questions.explanation: The more generous schedule in § 36B(b)(3)(A)(iii) applied only to taxable years beginning before 1 January 2026 and was not extended, so the credit is smaller across the income range; the restored ceiling matters only above 400 percent.

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: For purposes of computing the premium tax credit, whose income generally makes up 'household income' on Form 8962?
options: Only the taxpayer's own modified AGI
The modified AGI of the taxpayer, the taxpayer's spouse if filing jointly, and any dependents who are required to file a return
The modified AGI of every person listed on the Marketplace application, regardless of filing requirement
Gross income before any adjustments, for the taxpayer and spouse only
questions.explanation: Household income for the premium tax credit is the taxpayer's modified AGI plus the modified AGI of the spouse (if filing jointly) and of each dependent who is required to file a tax return for the year — not every dependent regardless of filing requirement.
questions.pageTitle: ACA requirements (e.g., health insurance coverage, total household income, advanced premium tax credit, household size)

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: A taxpayer received advance premium tax credit payments during the year that turned out to exceed the premium tax credit actually allowed based on year-end income. What happens on the return?
options: The excess is always forgiven and requires no repayment
The excess advance payments are reconciled on Form 8962 and generally must be repaid, subject to any applicable repayment limitation based on income
The taxpayer must amend the Marketplace application instead of addressing it on the tax return
The excess is treated as an itemized deduction reduction with no other adjustment
questions.explanation: Form 8962 reconciles advance payments against the premium tax credit actually computed from year-end household income and family size. Excess advance payments generally must be repaid as additional tax, though the amount owed can be limited depending on income — the mechanics of that limitation are set by the current-year rules rather than fixed permanently in the statute.
questions.pageTitle: ACA requirements (e.g., health insurance coverage, total household income, advanced premium tax credit, household size)

questions.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
questions.stem: Two separate tax families were both covered under a single Marketplace policy for part of the year (for example, divorced parents whose child is covered on one parent's policy while both parents are separate tax families). How is the premium tax credit computed for each family?
options: Only the policyholder may claim any premium tax credit for the policy
Each family computes its own credit independently with no allocation between them
The policy amounts (enrollment premium, applicable SLCSP premium, and advance payments) are allocated between the tax families, typically on Form 8962, Part IV
The premium tax credit is unavailable whenever more than one tax family is covered by the same policy
questions.explanation: When one Marketplace policy covers individuals from more than one tax family, the relevant policy amounts must be allocated between the families — commonly by an agreed percentage — using the shared policy allocation mechanics on Form 8962, rather than each family or only the policyholder claiming the credit unallocated.
questions.pageTitle: ACA requirements (e.g., health insurance coverage, total household income, advanced premium tax credit, household size)

questions.stem: Devi is a full-time life insurance salesperson working principally for one company. Her wage statement has the statutory employee box marked, with social security and Medicare withheld but no income tax. How does she report?
options: As an ordinary employee, with no deduction for her selling expenses
As self-employed, paying self-employment tax on the earnings
On a business schedule with her expenses deducted, but with no self-employment tax
As an independent contractor exempt from all employment taxes
questions.explanation: IRC § 3121(d)(3)(B) makes a full-time life insurance salesperson an employee for social security and Medicare, so those taxes are collected at source, while the earnings are reported as a business with expenses deducted against them.
questions.pageTitle: Taxability of wages, salaries and other earnings

questions.stem: Which is the last taxable year for which the qualified tips and qualified overtime deductions are available?
options: There is no end date; both are permanent
questions.explanation: IRC §§ 224(h) and 225(g) terminate both deductions for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2028, so they are a four-year window from 2026 rather than a permanent change.
questions.pageTitle: Taxability of wages, salaries and other earnings

questions.stem: A server's qualified tips of $20,000 are fully deductible under § 224. What is the effect on her adjusted gross income?
options: The tips are excluded from gross income and never enter it
The tips are removed from adjusted gross income as an adjustment
The tips remain in gross income and adjusted gross income, and are removed by a deduction below the line
The tips are excluded for income tax but included for social security wages only
questions.explanation: Neither § 224 nor § 225 is an exclusion: tips remain compensation for services under IRC § 61(a)(1), so they enter adjusted gross income and every threshold measured from it, including the modified adjusted gross income phase-out of the deduction itself.
questions.pageTitle: Taxability of wages, salaries and other earnings

questions.stem: Interest on which of the following bonds is includible in gross income?
options: A general obligation bond issued by a city
A private activity bond that is a qualified bond within § 141
An arbitrage bond within § 148 issued by a State
A State bond issued in registered form to finance a school
questions.explanation: IRC § 103(b) withdraws the § 103(a) exclusion for a private activity bond that is not a qualified bond, an arbitrage bond within § 148, and a bond not in registered form; a qualified private activity bond and an ordinary registered State or local bond remain excluded.

questions.stem: Priya lends her son $60,000 interest-free to help with a house purchase. The loan is well above the de minimis figure but within the larger gift loan threshold, and the son has $2,400 of net investment income for the year. How much is treated as retransferred to Priya as interest?
options: The full amount of foregone interest at the applicable federal rate
No more than $2,400, the son's net investment income for the year
Nothing, because gift loans between parent and child are outside § 7872
Nothing, because the loan was not used to buy income-producing assets
questions.explanation: IRC § 7872(d)(1)(A) caps the amount treated as retransferred to the lender on a gift loan within the larger threshold at the borrower's net investment income for the year; the cap falls away only where tax avoidance is a principal purpose under § 7872(d)(1)(B).

questions.stem: A cash-basis taxpayer elected years ago to report the annual increase in redemption value of her Series EE bonds as income each year. This year she buys new bonds of the same kind. How is the interest on the new bonds reported?
options: At redemption only, because the election covered only the bonds she held when she made it
Annually, because the election binds every obligation of the same kind held or later acquired
Bond by bond, at her choice each year
Annually for the first year only, after which she may revert to reporting at redemption
questions.explanation: IRC § 454(a): the election to include the annual increase in redemption price, once made, binds for that obligation and for all others of the same kind the taxpayer holds or later acquires.

questions.stem: Under a dividend reinvestment plan, Lidia buys 50 shares at $18 each on the payment date, when the market price is $20. She has:
options: No income, and a basis of $900
$100 of income, and a basis of $1,000
$100 of income, and a basis of $900
No income, and a basis of $1,000
questions.explanation: IRC § 305(b)(1) brings a distribution payable at the election of a shareholder in stock or in property within § 301, so the $100 discount is income, and Publication 550 gives basis at the full fair market value of $1,000 — recording it at cost would tax the same $100 again on sale.
questions.pageTitle: Dividends and other distributions from mutual funds, corporations, and other entities

questions.stem: A single taxpayer has $30,000 of net investment income, all dividends, and modified adjusted gross income that exceeds the § 1411 threshold by $60,000. The amount subject to the net investment income tax is:
options: Nothing
questions.explanation: IRC § 1411(a)(1), (b) imposes the tax on the lesser of net investment income or the excess of modified adjusted gross income over an unindexed threshold; the excess is $60,000, so the $30,000 of net investment income is the smaller figure and is the base.
questions.pageTitle: Dividends and other distributions from mutual funds, corporations, and other entities

questions.stem: A corporation with $40,000 of accumulated earnings and profits distributes $25,000 to its shareholders, and its board resolution describes the payment as a return of capital. For tax purposes the distribution is:
options: A return of capital, as the resolution states
A dividend, because every distribution is presumed made out of earnings and profits to the extent of them
Capital gain
A dividend only for the portion above the shareholders' basis
questions.explanation: IRC § 316(a) provides that, except as otherwise provided, every distribution is made out of earnings and profits to the extent of them and from the most recently accumulated; the label does not displace the presumption.
questions.pageTitle: Dividends and other distributions from mutual funds, corporations, and other entities

questions.stem: Sofia lets a warehouse to a fabrication business and, under the same lease, lets the tenant a forklift kept on the premises. Is the forklift rent subject to self-employment tax?
options: Yes, because personal property rental is always inside net earnings from self-employment
No, because personal property leased with the real estate is inside the rental exclusion
No, but only if the forklift is worth less than the warehouse
Yes, on the forklift portion of the rent only
questions.explanation: IRC § 1402(a)(1) excludes from net earnings from self-employment rentals from real estate and from personal property leased with the real estate; the exclusion is lost only where the personal property is let on its own.

questions.stem: An equipment rental activity has shown gross income exceeding deductions in enough recent years to meet the profit presumption. What is the effect?
options: The activity is conclusively treated as engaged in for profit
The activity is presumed to be for profit, but the Secretary may establish otherwise
Deductions are allowed only up to the gross income of the activity
The activity is treated as a trade or business subject to self-employment tax
questions.explanation: IRC § 183(d): an activity meeting the presumption is presumed to be engaged in for profit unless the Secretary establishes otherwise; it is a presumption, not a definition, and failing it does not by itself make the activity a hobby.

questions.stem: A client lets his boat out a few weekends a year without any profit motive. Because the expenses are not deductible, he proposes to leave the rent off the return entirely. Is that right?
options: Right, because hobby income and hobby expenses net to zero
Wrong, the rent is gross income in every case and characterisation decides only deductions and employment tax
Right, if the rent is below the information reporting threshold
Wrong, but he may report the rent net of the expenses
questions.explanation: IRC § 61(a)(5) enumerates rents in gross income, and nothing in the business or for-profit characterisation changes inclusion; the § 183(b)(2) deductions are disallowed by IRC § 67(h), so the income is taxed with nothing against it.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who takes the standard deduction wins $18,000 gambling online in 2026 and loses $17,000 over the same year, with a complete diary of every session. What does she report?
options: $1,000 of net gambling income
$18,000 of income with no deduction for the losses
$18,000 of income and a $15,300 deduction, being 90 percent of the losses
Nothing, because losses of 90 percent or more of winnings are netted before inclusion
questions.explanation: Topic no. 419: gambling losses are an itemized deduction available only to a taxpayer who itemizes, so the § 165(d) computation is never reached; the winnings are gross income in full under IRC § 61(a).

questions.stem: A recreational player bets $5 on a slot machine in 2026 and wins $6,500, well above the Form W-2G reporting threshold and more than 300 times the wager. Is regular gambling withholding taken from the payout?
options: Yes, because the proceeds exceed the withholding trigger and are at least 300 times the wager
No, regular gambling withholding never applies to slot machine winnings, though backup withholding can
No, because no Form W-2G issues for slot machine winnings
Yes, because every payment above the reporting threshold is subject to withholding
questions.explanation: The Form W-2G instructions state that regular gambling withholding does not apply to bingo, keno or slot machine winnings, though backup withholding can; the IRC § 3402(q)(3) proceeds-and-ratio test governs other wagering, and reporting under IRC § 6041(a) is a separate question from withholding.

questions.stem: A preparer tells a client who itemizes that gambling losses are miscellaneous itemized deductions and so are wholly disallowed for 2026 under the permanent suspension. Is the preparer right?
options: Right, because every miscellaneous itemized deduction is suspended
Wrong, gambling losses are excluded from miscellaneous itemized deductions and remain an itemized deduction subject to the § 165(d) ceilings
Wrong, gambling losses are an above-the-line deduction
Right, unless the client is a professional gambler reporting on a business schedule
questions.explanation: IRC § 67(b)(3) excludes the § 165(d) loss deduction from miscellaneous itemized deductions, so the § 67(h) suspension does not reach it; the losses are claimed on Schedule A subject to the 90 percent and gains ceilings.

questions.stem: A rental property with an adjusted basis of $200,000 secures a recourse mortgage of $260,000. The lender forecloses when the property is worth $230,000 and forgives the $30,000 shortfall. What are the consequences?
options: $60,000 of gain and no discharge income
$30,000 of gain and $30,000 of discharge of indebtedness income
$30,000 of discharge income only, because the property was lost
$60,000 of discharge of indebtedness income
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.1001-2(a)(2): for a recourse liability the amount realized excludes amounts that are discharge income, so gain is measured at the $230,000 fair market value against basis, and the forgiven $30,000 is separately income under IRC § 61(a)(11).
questions.pageTitle: Tax treatment of forgiveness of debt

questions.stem: A farmer's qualified farm indebtedness is discharged in a title 11 case at a time when he is also insolvent. Which exclusion applies?
options: The insolvency exclusion, to the extent of the insolvency
The title 11 exclusion, which displaces the others
Whichever the taxpayer elects on the return
The qualified farm indebtedness exclusion, as the most specific
questions.explanation: IRC § 108(a)(2)(A) provides that the title 11 exclusion displaces the other four, and § 108(a)(2)(B) that insolvency displaces the farm and real property business exclusions; the order of precedence is fixed by statute, not chosen.
questions.pageTitle: Tax treatment of forgiveness of debt

questions.stem: A homeowner's lender discharges $45,000 of qualified principal residence indebtedness in March 2026 under a written modification agreement signed in November 2025. Is the discharge excluded?
options: No, the exclusion has ended for every discharge after 2025
Yes, because the discharge was under an arrangement entered into and evidenced in writing before 1 January 2026
Yes, because the principal residence exclusion was made permanent
No, unless the homeowner is insolvent
questions.explanation: IRC § 108(a)(1)(E) reaches a discharge before 1 January 2026 or one under an arrangement entered into and evidenced in writing before that date, so the November 2025 agreement brings a 2026 discharge within it.
questions.pageTitle: Tax treatment of forgiveness of debt

questions.stem: A lawful permanent resident of the United States has lived in France with her tax home there for three full calendar years, returning to the United States for two weeks each year. Which route to the foreign earned income exclusion is open to her?
options: Bona fide residence, because she has lived abroad for an entire taxable year
Either route, at her election
Physical presence only, and only in a 12-month period with at least 330 full days abroad
Neither, because the exclusion is limited to citizens
questions.explanation: IRC § 911(d)(1)(A) opens the bona fide residence route to citizens only, while § 911(d)(1)(B) opens the physical presence route to a citizen or resident present in foreign countries for at least 330 full days in any 12 consecutive months.
questions.pageTitle: Tax treatment of a U.S. citizen or resident with foreign income

questions.stem: Malik and his wife file jointly and have $650 of creditable foreign tax withheld on qualified passive income reported on payee statements. May they elect out of the § 904(a) limitation?
options: Yes, the election is open to any individual whose only foreign income is passive
No, the creditable tax exceeds the $600 joint ceiling, so the full § 904(a) computation applies
Yes, on the first $600 of tax
No, the election is available only on a separate return
questions.explanation: IRC § 904(j) is a bright line, not a phase-out: the election is available only where creditable foreign taxes on qualified passive income are within the threshold, $600 on a joint return, and any excess loses the simplification entirely.
questions.pageTitle: Tax treatment of a U.S. citizen or resident with foreign income

questions.stem: A taxpayer claims the foreign tax credit for tax withheld on foreign dividends and, on the same return, deducts the foreign income tax paid on her foreign salary. Is that permitted?
options: Yes, the choice is made item by item
No, taking the § 901 benefits to any extent forecloses the deduction for the year
Yes, provided a treaty allows it
No, unless the deduction is smaller than the credit
questions.explanation: IRC § 275(a)(4): no deduction is allowed for foreign income taxes if the taxpayer chooses to take to any extent the benefits of § 901; the choice is annual and all-or-nothing for the year.
questions.pageTitle: Tax treatment of a U.S. citizen or resident with foreign income

questions.stem: Rafael settles a claim against a former employer for $120,000, allocated $30,000 to a back injury suffered at work, $70,000 to emotional distress arising from how he was treated, and $20,000 to punitive damages. How much is includible?
options: Nothing, because the claim arose from a physical injury
$20,000, the punitive damages only
$90,000, everything but the physical injury damages
$120,000, because settlement proceeds are compensation
questions.explanation: IRC § 104(a)(2) excludes damages other than punitive received on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness; emotional distress arising from treatment rather than from the injury is not a physical injury, and punitive damages are expressly carved out.

questions.stem: Under a divorce instrument executed in 2021, Dana pays her former spouse $2,000 a month. How are the payments treated in 2026?
options: Includible by the recipient and deductible by Dana
Neither includible by the recipient nor deductible by Dana
Includible by the recipient but not deductible by Dana
Deductible by Dana but excluded by the recipient
questions.explanation: Pub. L. 115-97 § 11051 repealed both IRC § 71 and IRC § 215 for an instrument executed after 2018, so neither side has anything to report; only a pre-2019 instrument not modified to adopt the new rule keeps the old treatment.

questions.stem: Which of the following receipts is excluded from gross income?
options: Unemployment compensation paid without withholding
A qualified disaster relief payment
Punitive damages awarded alongside a physical injury claim
A graduate stipend conditioned on research duties
questions.explanation: IRC § 139(a) expressly excludes qualified disaster relief payments, while IRC § 85(a) expressly includes unemployment compensation, § 104(a)(2) excludes only damages other than punitive, and § 117(c)(1) includes any portion paid for research.

questions.stem: A contractor and client dispute the amount due on a finished job. By agreement the client pays the disputed sum into an escrow held by a title company, to be released only when an arbitrator rules. The ruling comes the following year. The cash-basis contractor reports the income:
options: In the year the funds were escrowed, because they were set apart for him
In the year the arbitrator rules and the funds are released
In the year the work was completed
Half in each year
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.451-2(a) excludes income whose receipt is subject to substantial limitations or restrictions, and a bona fide dispute administered by a neutral third party is one — the contractor cannot draw on the funds by demand or by notice until the restriction lifts.

questions.stem: Interest coupons on a bond held by a cash-basis investor matured and became payable on 1 December 2026. She did not present them until February 2027. The interest is income in:
options: 2027, when the coupons were presented
2026, unless it is shown there were no funds available for payment that year
The year the bond itself is redeemed
2026 only if the issuer sent a notice
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.451-2(b): matured and payable but uncashed interest coupons are constructively received in the year they mature, unless it is shown that there were no funds available for payment during that year.

questions.stem: An accrual-method firm asks whether the constructive receipt doctrine decides which year a December-billed fee, collected in January, is included. It does not, because:
options: The doctrine applies only to interest and dividends
Constructive receipt is a cash-method doctrine, and an accrual taxpayer's timing is governed by the all events test in § 451
Accrual taxpayers report income only when cash is collected
The doctrine applies only where a cheque has been received
questions.explanation: Constructive receipt governs when a cash-basis taxpayer has received income; an accrual taxpayer's timing is governed by the all events test in IRC § 451(b) instead, so the two methods answer the timing question differently.

questions.stem: A corporation with no current or accumulated earnings and profits pays $12,000 of its sole shareholder's personal travel. Her basis in the stock is $50,000. The treatment is:
options: A $12,000 dividend included in gross income
A reduction of her stock basis to $38,000, with no dividend income
Deductible compensation to the corporation and wages to her
No tax consequence, because no dividend was declared
questions.explanation: The IRC § 301(c) ordering still applies to a constructive distribution: a dividend only to the extent of earnings and profits under § 316(a), then a reduction of basis under § 301(c)(2), then gain — with no earnings and profits, the payment reduces basis rather than producing dividend income.

questions.stem: Two founders each own half of a consultancy and each draw $150,000, an amount that regional comparables show is ordinary for their full-time roles. An examiner argues the identical salaries are constructive dividends because they match the stock split. The correct result is:
options: A dividend, because the payments correspond to the stockholdings
No dividend, because the inference requires salaries that exceed what is ordinarily paid as well as a relationship to the stockholdings
A dividend for the half of each salary above the median
A dividend unless the board formally declares the pay to be compensation
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.162-7(b)(1) draws the inference only where the salaries exceed those ordinarily paid for similar services and the excessive payments bear a close relationship to the stockholdings; proportionality alone is not enough, and the § 162(a)(1) deduction stands.

questions.stem: A corporation makes a small interest-free loan to a shareholder and argues the § 7872 de minimis exception applies. That exception is:
options: Available regardless of purpose, provided the amount is small
Unavailable where a principal purpose of the interest arrangements is the avoidance of any Federal tax
Never available for a loan between a corporation and its shareholder
Available only for loans between family members
questions.explanation: IRC § 7872(c)(3)(A) allows the de minimis exception for corporation-shareholder loans, but § 7872(c)(3)(B) removes it where a principal purpose of the interest arrangements is the avoidance of any federal tax; § 7872(c)(1)(C) names such loans expressly.

questions.stem: Deshawn actively participates in a rental in which he holds a 100 percent interest. The rental loses $30,000 in 2026 and his adjusted gross income is $120,000. How much of the loss offsets his other income?
questions.explanation: IRC § 469(i)(3)(A) reduces the $25,000 ceiling by 50 cents for every dollar of adjusted gross income over $100,000, so $20,000 of excess income cuts the allowance to $15,000; the remaining $15,000 of loss is suspended and carried forward under § 469(b).

questions.stem: On a joint return, one spouse spends 500 hours and the other 400 hours in real property trades or businesses in which they materially participate, and neither has other work. Together they exceed the hours test. Do they qualify as real estate professionals?
options: Yes, because spouses combine their hours on a joint return
No, because one spouse must satisfy both § 469(c)(7) tests alone
Yes, because more than half of the household's personal services are in real property trades
No, because real estate professional status requires the taxpayer to hold a broker's licence
questions.explanation: IRC § 469(c)(7)(B), final sentence: on a joint return one spouse must meet both real estate professional tests alone, and hours may not be combined for that purpose, though they may be for material participation itself.

questions.stem: A taxpayer holds a working interest in an oil well through a general partnership that does not limit his liability. He does no work on it and his share of the loss is $12,000. Is the loss passive?
options: Yes, because he does not materially participate
No, because a working interest held through an entity that does not limit liability is outside the passive activity definition
Yes, because a mineral interest is treated as rental activity
No, but only if he meets one of the seven material participation tests
questions.explanation: IRC § 469(c)(3)(A) expressly excludes from the definition of a passive activity a working interest in oil or gas held directly or through an entity that does not limit liability, so material participation is not required.

questions.stem: A partner's Schedule K-1 shows $10,000 of long-term capital gain from the partnership's sale of an investment. How is it reported on the partner's return?
options: As ordinary business income, because the partnership earned it
Separately, keeping its character as long-term capital gain in the partner's hands
As a qualified dividend under § 1(h)(11)
Not at all until the partnership distributes the cash
questions.explanation: IRC § 702(a) requires each partner to take into account separately their distributive share of the partnership's short-term and long-term capital gains and losses, so the item keeps the treatment it would have had if the partner had earned it directly.

questions.stem: Wei is a single owner of a specified service trade or business whose 2026 taxable income before the deduction is $37,500 above the threshold for her filing status. The phase-in range for a single filer is $75,000 wide. What fraction of her qualified business income deduction is phased out?
options: 75 percent, using the former range width
50 percent
25 percent
All of it, because a specified service business gets no deduction above the threshold
questions.explanation: IRC § 199A(b)(3)(B) and (d)(3), as widened by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70105(a), phase the deduction out on a straight line over a range now $75,000 wide for a single filer, so $37,500 of excess is halfway through the range.

questions.stem: Devi's distributive share of loss from a rental partnership in which she does not participate is $40,000. Her basis is $25,000, her amount at risk is $18,000, and she has no passive income. How much does she deduct this year?
options: $25,000, the basis limit
$18,000, the at-risk limit
Nothing, with $15,000 suspended for basis, $7,000 at risk and $18,000 as passive
$40,000, because at-risk and passive rules apply only to real estate held directly
questions.explanation: IRC § 704(d)(1) stops the loss at basis, IRC § 465(a)(1) then allows only the amount at risk, and IRC § 469(a) suspends what survives as a passive loss with no passive income to absorb it; the three amounts sit in separate queues with separate releases.

questions.stem: Odile inherited her father's textbook rights and receives $9,000 of royalties a year, paying a literary agent $900 to manage them. She does not itemize. How is the commission treated?
options: As an itemized deduction on Schedule A, so she gets nothing
Not deductible, because miscellaneous itemized deductions are suspended
Deductible above the line as attributable to property held for the production of royalties
Deductible only if she reports the royalties on Schedule C
questions.explanation: IRC § 62(a)(4) places deductions attributable to property held for the production of rents or royalties above the line, so the expense reduces adjusted gross income even though the activity is not a trade or business.

questions.stem: Youssef licenses his patent to a manufacturer for the North American market only, keeping the rights for Europe and Asia, in return for a fixed amount per unit sold. What is the character of the payments?
options: Long-term capital gain, because the payments are contingent on use
Ordinary royalty income, because not all substantial rights were transferred
Long-term capital gain on the North American share of the rights
Capital gain if the patent was held for more than one year
questions.explanation: IRC § 1235(a) requires a transfer of all substantial rights to the patent, or an undivided interest including a part of all such rights; a licence limited to one territory retains rights and so fails the test however the payments are calculated.

questions.stem: A royalty owner computes cost depletion of $4,000 and percentage depletion of $7,000 on a mineral property. The § 613(a) taxable-income ceiling for the property limits percentage depletion to $6,000. What is the depletion deduction?
questions.explanation: Cost and percentage depletion are compared and the greater taken, subject to the IRC § 613(a) ceiling on percentage depletion measured against taxable income from the property; the capped $6,000 still exceeds the $4,000 of cost depletion.

questions.stem: A preparer receives a client's Form 1099-G showing a $4,200 state income tax refund for a year in which the client itemized. What is the correct procedure?
options: Include $4,200, because the form fixes the amount
File an amended return for the earlier year reducing the deduction
Rework the earlier year's tax with and without the refunded deduction and include the difference on the current return
Exclude the refund, because state tax refunds are not income
questions.explanation: IRC § 111(a) measures the includible amount by how much the earlier deduction reduced tax, so the prior year is recomputed twice on a worksheet, no amended return is filed, and the difference is reported on the current return.
questions.pageTitle: State and local income tax refunds and other itemized deduction recoveries

questions.stem: Which of the following taxes is outside the state and local tax limitation?
options: State income tax withheld from wages
Real property tax on a rental property held in a § 212 activity
Personal property tax on a family car
State sales tax elected under § 164(b)(5) in place of income tax
questions.explanation: IRC § 164(b)(6) does not reach taxes under § 164(a)(1) and (2) paid or accrued in carrying on a trade or business or a § 212 activity, nor foreign taxes under § 164(a)(3); the other three are inside the aggregate it caps.
questions.pageTitle: State and local income tax refunds and other itemized deduction recoveries

questions.stem: A taxpayer's 2026 modified adjusted gross income is far above the phasedown threshold. What is her applicable limitation amount?
options: Zero, because the phasedown eliminates the deduction for high earners
Reduced, but never below the old ten-thousand-dollar figure
Unchanged, because the phasedown applies only to married taxpayers filing separately
Halved
questions.explanation: IRC § 164(b)(7)(B)(i) reduces the applicable limitation amount by a percentage of the excess over the threshold, but § 164(b)(7)(B)(iii) provides that the reduction may never bring it below the reversion figure.
questions.pageTitle: State and local income tax refunds and other itemized deduction recoveries

questions.stem: In 2026 a distributor sells $3,000 of consumer products to Mei, who resells them from her home rather than a permanent retail establishment. The amount is above the 2026 § 6041(a) general threshold but below the direct sales figure stated in § 6041A(b). Must the distributor file an information return on those sales?
options: Yes, because the sales exceed the § 6041(a) general threshold, which § 6041A now tracks
No, because the direct sales threshold in § 6041A(b) is a separately stated figure that did not change, and the sales are below it
Yes, because all consumer product sales for resale are reportable
No, because direct sales are reported by the buyer
questions.explanation: IRC § 6041A(b)(1)(A), (B) sets its own figure for direct sales, stated in the section itself and not tied to § 6041(a); only § 6041A(a)(2), for remuneration for services, was rewritten to track the general threshold.
questions.pageTitle: Forms 1099-MISC, 1099-NEC and 1099-K — reporting, irregularities and corrections

questions.stem: A platform reports $26,000 on Dalia's Form 1099-K. Her records show $3,000 of platform fees and $1,500 of customer refunds were taken out before the money reached her. On Schedule C she should report gross receipts of:
options: $26,000, deducting the fees as an expense and the refunds as returns and allowances
Nothing until the platform issues a corrected form
questions.explanation: IRC § 6050W reports the gross amount of reportable payment transactions before fees, refunds and chargebacks, so the form is not wrong; reporting the lower net figure as gross receipts produces a matching notice on a return that is arithmetically correct.
questions.pageTitle: Forms 1099-MISC, 1099-NEC and 1099-K — reporting, irregularities and corrections

questions.stem: A contractor engaged by a business refuses to furnish a taxpayer identification number. The business:
options: May withhold payment until a number is furnished
Must withhold on the payments at the statutory backup withholding rate
Files the information return without a number and has no further duty
Is excused from filing an information return
questions.explanation: IRC § 3406(a)(1): where a payee fails to furnish a taxpayer identification number, the payor must withhold at the statutory rate — backup withholding is the payer's remedy.
questions.pageTitle: Forms 1099-MISC, 1099-NEC and 1099-K — reporting, irregularities and corrections

questions.stem: Aisha has 200,000 dollars of pre-tax money in a traditional IRA and 50,000 dollars in a Roth IRA. She makes a 7,000-dollar nondeductible contribution to the traditional IRA and withdraws 7,000 dollars from it the same year. Is the Roth balance included in the denominator of her basis fraction?
options: Yes, because all individual retirement plans are treated as one contract
No, because the aggregation rule is applied separately to Roth IRAs and to other individual retirement plans
Yes, but only the Roth contributions, not the earnings
No, because a Roth IRA can never have basis
questions.explanation: IRC § 408A(d)(4)(A) applies § 408(d)(2) separately to Roth IRAs and to other individual retirement plans, so the Roth is never blended into the traditional pro-rata fraction. The traditional side is still aggregated under § 408(d)(2)(A).

questions.stem: Jonas has 300,000 dollars in his current employer's 401(k) plan and a single traditional IRA holding 7,000 dollars of basis. In 2026 he withdraws the IRA's entire 7,000-dollar balance, leaving it empty at year end, and takes nothing else. How much of the withdrawal is taxable?
options: Almost all of it, because the 401(k) balance is in the denominator
None of it, because an employer plan is not an individual retirement plan and sits outside the aggregation rule
Half of it, because the year-end value is increased by the distribution
All of it, because basis is recovered last
questions.explanation: IRC § 408(d)(2) reaches only individual retirement plans, and a 401(k) balance is outside it. The § 408(d)(2)(C) denominator is the year-end value of zero increased by the 7,000-dollar distribution, or 7,000 dollars, against 7,000 dollars of basis, so the withdrawal is a recovery of basis in full.

questions.stem: Priyanka is not an active participant in any employer plan and is fully eligible to deduct her 2026 traditional IRA contribution, but she chooses not to deduct it. Does the contribution create basis?
options: No, because basis arises only where the active-participant phase-out denies the deduction
Yes, because the nondeductible limit is increased where the taxpayer elects not to deduct an amount that would otherwise be deductible
No, because an undeducted contribution is treated as an excess contribution
Yes, but only if she has no other traditional IRA
questions.explanation: IRC § 408(o)(2)(B)(ii) increases the nondeductible limit where the taxpayer elects not to deduct an amount that would otherwise be deductible, so basis arises either from a § 219(g) denial or from that election. She must report it under § 408(o)(4)(A).

questions.stem: Which distribution from a Roth IRA counts as a qualified special purpose distribution — the fourth triggering event for a qualified distribution?
options: One used within 120 days for qualified acquisition costs of a principal residence of the individual's child
One used to pay a child's college tuition
One used for unreimbursed medical expenses
One used for health insurance premiums while unemployed
questions.explanation: IRC § 408A(d)(2)(C) defines a qualified special purpose distribution as one to which § 72(t)(2)(F) applies — a distribution used within 120 days for qualified acquisition costs of a principal residence of the individual, a spouse, or a child, grandchild or ancestor of either (IRC § 72(t)(8)(A)), subject to the lifetime limit in § 72(t)(8)(B).
questions.pageTitle: Traditional and Roth IRAs compared, and their distributions

questions.stem: Priya, now 62, made her first Roth IRA contribution nine years ago, later closed that account, and three years ago opened a new Roth IRA at a different custodian, where all her Roth money now sits. She withdraws earnings this year. Is the distribution qualified?
options: Yes — the five-year period runs from her first Roth contribution nine years ago, and she is over 59½
No — the five-year period restarted when the new account was opened
No — closing the original account erased the starting year
Yes, but only as to earnings that were in the original account
questions.explanation: IRC § 408A(d)(2)(B) measures the 5-taxable-year period from the first taxable year for which the individual made a contribution to a Roth IRA — it is personal, not per account — so both limbs of § 408A(d)(2) are met and nothing is includible.
questions.pageTitle: Traditional and Roth IRAs compared, and their distributions

questions.stem: A 50-year-old's Roth IRA holds $30,000 of regular contributions, a $20,000 conversion made in 2022, a $15,000 conversion made in 2025, and earnings. He takes a non-qualified distribution of $45,000. How is it treated?
options: $30,000 from regular contributions, then $15,000 from the 2022 conversion
$30,000 from regular contributions, then $15,000 from the 2025 conversion
Pro rata across contributions, conversions and earnings
Earnings first, so the whole $45,000 is includible
questions.explanation: IRC § 408A(d)(4)(B)(i), (ii): a distribution is treated as made from regular contributions first, then from qualified rollover contributions on a first-in first-out basis, with earnings reached last.
questions.pageTitle: Traditional and Roth IRAs compared, and their distributions

questions.stem: A taxpayer receives an eligible rollover distribution on 3 June; the plan's cheque is dated 28 May. She deposits the full amount into an IRA on 2 August, the sixtieth day after receipt. Is the rollover timely?
options: Yes — the period runs from the day of receipt, and a transfer on the sixtieth day is not made after it
No — the period runs from the date printed on the cheque
No — the deposit had to be made before the sixtieth day
Only if the Secretary grants a waiver for equity or good conscience
questions.explanation: IRC § 402(c)(3)(A) denies rollover treatment only to a transfer made after the 60th day following the day the distributee received the property; a deposit on the 60th day itself is timely, and the § 402(c)(3)(B) waiver is needed only for a late one.
questions.pageTitle: Distributions from qualified and nonqualified plans

questions.stem: A retiring employee is completing the paperwork for a lump-sum distribution of his 401(k) balance and wants the whole balance to reach his IRA with nothing withheld. What must he do?
options: Elect on the distribution paperwork to have the amount paid directly to the IRA
Take the cheque and complete the rollover within sixty days
Take the cheque and elect a lower withholding rate under the ordinary elective rules
Take the cheque and claim the withheld amount as a payment on his return
questions.explanation: IRC § 3405(c)(1) makes twenty percent withholding mandatory on an eligible rollover distribution and disapplies the elective rules, and § 3405(c)(2) lifts it only where the distributee elects under § 401(a)(31)(A) to have the distribution paid directly to an eligible retirement plan.
questions.pageTitle: Distributions from qualified and nonqualified plans

questions.stem: Ines earns $90,000; her husband Marco has no compensation of his own. They file jointly. May Marco contribute to an IRA for 2026?
options: Yes — he has his own limit, computed from the couple's combined compensation
No — a contribution requires the contributor's own compensation
Yes, but only to a joint IRA held with Ines under a single shared limit
Yes, but only up to half of Ines's limit
questions.explanation: IRC § 219(c) gives a non-earning spouse their own limit computed from the couple's combined compensation — a separate limit, not a joint limit on a shared account.
questions.pageTitle: Distributions from qualified and nonqualified plans

questions.stem: Bashir makes an excess Roth IRA contribution in 2026. In March 2027, before filing, his custodian returns the contribution together with $300 of net income attributable to it. In which year is the $300 taxable?
options: 2026, the year the contribution was made
2027, the year of the withdrawal
Neither — the net income comes back tax-free with the contribution
Half in each year
questions.explanation: IRC § 408(d)(4), closing sentence: the net income attributable to a timely returned contribution is treated as earned and receivable in the taxable year in which the contribution was made, not the year of withdrawal.
questions.pageTitle: Excess contributions and their tax treatment

questions.stem: In 2026 a taxpayer rolls $60,000 from a former employer's 401(k) into a traditional IRA and also makes a regular contribution at the full annual limit. Does the rollover create an excess contribution?
options: No — rollover contributions described in § 402(c) are excluded from the excess computation
Yes — anything above the § 219 limit is excess, whatever its source
Yes, unless the rollover was completed within sixty days
No, but only if the regular contribution is nondeductible
questions.explanation: IRC § 4973(b)(1) measures the excess by contributions other than rollover contributions described in §§ 402(c), 403(a)(4), 403(b)(8), 408(d)(3) or 457(e)(16), so the rollover is outside the computation entirely.
questions.pageTitle: Excess contributions and their tax treatment

questions.stem: A taxpayer over-contributes to a health savings account in 2026 and leaves the excess in place for three years. What is the consequence?
options: A 6 percent excise tax for each year the excess remains, capped at 6 percent of the account value
Nothing — the excise tax reaches only individual retirement accounts
A single 6 percent charge in the year of the contribution
A 10 percent additional tax on the excess in the year of withdrawal
questions.explanation: IRC § 4973(a)(1)–(6) lists six kinds of account, including a health savings account, and imposes the 6 percent tax for each taxable year the excess remains, limited to 6 percent of the account value at the close of the year.
questions.pageTitle: Excess contributions and their tax treatment

questions.stem: A 56-year-old separates from her employer in March 2026 and, before taking any distribution, rolls the entire 401(k) balance into an IRA. She then withdraws 40,000 dollars from the IRA the same month. Does the separation-from-service exception reach this withdrawal?
options: Yes — she is over 55 and separated from service
No — the exception is withheld from IRAs, and the rollover destroyed it
Yes, but only for the portion attributable to her own contributions
No, because a rollover is itself a taxable event
questions.explanation: IRC § 72(t)(3)(A) withholds the separation-after-55 exception in § 72(t)(2)(A)(v) from distributions out of an individual retirement plan; the exception is available only while the money stays in the employer's plan, and rolling the balance into an IRA first destroys it — the single most common error in the topic.
questions.pageTitle: Penalties and exceptions on premature distributions

questions.stem: A 45-year-old who takes the standard deduction withdraws from a 401(k) to pay unreimbursed medical expenses that exceed the § 213 floor. Does the medical exception reach the withdrawal?
options: Yes, to the extent the expenses exceed the § 213 floor, whether or not he itemizes
No — the exception requires the medical expenses to be actually deducted
Only if the withdrawal comes from an IRA rather than a plan
Yes, for the whole withdrawal regardless of the amount of expenses
questions.explanation: IRC § 72(t)(2)(B) excepts distributions to the extent they do not exceed the amount allowable as a § 213 deduction, determined without regard to whether the employee itemizes.
questions.pageTitle: Penalties and exceptions on premature distributions

questions.stem: A 50-year-old who is still employed wants to start a series of substantially equal periodic payments and is choosing between her current employer's 401(k) and her IRA. Which is available?
options: Only the IRA — a series from a qualified plan must begin after separation from service
Only the 401(k) — an IRA series must wait until age 55
Both, as long as the payments run for at least five years
Neither, because she is under 55
questions.explanation: IRC § 72(t)(3)(B) requires a series from a § 401(a) trust to begin after separation from service; there is no such requirement for an IRA, though any series must run the longer of five years or to age 59½ on pain of the § 72(t)(4)(A) recapture.
questions.pageTitle: Penalties and exceptions on premature distributions

questions.stem: Nadia's self-directed IRA owns a holiday cottage that is let commercially all year. In August she and her husband stay there for a long weekend and pay nothing. What is the consequence?
options: The account ceased to be an IRA on 1 January and is treated as having distributed everything at its value on that day
Nothing — no sale, loan or payment took place
Only the rental value of the weekend is treated as distributed
The account is destroyed as of August, the month of the stay
questions.explanation: IRC § 4975(c)(1)(D) reaches the use by or for the benefit of a disqualified person of plan assets, with no consideration needed; IRC § 408(e)(2)(A) then ends the account's IRA status as of the first day of the taxable year, and § 408(e)(2)(B) deems all its assets distributed at first-day fair market value.
questions.pageTitle: Prohibited transactions and their tax effects

questions.stem: A disqualified person engages in a prohibited transaction with an employer's qualified plan and does not correct it. What tax applies?
options: 15 percent of the amount involved for each year or part of a year in the taxable period, then a further 100 percent if not corrected within that period
A single 15 percent charge in the year of the transaction
Disqualification of the plan as of the first day of the year
A 10 percent additional tax on the amount involved
questions.explanation: IRC § 4975(a) imposes the first-tier tax for each year or part of a year in the taxable period on any participating disqualified person, and § 4975(b) imposes the 100 percent second-tier tax where the transaction is not corrected within the taxable period.
questions.pageTitle: Prohibited transactions and their tax effects

questions.stem: Kwame holds two traditional IRAs. In June 2026 he lends money from one of them to a company he controls. What happens to the accounts?
options: Only the lending IRA ceases to be an IRA, as of 1 January 2026, and is deemed distributed at its value on that day; the other survives
Both IRAs cease to be IRAs, because the owner is one taxpayer
Only the lending IRA, as of June 2026, the date of the loan
Only the amount lent is treated as distributed from the lending IRA
questions.explanation: IRC § 408(e)(2)(A)(iii) treats each individual retirement plan as a separate contract for this purpose, so the prohibited transaction destroys only the account involved; § 408(e)(2)(A) and (B) fix the disqualification and the deemed distribution at the first day of the taxable year, not the transaction date.
questions.pageTitle: Prohibited transactions and their tax effects

questions.stem: Devi holds a rollover IRA of $190,000, all pre-tax, and in 2026 makes a $7,500 nondeductible contribution to a separate new traditional IRA. Later that year she converts the new account, then worth $7,700, to a Roth IRA. Roughly how much is includible?
options: About $7,400 — basis is spread pro rata across all her traditional IRAs
$200 — only the growth on the nondeductible contribution
Nothing — the converted account held only after-tax money
$7,700 — basis cannot be used against a conversion
questions.explanation: IRC § 408(d)(2)(A) treats all individual retirement plans as one contract, so her $7,500 of basis is measured against a combined value of about $197,700 and only a little under four percent of the conversion is tax-free; the rest of the basis stays on the traditional side.

questions.stem: Two clients each converted $60,000 to a Roth IRA — one on 28 December 2021, the other on 3 January 2022. Both withdraw the full converted amount on 15 January 2026, before age 59½. Who faces recapture of the additional tax?
options: Only the January 2022 converter — her five taxable years run 2022 through 2026
Only the December 2021 converter — his conversion is older
Both — fewer than sixty months have passed for each
Neither — the additional tax never applies to converted amounts
questions.explanation: IRC § 408A(d)(3)(F)(i) counts a 5-taxable-year period beginning with the taxable year of the conversion; the 2021 conversion's period ended with 2025, while the 2022 conversion's runs through 2026, so the same-day withdrawal is inside one period and outside the other.

questions.stem: In 2026 a taxpayer converts her traditional IRA to a Roth IRA in four separate tranches, one each quarter. Is that permitted?
options: Yes — a conversion is disregarded for the one-rollover-per-year limit
No — after the first tranche the once-a-year rule bars any further rollover for twelve months
Only if the tranches are at least twelve months apart
Only if each tranche comes from a different traditional IRA
questions.explanation: The flush text of IRC § 408A(e)(1) disregards, for purposes of § 408(d)(3)(B), any qualified rollover contribution from a non-Roth individual retirement plan to a Roth IRA, so conversions may be done in any number of tranches in one year.

questions.stem: Nkem is 74, still working full time for an employer in which she owns no stock, and holds both that employer's 401(k) and a traditional IRA. Which required beginning date may she defer by continuing to work?
options: The 401(k) only — the retirement leg is withdrawn entirely for IRAs
Both — she has not retired
Neither — the applicable age alone fixes every required beginning date
The IRA only — employer plans must pay from the applicable age
questions.explanation: IRC § 401(a)(9)(C)(i) sets the required beginning date by the later of the applicable age or retirement, but § 401(a)(9)(C)(ii)(II) withdraws the retirement leg for purposes of § 408(a)(6) and (b)(3), and Reg. § 1.408-8(b)(1)(i) determines an IRA owner's date using the rules for 5-percent owners.
questions.pageTitle: Required minimum distributions and excess accumulations

questions.stem: Two co-founders, each 74 and still working full time, hold 401(k) accounts through the company's plan. One owns exactly 5 percent of its stock; the other owns 5.5 percent. Whose required beginning date can wait until actual retirement?
options: The co-founder at exactly 5 percent — a 5-percent owner is one owning more than 5 percent
Both — neither is a majority owner
Neither — any owner-employee loses the retirement leg
The co-founder at 5.5 percent — the exclusion applies only to owners of 10 percent or more
questions.explanation: IRC § 401(a)(9)(C)(ii)(I) excludes a 5-percent owner from the retirement leg of § 401(a)(9)(C)(i), and a 5-percent owner is one who owns more than 5 percent of the employer, so exactly 5 percent does not cross the line.
questions.pageTitle: Required minimum distributions and excess accumulations

questions.stem: An IRA owner's wife, fifteen years younger, is the sole beneficiary of his IRA from 1 January until November 2026, when he adds their son as a co-beneficiary. Which table sets his 2026 denominator?
options: The Uniform Lifetime Table — the spouse was not the sole beneficiary at all times during the year
The joint and last survivor table — she was the sole beneficiary on 1 January
The joint and last survivor table, prorated for the months she was sole beneficiary
The joint and last survivor table — a spouse more than ten years younger always qualifies
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.401(a)(9)-5(c)(2)(i), (ii) permits the joint and last survivor denominator only where the spouse is the sole beneficiary at all times during the distribution year; adding a co-beneficiary for even one day returns the owner to the Uniform Lifetime Table of § 1.401(a)(9)-5(c)(1).
questions.pageTitle: Required minimum distributions and excess accumulations

questions.stem: Rosa has a vested 401(k) balance of $300,000. She borrowed $50,000 in March 2025 and repaid it in full in November 2025. In February 2026 she asks for another $50,000. What is her ceiling for the new loan?
options: Zero — the capped limb is reduced by the $50,000 highest outstanding balance in the preceding year, less her current balance of nothing
$50,000 — the earlier loan was repaid before the new one was made
$150,000 — half her vested balance
$100,000 — the two limbs added together
questions.explanation: IRC § 72(p)(2)(A)(i) reduces the statutory cap by the excess of the highest outstanding balance during the year ending the day before the loan over the balance on the day of the loan; the look-back is what stops a participant repaying in one month and borrowing the full amount again the next.

questions.stem: A participant borrows from her plan to buy a house that will be her principal residence within a reasonable time. How does that change the § 72(p)(2) tests?
options: The five-year repayment term no longer applies; the ceiling is unchanged
The ceiling doubles; the term is unchanged
Both the term and the ceiling are relaxed
Nothing changes — the residence exception applies only to hardship distributions
questions.explanation: IRC § 72(p)(2)(B) lifts the five-year term for a loan used to acquire a dwelling unit that is to be the participant's principal residence, tested when the loan is made; it touches neither limb of the ceiling in § 72(p)(2)(A).

questions.stem: Ken's compliant plan loan calls for monthly payments. He misses the payment due 15 May 2026 and every payment after it, and the plan allows the longest cure period the regulations permit. When, at the latest, does the deemed distribution occur?
options: 30 September 2026 — the last day of the calendar quarter following the quarter in which the missed payment was due
15 May 2026 — the date of the first missed payment
30 June 2026 — the end of the quarter in which the payment was due
31 December 2026 — the end of the plan year
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.72(p)-1, A-10(a) allows a cure period that cannot run past the last day of the calendar quarter following the quarter in which the installment was due; if nothing is paid by then, the outstanding balance plus accrued interest is a deemed distribution in 2026.

questions.stem: A retired railroad worker receives one combined annuity from the Railroad Retirement Board. Which portion enters the IRC § 86 computation?
options: The whole annuity, since it is all railroad retirement
Only the tier 1 portion reported on Form RRB-1099
Only the tier 2 portion reported on Form RRB-1099-R
Neither portion, because railroad retirement is not social security
questions.explanation: IRC § 86(d)(1) defines a social security benefit to include a tier 1 railroad retirement benefit and nothing more; the tier 2 portion is outside § 86 and is taxed as a pension under the annuity rules of § 72.
questions.pageTitle: Taxability of Social Security and Railroad Retirement benefits

questions.stem: A nonresident alien receives 30,000 dollars of social security benefits in 2026 and has no other income. How much is included in gross income?
options: Nothing, because her other income is below the base amount
15,000 dollars, under the first tier
25,500 dollars, a flat 85 percent
30,000 dollars, the full benefit
questions.explanation: IRC § 871(a)(3)(A), (B) includes 85 percent of any social security benefit paid to a nonresident alien and provides that § 86 does not apply; there is no base amount and no two-tier computation.
questions.pageTitle: Taxability of Social Security and Railroad Retirement benefits

questions.stem: A taxpayer's disability claim is allowed in 2026 and he receives a lump sum covering 2024 through 2026, which pushes his 2026 sum past the adjusted base amount. What does the election in IRC § 86(e) allow?
options: Amending the 2024 and 2025 returns to report each year's portion
Limiting the 2026 inclusion for the prior-year portions to what those years would have included
Spreading the entire lump sum equally across three returns
Excluding the prior-year portions from gross income entirely
questions.explanation: IRC § 86(e)(1) caps the amount included by reason of the prior-year portion at the sum of the increases in gross income that would have resulted in the years to which it is attributable; it limits the current year's inclusion and does not reopen the earlier returns.
questions.pageTitle: Taxability of Social Security and Railroad Retirement benefits

questions.stem: Terrence separates from service and takes his entire profit-sharing plan account, receiving employer stock in kind worth 150,000 dollars against a trust cost of 30,000 dollars. He leaves 2,000 dollars in a second profit-sharing plan of the same employer. What is included in gross income for the year?
options: 30,000 dollars, the trust's cost
150,000 dollars, the full fair market value of the shares
120,000 dollars, the appreciation only
Nothing, because the shares were taken in kind
questions.explanation: IRC § 402(e)(4)(D)(ii)(I) treats all profit-sharing plans of the employer as a single plan, so the balance to his credit was not distributed within one taxable year, there is no lump sum distribution, and the § 402(e)(4)(B) exclusion never applies.

questions.stem: A participant separates from service in December. The plan distributes her employer stock in kind on 30 December and, after a processing delay, pays the remaining cash balance on 2 January. What is the effect on the exclusion?
options: None, because the delay was short and well documented
The exclusion applies to the stock, since it was paid within the year
There is no lump sum distribution, so the full fair market value of the stock is ordinary income
The exclusion applies, but only if she elects it on the return
questions.explanation: IRC § 402(e)(4)(D)(i) requires the balance to the credit to be paid within one taxable year of the recipient; a split across two taxable years, however short, means no lump sum distribution and no exclusion.

questions.stem: A qualifying lump sum distribution includes two blocks of employer stock: one worth 90,000 dollars against a trust cost of 40,000 dollars, and one worth 25,000 dollars against a trust cost of 35,000 dollars. What is the net unrealized appreciation excluded from gross income?
options: 50,000 dollars
40,000 dollars
60,000 dollars
115,000 dollars
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.402(a)-1(b)(2)(i) measures the figure net across all the employer securities in the distribution, so the 10,000 dollar loss on the second block reduces the 50,000 dollar gain on the first; the excluded amount is the net increase, not the sum of the winners.

questions.stem: An IRA owner dies in 2026 leaving the account to her 15-year-old daughter. Which distribution regime applies?
options: Life expectancy payments until the daughter's 21st birthday, then the remainder within ten years of that date
The ten-year rule, running from the year of death
The five-year rule, because a minor cannot be a designated beneficiary
Life expectancy payments for the rest of the daughter's life
questions.explanation: A child of the employee who has not reached majority is an eligible designated beneficiary under IRC § 401(a)(9)(E)(ii); majority is reached on the 21st birthday (Reg. § 1.401(a)(9)-4(e)(3)), and the remainder must then be distributed within ten years of that date (IRC § 401(a)(9)(E)(iii); Reg. § 1.401(a)(9)-5(e)(4)).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old is the sole beneficiary of his late aunt's 401(k) account and wants the money in an IRA rather than left in the employer plan. Which route is open to him?
options: A direct trustee-to-trustee transfer into an IRA that is itself treated as inherited
Electing to treat the account as his own, as a sole beneficiary may
Rolling it into his own existing IRA
None — an inherited plan balance cannot be moved anywhere
questions.explanation: IRC § 402(c)(11)(A) permits a non-spouse beneficiary of an employer plan a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer into an IRA treated as inherited; IRC § 408(d)(3)(C) denies rollover treatment to an inherited account, so moving the money into his own IRA is a distribution of the whole amount, and the treat-as-own election of Reg. § 1.408-8(c) belongs to a surviving spouse alone.

questions.stem: An owner dies in February 2026, aged 62, naming his daughter as primary beneficiary and a charity as contingent beneficiary. On 3 August 2026 the daughter executes a qualified disclaimer. Which rule governs the account?
options: The five-year rule — the charity is the beneficiary determined on 30 September 2027 and is not an individual
The ten-year rule — the daughter was the beneficiary as of the date of death
Life expectancy payments to the charity in the daughter's place
The daughter's own rule — a disclaimer after the date of death cannot change the beneficiary
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.401(a)(9)-4(c)(1), (2) disregards a beneficiary who makes a qualified disclaimer by 30 September of the year following death; the charity then determined is not a designated beneficiary, and because the owner died before the required beginning date IRC § 401(a)(9)(B)(ii) requires distribution within five years.

questions.stem: A United States resident holds a foreign employer's retirement account whose balance is far above the FBAR reporting figure. He argues the account is a retirement plan and so exempt from the FBAR. Is he right?
options: No — the retirement exception lists only plans under §§ 401(a), 403(a), 403(b), 408 and 408A, all of them domestic
Yes — retirement accounts of every kind are outside the FBAR
Yes, provided he qualifies for relief under Rev. Proc. 2020-17
Yes, provided he reports the account on Form 8938 instead
questions.explanation: 31 CFR 1010.350(g)(4) confines the retirement exception to domestic plans, so a foreign arrangement is not on the list; and Rev. Proc. 2020-17 § 4 states that its relief does not affect the FBAR.

questions.stem: A United States citizen's foreign employer contributed to her retirement fund in each of 2022 through 2026. Under the plan's vesting schedule her interest was subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture until 2026, when it lapsed entirely. No treaty applies. What does she include in 2026?
options: The entire account, including the contributions from earlier years
Only the 2026 contribution
Nothing until amounts are actually distributed
Only the earnings on the earlier contributions
questions.explanation: IRC § 402(b)(1) includes employer contributions in accordance with § 83, which does not tax property while it is subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture; vesting is the taxing event, so the whole buildup lands in gross income in the year the risk lapsed.

questions.stem: A foreign employer's trust is not exempt under § 501(a) because it fails the coverage tests of § 401(a)(26) and § 410(b). What does a highly compensated employee include for the year?
options: The whole vested accrued benefit, other than investment in the contract, as of the close of the trust's taxable year
Only the employer contributions that vested during the year
Nothing, because the coverage failure relieves employees of inclusion
Only the amounts actually distributed to him during the year
questions.explanation: IRC § 402(b)(4)(A): where the trust fails § 401(a)(26) or § 410(b), a highly compensated employee includes, in lieu of the ordinary amounts, the vested accrued benefit other than investment in the contract; § 402(b)(4)(B) relieves only non-highly compensated employees.

questions.stem: Owen gives his daughter a delivery van worth 95,000 dollars. His adjusted basis is 60,000 dollars, reduced from cost entirely by depreciation he deducted. How much ordinary recapture income does Owen report on the gift?
options: 35,000 dollars, the full built-in ordinary income
None, because neither recapture section applies to a disposition by gift, and his daughter takes his carryover basis
35,000 dollars as long-term capital gain
None, and his daughter takes a basis equal to the van's fair market value
questions.explanation: IRC § 1245(b)(1) and § 1250(d)(1) except a disposition by gift from recapture, however much depreciation was claimed. The built-in gain moves to the daughter's return through the carryover basis rather than disappearing.
questions.pageTitle: Sale or disposition of property and depreciation recapture

questions.stem: Lucía bought a machine for 50,000 dollars, never claimed any depreciation on it, and kept no records showing how much depreciation was actually allowed. She sells it for 45,000 dollars in 2026. Does the depreciation she never claimed enter the recapture computation?
options: No, because only depreciation actually deducted can be recaptured
Yes, because recomputed basis includes adjustments allowed or allowable, and the burden of proving less was allowed falls on the taxpayer
No, unless the IRS asserts the allowable depreciation on audit
Yes, but only half of the allowable amount
questions.explanation: IRC § 1245(a)(2)(A) builds recomputed basis from adjustments for depreciation allowed or allowable, and § 1245(a)(2)(B) substitutes allowed only where the taxpayer proves by adequate records that less was allowed than was allowable. Without records, the unclaimed depreciation counts.
questions.pageTitle: Sale or disposition of property and depreciation recapture

questions.stem: Tessa sells a rental building at a gain, of which 40,000 dollars is unrecaptured section 1250 gain. Her ordinary income is taxed at a marginal rate of 12 percent. At what rate is the 40,000 dollars taxed?
options: 25 percent, the fixed rate for unrecaptured section 1250 gain
12 percent, because 25 percent is a ceiling and a taxpayer whose ordinary rate is lower pays the lower rate
15 percent, the rate for adjusted net capital gain
20 percent
questions.explanation: IRC § 1(h)(1)(E) taxes unrecaptured section 1250 gain at 25 percent as a maximum, not a flat rate; a taxpayer whose ordinary rate is lower pays the lower rate. The gain remains capital gain throughout.
questions.pageTitle: Sale or disposition of property and depreciation recapture

questions.stem: A married couple filing jointly for 2026 have a 10,000-dollar net capital loss and no capital gains. Which allowance limits the amount that reduces their ordinary income this year?
options: Twice the allowance a single filer gets, because there are two taxpayers on the return
The same allowance a single filer gets, because the allowance is not doubled on a joint return
Half the allowance a single filer gets, because the halved figure applies to all married taxpayers
No allowance is needed, because a net capital loss offsets ordinary income without limit
questions.explanation: IRC § 1211(b): the annual allowance is not doubled on a joint return; the smaller figure is a halving for married taxpayers filing separately, not the joint amount halved. The excess carries forward under § 1212(b)(1).

questions.stem: Rafael buys common shares and holds them for 50 days within the 121-day period surrounding the ex-dividend date, receiving a dividend during that time. Is the dividend a qualified dividend?
options: Yes, because he held the shares more than 45 days
No, because the shares must be held more than 60 days within the 121-day period
No, because the shares must be held more than 90 days within a 181-day period
Yes, because any dividend on common stock is qualified regardless of holding period
questions.explanation: IRC § 1(h)(11)(B)(iii)(I) applies the § 246(c) holding period by substituting 60 days for 45 days and a 121-day period for the 91-day period; the 90-day and 181-day rule in § 246(c)(2) applies only to preference dividends attributable to periods aggregating more than 366 days.

questions.stem: Lena opens a regulated futures contract that is a section 1256 contract on 1 October 2026 and still holds it at year end. How is it treated on her 2026 return?
options: No gain or loss until she closes the position
Treated as sold at fair market value on the last business day, with gain or loss 40 percent short-term and 60 percent long-term
Treated as sold at year end, with gain or loss entirely short-term because held three months
Treated as sold at year end, with gain or loss 60 percent short-term and 40 percent long-term
questions.explanation: IRC § 1256(a)(1), (3): each section 1256 contract held at year end is treated as sold at fair market value on the last business day, and the gain or loss is split 40 percent short-term and 60 percent long-term however long the contract was held.

questions.stem: A couple bought a house for 300,000 dollars, holding it as community property. One spouse dies when it is worth 900,000 dollars and her half is includible in her gross estate. What is the survivor's basis in the whole house?
options: 300,000 dollars
600,000 dollars
900,000 dollars
450,000 dollars
questions.explanation: IRC § 1014(b)(6) treats the surviving spouse's own one-half share as also acquired from the decedent where at least half the community interest was includible, so the entire property takes a date-of-death basis rather than only the decedent's half.

questions.stem: Eight months before her uncle's death, a niece gives him appreciated land with a basis of 30,000 dollars and a value of 500,000 dollars; his will leaves it back to her. What is her basis after his death?
options: 500,000 dollars, the fair market value at death
30,000 dollars, the decedent's adjusted basis immediately before death
500,000 dollars, the fair market value at the date of the gift
Zero, because the gift is disregarded
questions.explanation: IRC § 1014(e)(1): where appreciated property was acquired by the decedent by gift within the one-year period ending on the date of death and passes back to the donor or the donor's spouse, basis is the decedent's adjusted basis immediately before death.

questions.stem: A donor with an adjusted basis of 50,000 dollars gives stock worth 80,000 dollars, the amount of the gift being 80,000 dollars, and pays 8,000 dollars of gift tax. What is the donee's basis for gain?
options: 50,000 dollars
53,000 dollars
58,000 dollars
80,000 dollars
questions.explanation: IRC § 1015(d)(1)(A) adds the gift tax paid, capped at fair market value, but § 1015(d)(6)(A) limits the increase to the portion the net appreciation bears to the amount of the gift: 30,000 over 80,000 of 8,000 dollars is 3,000 dollars.

questions.stem: Sasha holds common stock with a basis of 40,000 dollars and receives a preferred stock dividend excluded under § 305(a). On the record date the common is worth 130,000 dollars and the preferred 30,000; on the distribution date the common is worth 120,000 and the preferred 40,000. What basis attaches to the preferred?
options: 7,500 dollars
10,000 dollars
40,000 dollars
Zero
questions.explanation: IRC § 307(a) allocates the old basis between old and new stock, and Treas. Reg. § 1.307-1(a) fixes the allocation in proportion to fair market values on the date of distribution, not the record date, so one quarter of 40,000 dollars goes to the preferred.
questions.pageTitle: Basis of stock after stock splits and stock dividends

questions.stem: Rights distributed in a § 305(a) transaction are worth 20 percent of the old stock. The shareholder neither exercises nor sells them, and they lapse. What happens to the basis of the old stock?
options: Part is allocated to the rights under § 307(a) and lost as a capital loss on the lapse
None is allocated, because the allocation rule applies to rights only if they are exercised or sold
The rights take a zero basis under § 307(b)(1) and the old stock is unchanged
Part is allocated to the rights and carried forward to future distributions
questions.explanation: Treas. Reg. § 1.307-1(a), closing sentence: the general allocation rule applies to rights only if they are exercised or sold, so rights that lapse never engage it and the old stock keeps its full basis; the 15 percent rule in § 307(b)(1) is not reached because the rights are above it.
questions.pageTitle: Basis of stock after stock splits and stock dividends

questions.stem: A taxpayer has bought shares of one operating company directly through her broker over several years, outside any dividend reinvestment plan. May she use the average basis method when she sells some of them?
options: Yes, average basis is available for any identical shares
No, average basis is confined to regulated investment company shares and post-2010 dividend reinvestment plan shares left with a custodian
Yes, if she elects it on the return for the year of sale
No, because the average basis method was withdrawn when broker basis reporting began
questions.explanation: Treas. Reg. § 1.1012-1(e)(1)(i) allows average basis only for shares in a regulated investment company, or shares acquired after 31 December 2010 in connection with a dividend reinvestment plan, held with a custodian or agent; otherwise the lot rules of § 1.1012-1(c) apply.
questions.pageTitle: Basis of stock after stock splits and stock dividends

questions.stem: Delia actively participates in a rental real estate activity conducted through a publicly traded partnership, which allocates her a 12,000-dollar rental loss for 2026. Her modified adjusted gross income is 70,000 dollars. May she use the rental real estate allowance against her wages?
options: Yes, the full 12,000 dollars, because she actively participates
No, because the rental real estate allowance does not apply to items attributable to a publicly traded partnership
Yes, but only to the extent of her other passive income
No, because rental losses are never deductible against wages
questions.explanation: IRC § 469(k)(1) applies § 469 separately to each publicly traded partnership and provides that § 469(i), the rental real estate allowance, does not apply to those items at all. The loss is suspended within that partnership.

questions.stem: Bram, a United States citizen, sells his units in a publicly traded partnership through his broker. Part of the gain would be effectively connected income under § 864(c)(8). What must the transferee do, and how can Bram avoid it?
options: Nothing, because withholding never applies to a sale of a partnership interest
Withhold 10 percent of the amount realised, unless Bram furnishes an affidavit under penalty of perjury giving his taxpayer identification number and stating that he is not a foreign person
Withhold 10 percent of the gain, which Bram can avoid only by claiming a refund
Withhold 30 percent of the amount realised, with no exception for United States persons
questions.explanation: IRC § 1446(f)(1) requires the transferee to deduct and withhold 10 percent of the amount realised, and § 1446(f)(2)(A) switches the withholding off where the transferor furnishes a non-foreign affidavit with a taxpayer identification number.
