questions.stem: A partnership whose interests trade on an established securities market earns all of its gross income from interest and dividends, and it would be a regulated investment company if it were a domestic corporation. How is it classified for federal tax purposes?
options: A partnership, because more than 90 percent of its gross income is qualifying income
A corporation, because a partnership that would be a regulated investment company cannot use the qualifying income exception
A partnership, provided it elects out of subchapter K
A corporation, because interest and dividends are never qualifying income
questions.explanation: IRC § 7704(c)(3): a partnership that would be a regulated investment company if it were a domestic corporation cannot use the § 7704(c) exception, so the § 7704(a) corporate default applies even though interest and dividends are qualifying income under § 7704(d)(1).

questions.stem: Paulo and his wife owned and lived in their home for many years and met every joint condition. She died in March 2025. Paulo, who has not remarried, sells the home in January 2027 at a gain. Which dollar limit applies to his exclusion?
options: The single-filer limit, because he now files as a single taxpayer
The joint-return limit, because the sale is not later than 2 years after the date of death and the joint conditions were met immediately before it
No exclusion at all, because he no longer meets the joint use test
The joint-return limit, but only if the sale closes in the same taxable year as the death
questions.explanation: IRC § 121(b)(4): an unmarried individual whose spouse is deceased applies the joint limit on a sale not later than 2 years after the date of death, where the joint conditions were met immediately before that date. January 2027 is within 2 years of March 2025.

questions.stem: Greta bought a house in January 2004 and rented it out until January 2012, then lived in it as her principal residence until she sold it in January 2026. Ignoring depreciation, what fraction of the gain is allocated to nonqualified use?
options: Eight of twenty-two years, the whole rental period
Three of twenty-two years, the rental period after 1 January 2009
None, because she lived in the house for two of the last five years
Eight of fourteen years, measured from 2012
questions.explanation: IRC § 121(b)(5)(C)(i) excludes periods before 1 January 2009 from nonqualified use, so only the three rental years from January 2009 to January 2012 count, and § 121(b)(5)(B) allocates them over the whole twenty-two-year period of ownership.

questions.stem: Under their divorce decree, Nadine's former husband was granted use of the home they still co-own. He lived there for four years while she lived elsewhere, and she then sold her interest at a gain. Does Nadine meet the use test?
options: No, because she did not personally live in the home during the five years before the sale
Yes, because she is treated as using the home during any period of ownership while a former spouse is granted its use under a divorce instrument
Only if she qualifies for a reduced exclusion by reason of the divorce
Only if the home is sold within 2 years of the divorce
questions.explanation: IRC § 121(d)(3)(B): an individual is treated as using the property as a principal residence during any period of ownership while a spouse or former spouse is granted its use under a divorce or separation instrument.

questions.stem: Orla is a land developer who regularly sells subdivided lots to customers on deferred-payment contracts. In 2026 she sells a lot for 90,000 dollars, receiving 10,000 dollars down and the balance over four years. How is the gain reported?
options: Under the installment method, because at least one payment falls after the year of sale
In full in 2026, because a dealer disposition is excluded from the installment method
Under the installment method, but only if she elects in on a timely return
In full in 2026, because real property never qualifies for the installment method
questions.explanation: IRC § 453(b)(2) excludes a dealer disposition from the term installment sale, and § 453(l)(1) defines a dealer disposition to include real property held for sale to customers in the ordinary course. The whole gain is reported in the year of sale.

questions.stem: Nikhil sells machinery he owns personally to a corporation he controls for 600,000 dollars, payable over five years with 60,000 dollars down. The machinery is depreciable in the corporation's hands. What is the result in the year of sale?
options: Gain is spread over the payments, and the gain in excess of recapture is capital
Gain is spread over the payments, but all of it is ordinary income
All payments are treated as received in the year of sale, and the entire gain is ordinary income
All payments are treated as received in the year of sale, but the gain in excess of recapture is capital
questions.explanation: IRC § 453(g)(1) denies the installment method on a sale of depreciable property between related persons and treats all payments to be received as received in the year of disposition, and § 1239(a) independently makes the gain ordinary income where the property is depreciable in the transferee's hands.

questions.stem: Two years into an installment sale, Yara sells the buyer's remaining note to a bank for 150,000 dollars cash. Her basis in the note is 95,000 dollars. What happens?
options: Nothing until the buyer pays the bank; the deferral continues
She recognises 55,000 dollars of gain, treated as from the sale of the property for which the note was received
She recognises 150,000 dollars of gain, since the whole proceeds are a payment
She recognises interest income of 55,000 dollars
questions.explanation: IRC § 453B(a): where an installment obligation is sold or otherwise disposed of, gain or loss results to the extent of the difference between the basis of the obligation and the amount realised, and is treated as from the sale of the property for which the obligation was received.

questions.stem: Ravi exercises an incentive stock option in September 2026 with a 50,000-dollar bargain element and sells the shares in April 2027, less than a year after the transfer. In which year is the compensation income reported, and is withholding required?
options: 2026, with income tax withholding
2027, and no chapter 24 withholding is required
2026, and no withholding is required
2027, with income tax withholding
questions.explanation: IRC § 421(b): where the transfer would qualify but for a failure of the holding periods, the increase in income is treated as arising in the taxable year of the disposition, not the year of exercise, and no chapter 24 withholding is required on that increase.

questions.stem: Mei buys a call option on shares that would be a capital asset in her hands, paying a 2,000-dollar premium. She never exercises it and it expires worthless eight months later. What is the result?
options: An ordinary loss of 2,000 dollars, because an unexercised option is not a sale
A short-term capital loss of 2,000 dollars, the option being deemed sold on the day it expired
No deduction, because the option was never sold or exchanged
A long-term capital loss of 2,000 dollars, because a lapsed option takes the long-term character of the shares it covers
questions.explanation: IRC § 1234(a)(1) gives loss from failing to exercise an option the same character as the underlying property would have in the taxpayer's hands, and § 1234(a)(2) deems a lapsed option sold on the day it expired. The option was held eight months, so the capital loss is short term; the grantor rule in § 1234(b)(1) applies to the writer, not the purchaser.

questions.stem: An employer's employee stock purchase plan sets the option price at 85 percent of the share value on the date of exercise rather than on the date of grant. What is the longest period the option may remain outstanding?
options: 10 years from grant
5 years from grant
27 months from grant
There is no limit so long as the 85 percent floor is met
questions.explanation: IRC § 423(b)(7): where the option price is set against value at exercise, the option period is limited to 5 years. The 10-year term belongs to incentive stock options under § 422(b).

questions.stem: Soraya exchanges investment land with a basis of 400,000 dollars and a value of 350,000 dollars for like-kind land worth 320,000 dollars plus 30,000 dollars of cash. How much loss is recognised?
options: 30,000 dollars, to the extent of the cash received
50,000 dollars, the full realised loss
None, because no loss is recognised on an exchange that would otherwise qualify
20,000 dollars, the loss net of the cash received
questions.explanation: IRC § 1031(c): where an exchange would qualify but for the receipt of money or other property and produces a loss, no loss is recognised at all. Boot triggers gain under § 1031(b) but never loss.

questions.stem: Kenji exchanges a rental building in Ohio for a rental building of equal value in Portugal, both held for investment, and completes the identification and exchange within the statutory periods. Does the exchange qualify?
options: Yes, because both properties are real property held for investment
No, because real property in the United States and real property outside it are not of like kind
Yes, provided a qualified intermediary is used
No, because foreign property must be identified within 30 days
questions.explanation: IRC § 1031(h): real property located in the United States and real property located outside the United States are not property of a like kind.

questions.stem: Amara transfers her relinquished property on 1 March 2026. Her intermediary delivers a signed written identification of the replacement property on 20 April 2026, and she receives that property on 15 July 2026. Does the property received qualify as like-kind property?
options: Yes, because it was received within 180 days of the transfer
No, because the identification came after the 45-day identification period
Yes, because the identification only has to precede receipt
No, because identification must be made before the relinquished property is transferred
questions.explanation: IRC § 1031(a)(3)(A): property received is treated as not like-kind if it is not identified on or before the day 45 days after the taxpayer transfers the relinquished property. 20 April is day 50, so the identification is late and receipt within 180 days does not cure it.

questions.stem: Teodora advances 45,000 dollars to her brother to buy a food truck. There is no note, no interest rate and no repayment date, and she never asks to be repaid. The business fails in 2026. What may she deduct?
options: A short-term capital loss of 45,000 dollars
A long-term capital loss of 45,000 dollars
Nothing, because there was never a bona fide debt
A business bad debt, because the funds were used in a trade or business
questions.explanation: Treas. Reg. § 1.166-1(c): only a bona fide debt arising from a valid and enforceable obligation to pay a fixed or determinable sum qualifies, and a gift is not a debt for § 166 purposes. The advance is a completed gift with no income tax deduction.

questions.stem: Hugo buys a corporate bond, a security that is a capital asset in his hands, on 1 September 2025. The issuer collapses and the bond becomes wholly worthless on 1 March 2026. What is the character of his loss?
options: A short-term capital loss under the nonbusiness bad debt rule
A long-term capital loss, because the security is deemed sold on the last day of the taxable year
A short-term capital loss, because he held the bond for six months when it became worthless
An ordinary loss
questions.explanation: IRC § 165(g)(1) treats a worthless security that is a capital asset as sold on the last day of the taxable year, which is 31 December 2026 here, so the holding period runs past one year and the loss is long term. A debt described in § 165(g)(2)(C) is outside the nonbusiness bad debt rules under Treas. Reg. § 1.166-5(b).

questions.stem: Ines lent 30,000 dollars on a properly documented note that does not mature until 2028. In 2026 the borrower is adjudged bankrupt with no assets, and the debt is wholly worthless. May she deduct the loss in 2026?
options: No, because a debt cannot be worthless before its maturity date
Yes, because the fact that the debt is not yet due does not by itself prevent the deduction
No, until she has sued on the note and obtained a judgment
Yes, but only as a partial deduction until 2028
questions.explanation: Treas. Reg. § 1.166-1(c): the fact that a debt is not yet due does not by itself prevent the deduction. What matters is that the debt is bona fide and has become totally worthless within the year, as Treas. Reg. § 1.166-5(a)(2) requires.

questions.stem: Camila, an investor, pays 9,000 dollars of interest in 2026 on a margin loan used to buy stock. Her net investment income for the year is 6,000 dollars. How much of the interest is deductible?
options: None, because investment expenses are miscellaneous itemized deductions suspended by § 67
6,000 dollars, with the remaining 3,000 dollars treated as investment interest paid in the succeeding year
9,000 dollars in full
6,000 dollars, with the remaining 3,000 dollars permanently lost
questions.explanation: IRC § 163(d)(1), (2): for a taxpayer other than a corporation, investment interest is deductible up to net investment income, and any excess is treated as investment interest paid in the succeeding year. Investment interest is not a miscellaneous itemized deduction, so § 67(h) does not touch it.

questions.stem: Dmitri is a trader in securities who has made the § 475(f) election. His 2026 trading gains are ordinary income. Are they subject to self-employment tax?
options: Yes, because the election makes the gains ordinary and he carries on a trade or business
No, because the ordinary characterisation does not apply for purposes of § 1402
Yes, but only on gains from positions held less than a year
No, because trading gains are always capital gains
questions.explanation: IRC § 475(f)(1)(D) provides that § 475(d)(3) does not apply for purposes of §§ 1402 and 7704, so the ordinary character does not carry through to self-employment tax.

questions.stem: A securities dealer buys a block of shares and, before the close of that day, clearly identifies them in her records as held for investment. She later sells them at a loss. What is the character of the loss?
options: Ordinary, because a dealer's securities are always inventory
Capital, because a loss on a security identified as held for investment is never ordinary to a dealer
Ordinary, unless she held the shares for more than one year
Not deductible, because dealers may not hold investments
questions.explanation: IRC § 1236(b): a dealer's loss is never ordinary if the security was at any time clearly identified in the dealer's records as held for investment. The identification that secures capital gain treatment under § 1236(a) also fixes capital character for a loss.

questions.stem: Tariq is a limited partner. For 2026 his distributive share of partnership income is $30,000 and he also receives a $12,000 guaranteed payment for services he actually rendered. His net earnings from self-employment from the partnership are:
options: Nothing
questions.explanation: IRC § 1402(a)(13) excludes the distributive share of a limited partner as such, other than guaranteed payments under § 707(c) for services actually rendered to the extent they are remuneration for those services — so only the $12,000 is in.
questions.pageTitle: Self-employment tax deduction and the two halvings

questions.stem: Zoe is single. Her wages taken into account for FICA fall $50,000 short of the single-filer threshold for the additional hospital insurance tax, and after the base reduction she has $80,000 of self-employment income. The additional 0.9 percent tax applies to:
options: None of it, because her self-employment income alone is below the threshold
questions.explanation: IRC § 1401(b)(2)(B) reduces the threshold, but not below zero, by wages taken into account for the corresponding FICA tax, so only $50,000 of it remains for her self-employment income; $30,000 of the $80,000 sits above that and bears the additional tax, with no § 164(f) deduction for any part of it.
questions.pageTitle: Self-employment tax deduction and the two halvings

questions.stem: A part-time city council member receives $18,000 for the functions of that public office and has no other self-employment activity. Self-employment tax is owed on:
options: The whole $18,000
Nothing, because the functions of a public office are not a trade or business for this purpose
Only the hospital insurance components
The amount above the statutory floor
questions.explanation: IRC § 1402(c)(1) provides that a trade or business does not include the performance of the functions of a public office, other than certain State fee-basis positions, so the pay is outside net earnings from self-employment.
questions.pageTitle: Self-employment tax deduction and the two halvings

questions.stem: Lars, single, was an active participant in his employer's plan for January 2026 only and then left the job. His modified adjusted gross income is far above the active participant phase-out range. His traditional IRA deduction for 2026 is:
options: The full amount, because he was covered for only one month
Nothing, because active participation for any part of the plan year engages the § 219(g) phase-out and his income is above the range
The full amount reduced by one twelfth
Nothing, because an active participant may not contribute to an IRA at all
questions.explanation: IRC § 219(g)(1), (2) applies the phase-out where the individual was an active participant for any part of a plan year ending with or within the taxable year — a single month counts for the whole year, and above the range the deduction is gone; the contribution itself remains permitted.

questions.stem: Meret, aged 52, had wages of $190,000 from her employer in 2025, above the Roth catch-up wage threshold, and expects $120,000 in 2026, below it. Her 2026 catch-up contribution to that employer's 401(k) plan must be:
options: Pre-tax, because her 2026 wages are below the threshold
A designated Roth contribution, because her 2025 wages from that employer exceeded the threshold
Forgone, because the catch-up is unavailable above the threshold
Split equally between pre-tax and Roth
questions.explanation: IRC § 414(v)(7)(A) requires catch-up contributions to an applicable employer plan to be designated Roth contributions where the individual's wages from the employer for the preceding calendar year exceeded the threshold — the test looks at 2025 pay, not 2026.

questions.stem: Yusra works for two unrelated employers in 2026 and defers $15,000 into each plan, so that her total deferrals exceed the annual elective deferral limit. Which is correct?
options: There is no excess, because each plan is under the limit
She has an excess deferral, because the § 402(g)(1) limit applies to the individual across all plans
There is an excess only if the two employers are related
Each plan has failed the § 415(c) annual addition limit
questions.explanation: IRC § 402(g)(1) caps the exclusion for elective deferrals for the individual's taxable year across every plan they participate in; each plan is within § 415(c) on its own, which is why neither payroll flags the excess.

questions.stem: Priyanka, aged 67, retires in October 2026 and claims Social Security; her Medicare Part A entitlement is backdated to April. She had self-only coverage under a qualifying plan all year and contributed the full annual amount in January. Her monthly limitation is zero from:
options: October, the month she enrolled
April, the first month of entitlement
January 2026, because she was already past 65
January 2027, the year after enrolment
questions.explanation: IRC § 223(b)(7) makes the monthly limitation zero for the first month the individual is entitled to Medicare benefits and for each month thereafter — entitlement, not age or the enrolment date, controls, so nine twelfths of her January contribution is an excess.

questions.stem: In March 2027 Ola discovers a 2026 excess contribution. He extends his 2026 return to 15 October 2027 and withdraws the excess, with the net income attributable to it, in September 2027. The result is:
options: The excess is included in gross income and the tax is increased by 20 percent of it
The excess escapes the inclusion rule, because the withdrawal with its net income was made by the due date of the return including extensions
The excess escapes only if withdrawn by the unextended due date
The excess escapes inclusion but the 10 percent additional tax still applies
questions.explanation: IRC § 223(f)(3)(A): an excess contribution withdrawn with the net income attributable to it on or before the due date of the return, including extensions, escapes the inclusion rule.

questions.stem: Mira, aged 22, is claimed as a dependent on her parents' return. She has her own qualifying high deductible health plan through her job and contributes $2,000 to an HSA in her own name. Her deduction is:
options: $2,000, because she has her own qualifying coverage
$2,000 prorated for the months she was covered
Nothing, because another taxpayer is allowed a § 151 deduction for her
Nothing, unless her parents also contribute to the account
questions.explanation: IRC § 223(b)(6) allows no deduction to an individual for whom another taxpayer is allowed a § 151 deduction for a taxable year beginning in the same calendar year; her own coverage and eligibility do not matter.

questions.stem: Dara pays alimony under a 2017 divorce decree. In 2023 the parties modified the decree and expressly adopted the post-2018 treatment. Her 2026 payments are:
options: Deductible, because the date of the original instrument controls
Not deductible by her and not includible by the recipient
Deductible by her but not includible by the recipient
Deductible only for payments made before the modification
questions.explanation: IRC § 215 was repealed by Pub. L. 115-97 § 11051(a), and the repeal reaches an instrument executed before 2019 that is modified after 2018 to adopt the change — the modification moves her onto the new regime.

questions.stem: A member of a reserve component travels 80 miles from home for weekend drills and pays lodging within the Federal travel rates. The expenses are:
options: An adjustment to income under § 62
Not an adjustment, because the travel must be more than 100 miles from home
An itemized deduction only
An adjustment for the lodging but not the mileage
questions.explanation: IRC § 62(a)(2)(E) reaches reservist expenses only for a period during which the individual is more than 100 miles from home in connection with the services; at 80 miles the above-the-line treatment is unavailable.

questions.stem: A part-time aide at a public elementary school works 700 hours during the school year and spends $300 on classroom supplies. The educator adjustment is:
options: Capped at the indexed figure, because an aide is a listed role
Nothing, because the 900-hour test is not met
Nothing, because aides are not eligible educators
questions.explanation: IRC § 62(d)(1)(A) requires a kindergarten through grade 12 teacher, instructor, counselor, principal or aide to be in a school for at least 900 hours during a school year; an aide is a listed role, but 700 hours fails the test.

questions.stem: Bettina runs two sole proprietorships: a consultancy earning $50,000 and a bakery that shows a loss. Her health policy is established with respect to the bakery, and she pays $7,000 of premiums. Her § 162(l) deduction is:
options: $7,000, because her total self-employment earnings exceed the premium
Nothing, because the business with respect to which the plan is established has no earned income
$7,000, reduced by the bakery's loss
Half of $7,000
questions.explanation: IRC § 162(l)(2)(A) caps the deduction at earned income derived from the trade or business with respect to which the plan is established; the consultancy's profit is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Where does a sole proprietor take the self-employed health insurance deduction?
options: On Schedule A, subject to the § 213 percentage floor
In computing adjusted gross income, whether or not the taxpayer itemizes
On Schedule C, reducing net profit and self-employment tax
As a nonrefundable credit
questions.explanation: IRC § 62(a)(1): the deduction is attributable to a trade or business not consisting of the performance of services as an employee, so it is allowed in computing adjusted gross income — above the line, but kept out of net earnings from self-employment by § 162(l)(4).

questions.stem: Hugo's wife is eligible for her employer's subsidised medical plan, which has no long-term care component, and declines it. Hugo, self-employed, pays his own medical premiums and a premium for a qualified long-term care insurance contract. For those months:
options: Both premiums are denied
The medical premiums are denied, but the eligible long-term care premiums remain deductible because the two tests are applied separately
Neither premium is denied, because the plan was declined
The long-term care premium is denied and the medical premiums allowed
questions.explanation: IRC § 162(l)(2)(B)(i), (ii) applies the other-coverage test separately for plans that include qualified long-term care coverage and plans that do not, so eligibility for a medical-only plan denies the medical premiums for the month without reaching the long-term care premiums, which are limited instead by § 162(l)(2)(C).

questions.stem: Vera, 72, pays 7,500 dollars of premiums during 2026 on a qualified long-term care insurance contract. How much of the premium is taken into account as medical care?
options: All 7,500 dollars
Nothing, because premiums count only for a self-employed taxpayer
Only the eligible long-term care premium for her age band under § 213(d)(10)
Only the portion exceeding 7.5 percent of adjusted gross income
questions.explanation: IRC § 213(d)(10) counts only eligible long-term care premiums, on a five-band scale by attained age before the close of the year, so a premium above the figure for her band is excluded to that extent. Insurance covering medical care is otherwise within § 213(d)(1)(D), and the floor is applied afterwards to the total.
questions.pageTitle: Medical, dental, vision and long-term care expenses

questions.stem: Xavier's mother lives with him. Her own gross income is too high for him to claim her as a dependent, but she otherwise meets the § 152 tests, and he pays 6,000 dollars of her unreimbursed medical bills in 2026. May those bills count toward his § 213 deduction?
options: No, because she is not his dependent
Yes, because § 213(a) applies § 152 without regard to the gross income test
Only if he claims her for the credit for other dependents
Only the portion exceeding her own income
questions.explanation: IRC § 213(a) determines dependency under § 152 without regard to the gross income test, the not-a-dependent-of-another test and the joint return test, so a person who is not a dependent for credit purposes can still have their medical expenses paid and deducted, subject to the 7.5 percent floor.
questions.pageTitle: Medical, dental, vision and long-term care expenses

questions.stem: Yara uses a wheelchair and rents her apartment. In 2026 she spends 2,000 dollars on a ramp to the entrance and has 3,500 dollars of other unreimbursed medical expenses. Her adjusted gross income is 40,000 dollars. What is her medical deduction?
options: 500 dollars
2,500 dollars
5,500 dollars
2,000 dollars
questions.explanation: The ramp is a capital expenditure for the purpose of affecting a structure or function of the body within IRC § 213(d)(1)(A), and because she does not own the property there is no increase in the value of her property to offset against it, so the full 2,000 dollars counts. The 5,500-dollar total less the 3,000-dollar floor under § 213(a) leaves 2,500 dollars.
questions.pageTitle: Medical, dental, vision and long-term care expenses

questions.stem: Beatrix files jointly for 2026 with modified adjusted gross income $20,000 above the threshold amount for the applicable limitation amount. Her cap on the capped pile of State and local taxes is:
options: Reduced by $6,000, being 30 percent of the excess
Reduced by $20,000, dollar for dollar
Unchanged, because the phasedown applies only to years beginning after 2029
Halved
questions.explanation: IRC § 164(b)(7)(B)(i) reduces the applicable limitation amount by 30 percent of the excess of modified adjusted gross income over the threshold amount for a taxable year beginning before 1 January 2030 — so $20,000 of excess costs $6,000 of cap.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor pays a State real estate transfer tax when buying a warehouse for the business. Under § 164 the tax is:
options: Deducted in the year paid as a tax paid in carrying on a trade or business
Treated as part of the cost of the property acquired
Added to the capped pile with the proprietor's home property taxes
Nondeductible as a personal expense
questions.explanation: IRC § 164(a), flush text: a tax paid in connection with an acquisition or disposition of property is treated as part of the cost of the property acquired, or as a reduction in the amount realised on a disposition, rather than deducted in the year paid.

questions.stem: In 2026 Rosa, a single individual below the phasedown threshold, pays $9,000 of foreign income tax and $38,000 of State income tax, and deducts the foreign tax rather than crediting it. For the applicable limitation amount:
options: Both amounts go into the capped pile
The foreign income tax is excluded from § 164 entirely, like a foreign real property tax
Only the $38,000 is measured against the cap; the foreign income tax sits outside it
The foreign income tax is deductible only if she elects general sales taxes instead
questions.explanation: The sentence following IRC § 164(b)(6)(B) provides that the limitation does not apply to foreign taxes described in § 164(a)(3), so foreign income taxes are deductible outside the cap — only foreign real property taxes are removed altogether, by § 164(b)(6)(A).

questions.stem: Kai took out an 850,000-dollar mortgage in 2016 to buy his principal residence. In 2026 he borrows a further 250,000 dollars, secured by the same house, to add a second storey. Which interest is deductible as qualified residence interest?
options: Interest on both loans in full
Interest on the 2016 loan only
Interest on the 2026 loan only, because it is the more recent acquisition debt
Neither, because the combined debt exceeds the cap
questions.explanation: IRC § 163(h)(3)(F)(i)(IV) keeps debt incurred on or before 15 December 2017 on the higher pre-2018 cap, and the 2016 balance sits within it, but that grandfathered balance reduces the lower cap available for later borrowing and already exceeds it. The 2026 loan is acquisition indebtedness, yet no interest on it is deductible.

questions.stem: Lila draws 60,000 dollars on a home equity line of credit secured by her principal residence and uses all of it to build an extension on that house. Is the interest deductible for 2026?
options: No, because home equity indebtedness has been permanently disallowed
Yes, because the borrowing substantially improves the residence and is secured by it, making it acquisition indebtedness
Yes, but only as investment interest
No, because a line of credit is never acquisition indebtedness
questions.explanation: IRC § 163(h)(3)(B)(i) defines acquisition indebtedness as debt incurred in acquiring, constructing or substantially improving a qualified residence and secured by it. Trace the borrowing, not the label: the same line used to buy a car would be personal interest, but used to improve the home it is deductible within the cap.

questions.stem: Mateo pays 20,000 dollars of interest on a margin loan used to buy stock held for investment. His investment income is 8,000 dollars of interest and dividends plus 15,000 dollars of net capital gain. How much investment interest can he deduct for 2026?
options: 8,000 dollars, with the balance lost
20,000 dollars automatically, because total investment income exceeds the interest
8,000 dollars without an election, or 20,000 dollars if he elects to treat enough of the net capital gain as investment income at ordinary rates
23,000 dollars
questions.explanation: IRC § 163(d)(1) limits the deduction to net investment income, with the excess carried forward under § 163(d)(2), and § 163(d)(4)(B) lets him elect to treat net capital gain as investment income, raising the ceiling at the cost of the preferential rate on the amount elected.

questions.stem: Gideon has a contribution base of 300,000 dollars for 2026 and itemizes. He gives 100,000 dollars of cash to public charities and 4,000 dollars of appreciated stock to a private foundation. How is the 0.5 percent floor absorbed?
options: The cash is reduced to 98,500 dollars and the stock is untouched
The stock is reduced to 2,500 dollars and the cash is untouched
The 1,500 dollars is split between the two gifts in proportion to their amounts
Each gift is reduced by 1,500 dollars
questions.explanation: IRC § 170(b)(1)(I) absorbs the floor in a prescribed order that runs from the least favourably treated categories to the 60 percent cash category last, so the 1,500 dollars comes out of the private foundation gift before it touches the cash to public charities. Simply subtracting 0.5 percent from the total is wrong whenever there is more than one category of giving.

questions.stem: Helene does not itemize for 2026. She gives 800 dollars in cash, by cheque, to a donor advised fund maintained by her community foundation, and keeps the cancelled cheque. What is her deduction under § 170(p)?
options: 800 dollars
800 dollars less the 0.5 percent floor
Nothing, because § 170(p) does not reach a gift to establish or maintain a donor advised fund
Nothing, because a non-itemizer has no charitable deduction in 2026
questions.explanation: IRC § 170(p)(2) excludes a contribution for the establishment or maintenance of a donor advised fund, just as § 170(p)(1) excludes a § 509(a)(3) supporting organization. The gift is cash and properly recorded, but the donee is the wrong kind for this provision.

questions.stem: Iris donates publicly traded shares with a claimed deduction of 30,000 dollars to a public charity in 2026. Which is correct about the appraisal requirements?
options: She must obtain a qualified appraisal, because the deduction exceeds the middle threshold
She must obtain a qualified appraisal and attach it to the return
No qualified appraisal is required, because publicly traded securities are excepted
No documentation of any kind is required for a gift of securities
questions.explanation: IRC § 170(f)(11)(A)(ii)(I) excepts cash, inventory, publicly traded securities and a qualified vehicle with the donee acknowledgment from the appraisal requirements, whatever the amount claimed. The § 170(f)(8) contemporaneous written acknowledgment is still needed.

questions.stem: After applying the per-event floor to each of two federally declared disaster events, Nadia's personal casualty losses for 2026 total $20,000. She has no personal casualty gains, and her adjusted gross income is $150,000. What is her itemized deduction?
options: Nothing, because losses from two events cannot be aggregated
questions.explanation: IRC § 165(h)(2)(A) allows losses exceeding gains only to the extent the excess exceeds 10 percent of adjusted gross income, $15,000 here, so $5,000 remains. The per-event floor was applied first, as § 165(h)(3)(B) requires.
questions.pageTitle: Nonbusiness casualty and theft losses in declared disaster areas

questions.stem: Omar's insurance recovery on a boat destroyed in a declared hurricane exceeds his basis by $10,000, a personal casualty gain. In the same year an undeclared kitchen fire destroys $6,000 of uninsured contents. How is the fire loss treated?
options: Not deductible at all, because no disaster was declared
Deductible in full without any floor, because casualty losses are always allowed against gains
Allowed, less the per-event floor, because the disaster requirement is disapplied to the extent of his personal casualty gains
Allowed only if he elects to take it in the preceding year
questions.explanation: IRC § 165(h)(5)(B)(i) disapplies the disaster requirement to a non-disaster loss up to the amount of personal casualty gains, and clause (ii) then removes the gains so used from the § 165(h)(2)(A) computation for the disaster losses. The loss is below the gain, so all of it comes through after the per-event floor.
questions.pageTitle: Nonbusiness casualty and theft losses in declared disaster areas

questions.stem: Gwen's home is destroyed in a federally declared disaster in April 2026. Her adjusted gross income was $200,000 in 2025 and is $50,000 in 2026. If she elects under § 165(i)(1) to take the loss in 2025, how does the 10 percent floor apply?
options: Against 2026 adjusted gross income, whichever year the loss is claimed in
Against 2025 adjusted gross income, so $20,000 of the loss is absorbed rather than $5,000
The floor does not apply to an elected loss
The election is unavailable, because it is limited to State declared disasters
questions.explanation: IRC § 165(i)(1) moves the loss to the year immediately preceding the disaster, and the § 165(h)(2)(A)(ii) floor is then measured against that preceding year's adjusted gross income. The election can produce a refund quickly, but it carries a real price when the prior year's income was higher.
questions.pageTitle: Nonbusiness casualty and theft losses in declared disaster areas

questions.stem: Nia, a self-employed sales agent, repaid 2,600 dollars in 2026 of a commission from her own business that had been included in her 2024 income because it appeared she had an unrestricted right to it, which proved wrong. How is the repayment treated?
options: Under the § 1341 lesser-of computation, comparing 2026 tax with and without the deduction
As an ordinary business deduction in 2026, because § 1341 applies only where the deduction exceeds 3,000 dollars
By amending the 2024 return to exclude the commission
Not deductible, because repayments are miscellaneous itemized deductions
questions.explanation: IRC § 1341(a)(4) applies its special computation only where the deduction exceeds 3,000 dollars, so the repayment is simply an ordinary business deduction in 2026 with no comparison to what the 2024 tax would have been. A few hundred dollars more would have opened up the computation.

questions.stem: Pavel, who is blind, pays 4,000 dollars in 2026 for a reader at his workplace, without which he could not do his job. He also pays 1,200 dollars of union dues. Which is deductible as an itemized deduction?
options: Both, subject to the 2 percent floor
The reader only, in full and without a floor
The union dues only
Neither, because both are employee expenses
questions.explanation: IRC § 67(d) defines impairment-related work expenses as expenses of a handicapped individual for attendant care services at the place of employment and other expenses necessary for the individual to be able to work; the class is on the § 67(b) list, so it survives § 67(h) and is deductible in full. Union dues are an ordinary employee expense, disallowed as a miscellaneous itemized deduction.

questions.stem: A study source cites "§ 67(g)" for the disallowance of miscellaneous itemized deductions. What does § 67(g) now contain?
options: The disallowance, unchanged
The 2 percent floor
A definition of educator expenses, the disallowance having been redesignated § 67(h)
Nothing, because the subsection was repealed
questions.explanation: Pub. L. 119-21 § 70110(b) redesignated the disallowance as § 67(h) after § 70110(a) struck its "before January 1, 2026" limitation, and a new § 67(g) defining educator expenses now occupies the old address. A citation to § 67(g) for the disallowance points at a provision about something else entirely.

questions.stem: Ines, a nonresident alien with effectively connected income, loses a house she owns in her home country to a flood that is the subject of a declared disaster there. May she deduct the casualty loss on Form 1040-NR?
options: Yes, because § 873(b) allows casualty losses whether or not connected with effectively connected income
No, because § 873(b)(1) reaches only a loss of property located within the United States
Yes, but only to the extent connected with her effectively connected income
Yes, but only against her § 871(a) income
questions.explanation: IRC § 873(b)(1) preserves casualty and theft losses within § 165(c)(2) or (3) only if the loss is of property located within the United States, and since 2018 the loss must also satisfy the § 165(h)(5) declared-disaster requirement. A foreign property fails the location limb whatever the declaration.

questions.stem: Rafael, a resident of Mexico with effectively connected income, points out that § 873(b)(3) lifts the "only one" personal exemption limit for a resident of a contiguous country. What is the result on his 2026 return?
options: He may claim a personal exemption for himself, his spouse and each dependent at the full amount
He is limited to one personal exemption
He is entitled to more than one exemption, but each is worth zero because the exemption amount is zero
He may claim the standard deduction in place of the exemptions
questions.explanation: IRC § 873(b)(3) genuinely lifts the single-exemption limit for a resident of a contiguous country, but § 151(d)(5)(A) has set the exemption amount at zero for taxable years beginning after 2017 and Pub. L. 119-21 left that in place, so the exception is a live cross-reference to an amount that is zero.

questions.stem: Sunita is a nonresident alien on a temporary assignment in the United States earning effectively connected wages. She has 4,000 dollars of unreimbursed employee expenses connected with those wages. Are they deductible on Form 1040-NR?
options: Yes, under § 873(a), because they are connected with effectively connected income
Yes, as one of the three § 873(b) exceptions
No, because the § 67 suspension of miscellaneous itemized deductions applies to everyone and § 873 did not preserve them
No, because a nonresident alien may deduct nothing against wages
questions.explanation: Unreimbursed employee expenses went with the rest of the miscellaneous class under the § 67 suspension, and nothing in § 873 preserved them, because the disallowance operates on the definition of an itemized deduction rather than on who may claim it. Being connected with effectively connected income does not revive a deduction that no longer exists.

questions.stem: Renata earns $95,000 of W-2 wages as a staff architect and has no other income; her taxable income is far below the threshold amount. Her § 199A deduction on those wages is:
options: 20 percent of the wages, because she is below the threshold
20 percent of the wages, because architecture is read out of the specified service list
Nothing, because performing services as an employee is excluded at every income level
Nothing, because an architect is a specified service trade
questions.explanation: IRC § 199A(d)(1)(B) excludes the trade or business of performing services as an employee from the definition of a qualified trade or business, and unlike the specified service exclusion the threshold never rescues it — the architecture carve-out is irrelevant to wages.

questions.stem: A single taxpayer's business is not a specified service trade or business. It produces $100,000 of qualified business income and pays $30,000 of W-2 wages, with no qualified property. Her taxable income is above the threshold and has used one fifth of the phase-in range. Her deduction for that business is:
questions.explanation: IRC § 199A(b)(3)(B)(i)–(iii): 20 percent of QBI is $20,000, the wage figure is the greater of $15,000 or $7,500, so the excess amount is $5,000; one fifth of that, $1,000, comes off, leaving $19,000 — the ratio reduces the gap, not the deduction, so the cliff answer of $15,000 is wrong.

questions.stem: Devika is single with $80,000 of qualified business income from a business in which she materially participates. Her taxable income is $70,000, of which $50,000 is net capital gain. Her § 199A deduction is:
questions.explanation: IRC § 199A(a)(2) caps the deduction at 20 percent of taxable income over net capital gain — 20 percent of $20,000, or $4,000 — and that ceiling binds well below the $16,000 combined amount; net capital gain is already out of QBI and comes out of the ceiling a second time.

questions.stem: Ana has one child in daycare at a cost of $8,000 and excludes $7,500 from income under her employer's § 129 plan. Her adjusted gross income after the exclusion is $61,000. What is her credit?
options: The applicable percentage of $3,000, because the exclusion and the credit operate independently
The applicable percentage of $500, the expenses left after the exclusion
Nothing, because the § 129 exclusion reduces her $3,000 expense cap to zero
The applicable percentage of $8,000, less the amount excluded
questions.explanation: IRC § 21(c) caps employment-related expenses at $3,000 for one qualifying individual and reduces that cap by the amount excluded under § 129. The reduction operates on the cap, not on the expenses, so a $7,500 exclusion leaves no creditable expenses at all.

questions.stem: Marcus earns $88,000. His wife Delia had no wages all year and was a full-time student from September to December, four calendar months. They pay $7,200 for the care of their 3-year-old and file jointly. What is the credit?
options: The applicable percentage of $1,000, her deemed earned income for four months
The applicable percentage of $3,000, because Marcus's earnings exceed the cap
Nothing, because she is not a student for § 21 and her earned income is zero
The applicable percentage of $7,200
questions.explanation: IRC § 21(e)(7) treats a person as a student only if a full-time student for each of five calendar months in the year, so with four months § 21(d)(2) supplies no deemed earned income. The § 21(d)(1)(B) limitation is the lesser of the two spouses' earned incomes, which is Delia's nil, and so is the credit.

questions.stem: Divorced parents' son lives with his mother for most of the year, and she has signed Form 8332 releasing the dependency claim to the father, who pays $4,000 for after-school care so he can work. For which parent is the boy a qualifying individual under § 21?
options: The father, because he holds the dependency release and paid the expenses
The mother, because the child is a qualifying individual only of the custodial parent
Either parent, by agreement between them
Neither, because the parent who paid is not the parent who claims the child
questions.explanation: IRC § 21(e)(5): where § 152(e) applies to a child, the child is a qualifying individual of the custodial parent and not of the noncustodial parent, whichever of them claims the dependency. The noncustodial parent claiming the child cannot claim this credit.

questions.stem: Sunil's only dependent is his mother, a qualifying relative under § 152(d). His income tax before credits is zero and his earned income is $30,000. What refund does the $500 credit for other dependents produce?
options: $500, because the credit is refundable up to the per-child cap
$500, because his earned income exceeds the floor by enough to support it under the 15 percent formula
Nothing, because the other-dependent amount is excluded from the refundable computation
Nothing this year, but the unused $500 carries forward to next year
questions.explanation: IRC § 24(h)(5) directs that § 24(d)(1)(A) be applied without regard to § 24(h)(4), so the $500 increase for other dependents is never refundable. It shares the threshold and the phase-out of the child tax credit but not its refund, and nothing carries forward.
questions.pageTitle: Child tax credit and credit for other dependents

questions.stem: A taxpayer changes from a calendar year to a fiscal year with the Secretary's consent, producing a short taxable year of eight months in 2026. She has a qualifying child aged 5. What child tax credit is allowed for the short year?
options: The full $2,200
Eight-twelfths of $2,200
None, because no credit is allowable for a taxable year of fewer than 12 months
$500, the other-dependent amount
questions.explanation: IRC § 24(f): no credit is allowable for a taxable year of fewer than 12 months, with the sole exception of a year closed by the taxpayer's death. A short year for any other reason kills the credit entirely.
questions.pageTitle: Child tax credit and credit for other dependents

questions.stem: A married couple file jointly with two qualifying children who each hold valid social security numbers. The husband has a social security number; the wife has only an individual taxpayer identification number. Is the child tax credit allowed?
options: No, because every person on the return must have a social security number
Yes, because only the children's numbers matter
Yes, because on a joint return the number of at least one spouse satisfies the taxpayer identification requirement
Only the $500 other-dependent amount for each child
questions.explanation: IRC § 24(h)(7)(A)(i), as rewritten by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70104, requires the return to carry the taxpayer's social security number, but on a joint return the number of at least one spouse is enough. A single filer with an ITIN would lose the credit, and the former paragraph, which required only the child's number, no longer states the rule.
questions.pageTitle: Child tax credit and credit for other dependents

questions.stem: Nadia is enrolled half time in a certificate programme that does not lead to a degree. She pays $4,000 of tuition to the institution and buys $700 of required textbooks at the campus bookstore. What is her Lifetime Learning credit?
questions.explanation: The credit is 20 percent of qualified expenses, and the textbooks are not qualified: IRC § 25A(f)(1)(D) extends the definition to course materials only for the American Opportunity credit, and Reg. § 1.25A-2(d)(2)(ii) admits books only where the fee must be paid to the institution as a condition of enrollment. Twenty percent of $4,000 is $800.

questions.stem: Owen, 20, is a full-time degree student whose parents are entitled to claim him as a dependent. He paid his own $6,000 of tuition from summer earnings and received the Form 1098-T in his name. Who may claim the American Opportunity credit for those expenses?
options: Owen, because he paid the tuition
His parents, with the payments and the Form 1098-T treated as theirs
Either Owen or his parents, whichever produces the larger credit
Neither, because a dependent's own payments do not count for anyone
questions.explanation: IRC § 25A(g)(3) provides that where another taxpayer is entitled to claim the student as a dependent, the student may claim no credit, the student's own payments are treated as paid by that taxpayer, and the Form 1098-T is treated as received by that taxpayer. The rule does not turn on who wrote the cheque.

questions.stem: Priya, 18, is a first-year full-time degree student who files her own return and is a child subject to the § 1(g) kiddie tax. Nobody can claim her as a dependent, her tuition supports a full American Opportunity credit, and her tax liability is zero. What refund does the credit produce?
options: Nothing
questions.explanation: IRC § 25A(i) makes 40 percent of the credit refundable, but the whole refundable rule is switched off for a taxpayer who is a child subject to the § 1(g) kiddie tax, which catches a student claiming in her own right far more often than it catches a parent.

questions.stem: Marcus bought shares in a foreign company five days before the ex-dividend date and sold them four days after it, receiving a dividend from which foreign tax was withheld. May he credit the withholding?
options: Yes, in full, because withholding tax on a dividend is a tax in lieu of an income tax
Yes, but only under the § 904(j) election
No, because the stock was not held long enough under the § 901(k) holding period
No, but he may deduct it in the same year he credits his other foreign taxes
questions.explanation: IRC § 901(k) denies the credit for withholding tax on a dividend where the stock was held for too short a period around the ex-dividend date; the rule exists to stop a taxpayer buying a foreign stock immediately before its ex-dividend date purely to acquire a creditable tax. That period is different from, and shorter than, the § 1(h)(11) qualified dividend holding period.

questions.stem: Dana has US tax before credits of $20,000 and entire taxable income of $100,000. Her foreign source gross income is $30,000, against which $10,000 of deductions are properly allocable, and she paid $7,000 of foreign income tax on it, all general category. What is the § 904(a) limitation?
questions.explanation: IRC § 904(a) uses foreign source taxable income in the numerator, not gross income: $20,000 multiplied by $20,000 over $100,000 is $4,000. Using the $30,000 gross figure gives $6,000 and overstates the credit; the $3,000 excess carries back one year and forward ten within the general basket under § 904(c).

questions.stem: Ravi carried forward $900 of unused passive basket foreign tax credit from 2025. In 2026 his only foreign income is $3,000 of fund dividends on a Form 1099-DIV with $210 withheld, and he makes the § 904(j) election. What happens to the $900 carryforward in 2026?
options: It is used in 2026 against his US tax, because the limitation does not apply
It cannot be used in 2026, because the election blocks carryovers into or out of that year
It converts to a deduction for 2026
It is used in 2026, but only if he also files a Form 1116
questions.explanation: IRC § 904(j)(1)(B) and (C) block any carryback or carryover into or out of an electing year. The election gives him the full $210 without a Form 1116, but nothing from another year can enter 2026, which is the price the election carries for a taxpayer with an excess.

questions.stem: Sergeant Okafor's Form W-2 shows $16,000 of taxable wages and $9,000 of nontaxable combat pay excluded under § 112. He has two qualifying children. How is the combat pay treated in computing his earned income credit?
options: It must be included in earned income because it is compensation for services
It is never earned income because it is excluded from gross income
He may elect to treat it as earned income, and should compute the credit both ways before deciding
It is included automatically whenever doing so increases the credit
questions.explanation: IRC § 32(c)(2)(B)(vi) says a taxpayer "may elect" to treat § 112 combat pay as earned income. The election is optional and can raise or lower the credit depending on where the taxpayer sits on the curve, so the credit is computed both ways before deciding.

questions.stem: Lena is single with one qualifying child, earned income of $22,000, and $13,400 of capital gain net income from selling shares during 2026, with no other investment income. What is her earned income credit?
options: The full credit read from the table for one qualifying child
The table credit reduced by the amount of the gain
The table credit, because capital gains are not disqualified income
Nothing, because her disqualified income exceeds the 2026 ceiling
questions.explanation: Capital gain net income is disqualified income under IRC § 32(i)(2)(D), and § 32(i)(1) denies the credit entirely where disqualified income exceeds the ceiling, which $13,400 does for 2026. It is a cliff, not a phase-out, so the credit is not reduced but eliminated.

questions.stem: Marisol's 20-year-old son is a full-time student who lived with her all year and paid all of his own expenses from a part-time job and a scholarship, so he provides more than half of his own support. Which is correct for 2026?
options: He is not a qualifying child for either credit, because he supports himself
He is a qualifying child for the earned income credit but not for the child tax credit
He is a qualifying child for both the earned income credit and the child tax credit
He is a qualifying child for the child tax credit but not for the earned income credit
questions.explanation: IRC § 32(c)(3)(A) applies § 152(c) without paragraph (1)(D), the support test, so a self-supporting student who meets the relationship, abode and age tests is a qualifying child for this credit. For the child tax credit he fails twice, on age and on support.

questions.stem: Nadia pays $8,000 in 2026 to adopt her husband's daughter from his first marriage. Tomas pays $8,000 to adopt the son of the partner he lives with but has never married. Whose expenses are qualified adoption expenses?
options: Both, because each is adopting a child already living in the household
Neither, because each child already has a legal parent in the home
Only Nadia's, because adoption of a stepchild is favoured
Only Tomas's, because the exclusion reaches the child of the taxpayer's spouse and his partner is not his spouse
questions.explanation: IRC § 23(d)(1)(C) excludes expenses in connection with the adoption by an individual of a child of that individual's spouse. Tomas's partner is not his spouse, so his expenses are qualified adoption expenses on the ordinary tests; the provision turns on the marriage, not on the household.

questions.stem: The Delacroix family finalise a domestic adoption in 2026 with qualified adoption expenses above the per-child cap. Their modified adjusted gross income of $285,000 sits inside the 2026 phase-out band. How is their credit affected?
options: It is eliminated, because the income limitation operates as a cliff
It is unaffected, because expenses above the cap absorb the reduction
It is reduced ratably, so they keep a fraction of the capped credit that depends on where in the band their income falls
It is reduced dollar for dollar by the amount by which their income exceeds the floor
questions.explanation: IRC § 23(b)(2)(A), (B): the credit, as already capped by the dollar limitation, is reduced ratably across the phase-out range. It is a ratio rather than a dollar-for-dollar reduction, and for a family partway across the band it is neither zero nor total.

questions.stem: A couple adopt a child with serious physical disabilities, finalised in 2026, having paid $3,000 of qualified adoption expenses. No State or Indian tribal government has made any determination about the child. May they claim the special needs deemed amount?
options: Yes, because the child's disabilities make it a special needs adoption
Yes, if a physician certifies the disability
No, because special needs requires the two determinations by a State or Indian tribal government plus United States citizenship or residence
No, because the deemed amount is available only for foreign adoptions
questions.explanation: IRC § 23(d)(3)(A)–(C): a child with special needs is one that a State or Indian tribal government has determined cannot or should not be returned to the parents' home, and for which the same authority has determined that a specific factor makes placement unreasonable without adoption assistance, and who is a citizen or resident of the United States. Special needs is a legal determination, not a medical one, so their credit rests on the $3,000 actually paid.

questions.stem: A married couple live together all year and each buys a silver plan on the Exchange. The wife files married filing separately so as not to be responsible for her husband's tax debt. Is she an applicable taxpayer for 2026?
options: Yes, if her household income is between 100 and 400 percent of the poverty line
Yes, but only for months in which her husband had no coverage of his own
No, because a married taxpayer must file a joint return to be an applicable taxpayer
No, unless she repays every advance payment made on her behalf
questions.explanation: IRC § 36B(c)(1)(C) requires a married taxpayer to file a joint return, so the joint-return requirement fails before household income is even checked. The only relief is the regulatory exception for domestic abuse or spousal abandonment, which the statute itself does not provide.

questions.stem: Which of these Pub. L. 119-21 amendments to § 36B is not yet in effect for taxable year 2026?
options: Section 71305, striking the limitation on repayment of excess advance payments
Section 71302, repealing the special rule for certain lawfully present individuals with income below the poverty line
Section 71304, excluding plans enrolled in during an income-based special enrollment period
Section 71303, requiring the Exchange to run pre-enrollment verification of income and eligibility
questions.explanation: Pub. L. 119-21 § 71303 added § 36B(c)(3)(A)(ii) for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2027, so it is not yet in effect. Sections 71302 and 71305 apply to taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025 and § 71304 to plan years beginning after that date.

questions.stem: In 2026 a taxpayer enrols in an Exchange plan during a special enrollment period the Exchange offered solely on the basis of her expected household income relative to the poverty line, with no change in her circumstances. Are her months under that plan coverage months?
options: Yes, provided the plan is a silver plan
No, because a plan enrolled in during an income-based special enrollment period is not a qualified health plan for § 36B
Yes, because the route by which a taxpayer enrolled never affects the credit
No, until the Exchange completes pre-enrollment verification of her income
questions.explanation: IRC § 36B(c)(3)(A)(iii), added by Pub. L. 119-21 § 71304 for plan years beginning after 31 December 2025, provides that a plan enrolled in during an income-based special enrollment period not tied to a change in circumstances is not a qualified health plan for this section. The pre-enrollment verification rule in § 36B(c)(3)(A)(ii) does not apply until a later year.

questions.stem: Theo, 20, is a full-time university student with adjusted gross income of $15,000 from a part-time job, and nobody claims him as a dependent. He contributes $1,000 to a Roth IRA during 2026. What is his saver's credit?
options: Nothing
questions.explanation: IRC § 25B(c)(1)(B) excludes a full-time student from being an eligible individual, whatever their income. The Roth contribution would otherwise have counted as a qualified retirement savings contribution, but the eligibility test comes first.

questions.stem: Bianca is single, 40, not a student and not a dependent, with adjusted gross income of $20,000 for 2026. She contributes $2,000 to a traditional IRA for 2026, but took a $1,500 distribution from an old 401(k) plan in 2025. What is her saver's credit?
questions.explanation: IRC § 25B(d)(2) reduces qualified retirement savings contributions by distributions received during a testing period that runs from two years before the year through the due date of the return, so her base is $500, not $2,000. At her income she is in the 50 percent band, giving $250.

questions.stem: Hugo took delivery of a new electric vehicle on 20 October 2025 that would otherwise have qualified for the § 30D clean vehicle credit. Which is correct?
options: He has the credit, because the vehicle credits ran to 31 December 2025
He has no credit, because §§ 30D and 25E allow none for a vehicle acquired after 30 September 2025
He has a reduced credit under the step-down percentages
He has no § 30D credit, but may claim the § 25E previously-owned vehicle credit instead
questions.explanation: Pub. L. 119-21 § 70502 ended the § 30D clean vehicle credit and the § 25E previously-owned clean vehicle credit for vehicles acquired after 30 September 2025, a different date from the 31 December 2025 cut-off for §§ 25C and 25D property. The credits stopped; they were not phased down.

questions.stem: For 2026 a taxpayer's regular tax is $31,000 and tentative minimum tax is $36,500. What is the alternative minimum tax reported on Form 6251?
options: Zero, because the regular tax was paid
questions.explanation: IRC § 55(a) imposes a tax equal to the excess of the tentative minimum tax over the regular tax — $5,500 — which is added to the regular tax rather than replacing it.
questions.pageTitle: Alternative minimum tax and credit for prior year

questions.stem: Which of the following was not among the changes Pub. L. 119-21 made to the alternative minimum tax for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025?
options: The sunset on the enlarged exemption was struck
The phase-out threshold was reset and re-indexed from calendar year 2025
The phase-out rate was doubled to 50 percent
The exemption amounts were increased and given a new indexing base
questions.explanation: Pub. L. 119-21 § 70107 struck the sunset, reset the threshold with a 2025 indexing base, and doubled the phase-out rate; the exemption amounts themselves kept their 2017 base and their existing indexed values.
questions.pageTitle: Alternative minimum tax and credit for prior year

questions.stem: A child subject to the § 1(g) kiddie tax has alternative minimum taxable income in 2026. Does the § 59(j) limit on the child's exemption apply?
options: Yes, as published in the annual revenue procedure
No; the statute disapplies § 59(j) for every year the permanent exemption rules cover
Only if the child's parents themselves owe alternative minimum tax
Only for a child under 18
questions.explanation: IRC § 55(d)(4)(A)(iii) provides that § 59(j) shall not apply for any taxable year to which § 55(d)(4) applies, and with the sunset struck by Pub. L. 119-21 that is now every year; the statute controls over the figure the revenue procedure still publishes.
questions.pageTitle: Alternative minimum tax and credit for prior year

questions.stem: A family pays a plumber $3,800 during 2026 for repairs; he runs his own business, sets his own hours and serves the public. Do household employment taxes apply?
options: Yes, because cash payments exceed the threshold
No; he is an independent contractor, not a household employee
Yes, but only Medicare tax
Only if he worked more than one day a week
questions.explanation: IRS Topic no. 756: household workers are employees only where the payer controls both the work and how it is done; repairmen, plumbers and contractors providing services as independent contractors are not, so no Schedule H, Form W-2 or employer tax applies.

questions.stem: A family pays a live-in housekeeper $2,400 in cash plus room and board worth $9,000 in 2026. On what amount is social security and Medicare tax due?
options: Nothing
questions.explanation: IRC § 3121(a)(7)(A) excludes remuneration for domestic service paid in any medium other than cash, so the room and board never counts and never pushes the employee over the threshold, and the $2,400 of cash wages is itself below the year's threshold.

questions.stem: Why does the household employee cash wage threshold not appear in the annual inflation revenue procedure with the rest of an individual return's figures?
options: It is fixed in the statute and never changes
It is defined by § 3121(x) through its own adjustment mechanism, which rounds down, and is carried by IRS Topic 756 and Publication 926 instead
It is set each year by the Schedule H instructions alone
It changes only when Congress amends § 3121
questions.explanation: IRC § 3121(x) defines the applicable dollar threshold by an adjustment mechanism outside the annual inflation revenue procedure, so it is sourced from IRS Topic 756 and Publication 926, and because it rounds down it can stand still for a year while the underlying index rises.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's income arrives almost entirely in December. Using the annualised income method, her first-quarter instalment is reduced below 25 percent of the required annual payment. What happens to the reduction?
options: It is forgiven permanently
It is recaptured by increasing the next instalment, and later ones until fully recovered
It is added to the following year's first instalment
It becomes interest under § 6601
questions.explanation: IRC § 6654(d)(2)(A)(i), (ii): the lower annualised instalment becomes the required instalment for that quarter, but the reduction is recaptured by increasing the next instalment and later ones until it is fully recovered.

questions.stem: Hana, 67, retired four years ago and this year underpays her estimated tax through an honest misunderstanding. Does the retirement waiver relieve her?
options: Yes; she is over 62 and retired
Yes, automatically, once she shows reasonable cause
No; the retirement must have occurred in the year the payments were due or the year before, and even then the waiver is discretionary
No; the waiver applies only to disability
questions.explanation: IRC § 6654(e)(3)(B): the Secretary must determine both that the taxpayer retired after attaining 62, or became disabled, in the year the payments were due or the preceding year, and that the underpayment was due to reasonable cause and not willful neglect — a retirement four years earlier fails the first limb.

questions.stem: A taxpayer filed on time, could not pay, and entered an instalment agreement. What monthly failure to pay rate applies while the agreement is in effect?
options: 0.5 percent
0.25 percent
1 percent
5 percent
questions.explanation: IRC § 6651(a)(2), (d), (h): the failure to pay addition is 0.5 percent a month, reduced to 0.25 percent while an instalment agreement is in effect for a return filed on time, and raised to 1 percent after a notice of intent to levy.

questions.stem: Keiko's non-farm business shows a tiny profit this year. She had net earnings of $2,000 two years ago and $150 in each of the other two preceding years, and has never used an optional method. May she use the non-farm optional method?
options: Yes; she has all five years available
No; she was not self-employed on a regular basis, having had at least $400 of net earnings in only one of the three preceding years
Yes, because her current profit is below the lower limit
No; the non-farm method requires some farm income
questions.explanation: IRC § 1402(h) defines being self-employed on a regular basis by reference to net earnings of at least $400 in at least two of the three immediately preceding years; with only one qualifying year the method is closed to her this year, however low her current earnings.
questions.pageTitle: Self-employment tax: who owes it and the optional methods

questions.stem: A married couple run an unincorporated shop together and report all its profit on one spouse's Schedule C without electing qualified joint venture treatment. What is the principal consequence?
options: Total self-employment tax is doubled
The other spouse gets no social security earnings record for the year
The business loses its § 162 deductions
The profit becomes exempt from self-employment tax
questions.explanation: IRC § 1402(a)(17) and § 761(f): the qualified joint venture election lets each spouse's share be taken into account in that spouse's own net earnings. Without it the business is a partnership, and reporting everything on one Schedule C leaves the other spouse with no earnings record — the election is about coverage, not total tax.
questions.pageTitle: Self-employment tax: who owes it and the optional methods

questions.stem: A newly self-employed taxpayer with no withholding projects $4,000 of income tax and $9,000 of self-employment tax for the year. What must the estimated tax instalments be measured against?
options: The $4,000 of income tax only
The $9,000 of self-employment tax only
Both, $13,000 in total
Neither; self-employment tax is paid only with the return
questions.explanation: IRC § 6654(f)(2) brings the chapter 2 self-employment tax into the figure the instalments are measured against, alongside the income tax, so a new self-employed client with no withholding needs estimated payments covering both.
questions.pageTitle: Self-employment tax: who owes it and the optional methods

questions.stem: A taxpayer with two employers has combined 2026 social security wages $2,000 above the contribution and benefit base, each employer having withheld at 6.2 percent on everything it paid. What is the special refund?
options: Nothing, because each employer withheld correctly
questions.explanation: IRC § 6413(c)(1): the refund is the § 3101(a) tax withheld above what the base would have produced — 6.2 percent of the $2,000 excess. That each employer withheld correctly on its own wages is exactly why the employee, not the employer, is put right.

questions.stem: A taxpayer with a fiscal year ending 30 June received wages from two employers during calendar year 2026 that together exceeded the base. For which taxable year is the credit allowed?
options: The taxable year in which the second Form W-2 is received
The taxable year beginning in calendar year 2026
Either year, at the taxpayer's election
The taxable year ending in calendar year 2026
questions.explanation: IRC § 31(b)(2) allows the credit for the taxable year beginning in the calendar year in which the wages were received.

questions.stem: A taxpayer worked for a private company and, later the same year, for a railroad that withheld tier 1 railroad retirement tax. Does the tier 1 tax count toward the excess?
options: No; railroad retirement is a separate system
Yes, in full at whatever tier 1 rate applied
Yes, but only to the extent of the rate that does not exceed the § 3101(a) rate
Only if both employers were railroads
questions.explanation: IRC § 6413(c)(1): tier 1 tax under § 3201(a) counts toward the same ceiling only to the extent of the rate not exceeding the § 3101(a) rate, and § 3231(e) compensation is treated as wages for this purpose.

questions.stem: A congregation designates $30,000 of Reverend Idowu's 2026 pay as a housing allowance in advance. She spends $22,000 on rent and utilities; the fair rental value of the home with furnishings plus utilities is $26,000. How much is excluded from gross income?
options: Nothing, because the allowance exceeded the rent
questions.explanation: IRC § 107(2) excludes a cash allowance only to the extent used to rent or provide a home, only up to fair rental value plus utilities, and never beyond the amount designated — the lowest of the three caps, $22,000, with the $8,000 excess taxed as ordinary income.
questions.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the clergy

questions.stem: A minister's Form W-2 shows salary in box 1 but nothing withheld for social security, Medicare or federal income tax. The minister filed no exemption application. Is the form wrong?
options: Yes; FICA should have been withheld
Yes; income tax withholding is mandatory on salary
No; ministerial services are outside FICA and outside income tax withholding, and the minister pays by estimated tax or a voluntary agreement
No, because ministers are exempt from all employment taxes
questions.explanation: IRC §§ 3401(a)(9) and 3121(b)(8)(A) exclude ministerial services from wages for income tax withholding and from employment for FICA. The minister still owes self-employment tax under § 1402(c) and income tax, met by estimated payments or a voluntary withholding arrangement.
questions.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the clergy

questions.stem: A minister takes the standard deduction rather than itemizing. May a properly designated housing allowance still be kept out of income?
options: No; it is an itemized deduction
Yes; § 107 is an exclusion from gross income, available whether or not the minister itemizes
Only if the minister files Schedule A
Only up to the amount of the standard deduction
questions.explanation: IRC § 107 operates as an exclusion from gross income rather than a deduction, so it is available whether or not the minister itemizes and appears as a deduction nowhere on the return.
questions.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the clergy

questions.stem: A member serves for three months at a base abroad under sustained hostile fire, but the President has issued no Executive order designating the area a combat zone. Is the pay excluded under § 112?
options: Yes; the danger is what qualifies the service
No; without an Executive order there is no combat zone
Yes, but only for enlisted members
Yes, for the months in which fire was actually received
questions.explanation: IRC § 112(c)(2), (3): a combat zone exists only where the President designates one by Executive order, and service counts only between the Executive-order dates for the commencement and termination of combatant activities. Danger is not the test.
questions.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the military

questions.stem: A member leaves a combat zone on 1 March 2026 with no hospitalization. For how long after that are her filing and payment deadlines, and the Service's assessment and collection deadlines, disregarded?
options: 180 days after 1 March
Until the following 15 April only
180 days for her deadlines, but the Service's run normally
Until the end of the calendar year
questions.explanation: IRC § 7508(a) disregards the period of service plus 180 days for filing, payment, assessment, collection, refund claims and Tax Court petitions alike — the Service's clock stops as well as the taxpayer's.
questions.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the military

questions.stem: A member first served in a combat zone in 2024 and dies there in active service in 2026. For which years is income tax forgiven?
options: 2026 only
2026 and any earlier year ending on or after the first day of combat zone service, with tax already assessed abated
Only the months of combat zone service
None; § 692 only suspends deadlines
questions.explanation: IRC § 692(a): no income tax applies for the year of death or for any earlier year ending on or after the first day of combat zone service, and § 692(a)(2) abates tax already assessed for those earlier years.
questions.pageTitle: Tax provisions for members of the military

questions.stem: An estate holds the right to a decedent's unpaid $12,000 commission, distributes that right to the residuary legatee, and the payer then pays the legatee. Who reports the $12,000?
options: The estate, on Form 1041
The decedent, on the final Form 1040
The legatee
Half each to the estate and the legatee
questions.explanation: IRC § 691(a)(1)(A)–(C) runs in sequence — the estate, the person acquiring the right by reason of the death, or the legatee where the estate has already distributed the right — and only one limb applies to any item; here the estate distributed the right before collection.

questions.stem: A homeowner receives an offer on her house but dies before signing any contract. The executor negotiates and closes the sale after death at a gain. Is the gain income in respect of a decedent?
options: Yes, because the sale was in progress at death
No; the decedent held no enforceable right at death, so § 1014(a) gives a date-of-death basis
Yes, to the extent of the offer price
No, because an estate can never have income in respect of a decedent
