questions.explanation: With only a listing and an unsigned offer, no right to any amount existed at death, so the gain is not income in respect of a decedent; IRC § 1014(a) applies and the step-up shelters the pre-death appreciation. A binding contract signed before death would flip the result.

questions.stem: A beneficiary receives $80,000 from an inherited traditional individual retirement account. The estate was well below the exemption and paid no federal estate tax. What § 691(c) deduction is available?
options: The estate tax that would have been due at the highest rate
None
An amount equal to the income tax on the $80,000
40 percent of $80,000
questions.explanation: IRC § 691(c) gives a deduction for the federal estate tax attributable to the item; with no federal estate tax paid there is nothing to deduct, however large the item.

questions.stem: A trustee asks how the net investment income tax on $50,000 of a complex trust's undistributed dividends could have been avoided for 2026. Which is correct?
options: Nothing; trusts are outside the tax
Distributing the income to a beneficiary whose own modified adjusted gross income is below the individual threshold
Electing to be taxed at the individual thresholds
Holding the dividends in a money market fund instead
questions.explanation: IRC § 1411(a)(2) taxes a trust on the lesser of undistributed net investment income or adjusted gross income over the start of the highest § 1(e) bracket — a far lower threshold than an individual's — so income carried out to a beneficiary below $200,000 bears no net investment income tax at all.

questions.stem: A retiree with modified adjusted gross income well above the threshold receives $15,000 of municipal bond interest. How much of it is net investment income?
options: The lesser of $15,000 and the excess over the threshold
None
Half, because it is tax-exempt
questions.explanation: Tax-exempt interest is not gross income, so it never reaches the IRC § 1411(c)(1) definition of net investment income and escapes both this tax and the income tax.

questions.stem: An active sole proprietor who materially participates earns $6,000 of interest on the business's working capital held in a bank account. Is that interest net investment income?
options: No; it arises in an active trade or business
Yes; income from investing working capital is not treated as derived in the ordinary course of the business
No; it is self-employment income
Only if the business is a trading business
questions.explanation: IRC § 1411(c)(3) applies a rule similar to § 469(e)(1)(B): income from investing working capital is not treated as derived in the ordinary course of the trade or business, so it is net investment income even where the business itself is active.

questions.stem: An employer withholds additional Medicare tax from an employee's wages above the withholding trigger. What is the employer's own liability for this tax?
options: A matching 0.9 percent
A matching 1.45 percent
Nothing
Half of the amount withheld
questions.explanation: IRC § 3101(b)(2) imposes the tax on the employee alone; the employer withholds and remits but pays nothing of its own, unlike the ordinary 1.45 percent hospital insurance tax, which has an employer match.

questions.stem: Bianca earns $230,000 of wages; her husband earns nothing. They file jointly. Her employer withholds additional Medicare tax of $270 on her wages above $200,000. What happens on the return?
options: The $270 withheld is the liability and nothing more is due
The $270 is refunded, because combined wages are below the joint threshold
They owe a further $180 on the joint threshold
The withheld amount is kept as the employer's share
questions.explanation: IRC § 3102(f)(1) makes the employer withhold on its own wages above $200,000, but the couple's liability is measured against the $250,000 joint threshold, which $230,000 does not reach; the $270 is credited against a liability of zero and comes back as an overpayment.

questions.stem: A self-employed consultant has net self-employment income well above the threshold and no investment income. How do the additional Medicare tax and the net investment income tax interact on that income?
options: Both apply, since the thresholds are the same
Only the additional Medicare tax applies; the same dollar is never in both
Only the net investment income tax applies to self-employment income
The taxpayer elects which one applies
questions.explanation: IRC § 1411(c)(6) keeps the same dollar out of both taxes: this tax reaches earned income under § 1401(b)(2), while § 1411 reaches investment income, and the two share only their threshold figures.

questions.stem: A sommelier receives $600 of cash tips in a month and, separately, two bottles of wine from a regular customer. What is subject to social security and Medicare tax?
options: The cash and the value of the wine
The cash tips only
The wine only
Neither, because tips are not wages
questions.explanation: IRC § 3121(a)(12)(A): tips paid in any medium other than cash are never wages, so the wine produces income tax but no FICA; the cash tips are wages and reportable under § 6053(a).
questions.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

questions.stem: A server receives $900 of cash tips in March and furnishes the written statement to her employer on 8 April. When are the tips deemed paid for employment tax purposes?
options: When received in March
On 8 April, when the statement was furnished
On 10 April, the statutory deadline
On the next regular payday
questions.explanation: IRC § 3121(q): reported tips are deemed paid at the time the written statement is furnished to the employer; only where no statement is furnished are they deemed paid when received. That date starts the employer's collection window.
questions.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

questions.stem: A retired employee remains covered under her former employer's group-term life policy well above $50,000 of coverage. How does the social security and Medicare tax on the cost of the excess reach her?
options: It is withheld from her pension
As codes A and B in box 12, added to tax
As codes M and N in box 12, added to her own tax because there are no wages to withhold from
It does not apply to a former employee
questions.explanation: IRC § 79(a) includes the cost of coverage above $50,000 in gross income; with no wages from which to withhold, the employer reports the uncollected tax as codes M and N in box 12 and the individual pays it on the return. Codes A and B are for tips.
questions.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

questions.stem: A couple with $1,800 of unrecaptured 2008 first-time homebuyer credit sell the home to their daughter in 2026 for $3,000 less than their adjusted basis. What is added to their 2026 tax?
options: Nothing, because there was no gain
questions.explanation: IRC § 36(f)(2) accelerates the unrecaptured balance on disposition, and the § 36(f)(3) gain cap applies only to a sale to an unrelated person — a sale to a daughter is not that, so the full $1,800 is due regardless of the price.

questions.stem: An individual elected under § 965(h) to pay the transition tax in instalments and is now paying the eighth and final one. What percentage of the net tax liability is it?
options: 8 percent
12.5 percent
15 percent
25 percent
questions.explanation: IRC § 965(h): the instalments are not equal — they rise from 8 percent in the early years to 25 percent in the eighth — so a taxpayer who budgeted the first year's figure will be short.

questions.stem: Nadia, 41, withdraws $20,000 from a traditional individual retirement account to pay for a holiday. The whole amount is includible in gross income and no § 72(t)(2) exception applies. What additional tax is due?
options: Nothing, because income tax is already paid on it
questions.explanation: IRC § 72(t): 10 percent of the portion of an early distribution includible in gross income, on top of the income tax, where none of the § 72(t)(2) exceptions fits — $2,000 here. The 25 percent figure belongs to § 4974 and the 6 percent figure to § 4973.

questions.stem: A small corporation pays a shareholder $2,500 in dividends during 2026, an amount above the § 6041 threshold. Must it file an information return under § 6041?
options: Yes, because the payment exceeds the threshold and was made in the course of a trade or business
No, because dividends are reported under § 6042 and § 6041 excludes payments covered by another reporting section
Yes, but only if the shareholder is an individual rather than a corporation
No, because dividends are never subject to information reporting
questions.explanation: IRC § 6041(a): payments already covered by another reporting section, such as dividends under § 6042, patronage dividends under § 6044, interest under § 6049 and broker transactions under § 6045, are excluded to prevent duplicate reporting. The corporation's obligation, if any, runs through the dividend rules, and the size of the payment was never the issue.

questions.stem: A business with a fiscal year ending 30 June pays an unincorporated contractor throughout 2026. Over which period does § 6041(a) now measure the payments against the threshold?
options: The payer's taxable year, so the fiscal year controls
The calendar year, following the wording change made by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70433
Either period, at the payer's election
The recipient's taxable year
questions.explanation: Pub. L. 119-21 § 70433 substituted "calendar year" for "taxable year" in § 6041(a), so a fiscal-year business tests its payments on the calendar year like everyone else. The same section raised the threshold and added § 6041(h) to index it.

questions.stem: A payment app processes exactly 200 transactions for a seller in 2026, totaling $25,000. Is a Form 1099-K required?
options: Yes, because the dollar amount alone is well past its threshold
Yes, because both tests are satisfied once the count reaches 200
No, because § 6050W(e) requires more than 200 transactions and exactly 200 does not satisfy it
No, because the dollar test has not been met
questions.explanation: IRC § 6050W(e) as restored by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70432 requires more than $20,000 of payments and more than 200 transactions. The dollar test is met, but exactly 200 is not "more than" 200, so a single additional transaction, not a single additional dollar, is what would change the answer.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's net capital gain for the year includes unrecaptured section 1250 gain, collectibles gain and gain on listed stock held three years, and she also received qualified dividends. Which of these amounts are taxed on the zero, 15 and 20 percent ladder?
options: All of the net capital gain, with the qualified dividends taxed at ordinary rates
The stock gain and the qualified dividends, after the unrecaptured section 1250 gain and the 28-percent rate gain are carved out
Only the stock gain
The stock gain and the collectibles gain, with the unrecaptured section 1250 gain taxed as ordinary income
questions.explanation: IRC § 1(h)(3): adjusted net capital gain is net capital gain reduced by unrecaptured section 1250 gain and 28-percent rate gain, plus qualified dividend income. The two special categories come out first, and only the residual gets the zero, 15 and 20 percent ladder.

questions.stem: A taxpayer whose income is above the § 1411 threshold sells a passive rental building at a gain that includes $70,000 of straight-line depreciation. What does the net investment income tax do to the rates on the sale?
options: Nothing, because gain on real property is outside the net investment income tax
It applies only to the unrecaptured section 1250 portion of the gain
It adds 3.8 percent to every layer of the gain, the 25 percent portion and the 15 or 20 percent portion alike
It raises the 20 percent rate to 23.8 percent but leaves the 25 percent layer untouched
questions.explanation: IRC § 1411(c)(1)(A)(iii): gain on the sale of property not held in a non-passive trade or business is net investment income, so for a client above the threshold every rate quoted on the sale is effectively 3.8 points higher. The combined figure, not the headline one, is the number to give the client.

questions.stem: A client holds a painting for investment and wants to exchange it for another painting of equal value, deferring the gain under § 1031. Is the deferral available in 2026?
options: Yes, because both paintings are held for investment
Yes, provided the two paintings are of like kind within the § 408(m) definition
No, because since 2018 § 1031 reaches only real property
No, because a collectible can never be exchanged without recognising gain at ordinary rates
questions.explanation: Section 1031 has reached only real property since 2018, so a client planning to exchange business equipment or artwork cannot defer the gain that way. The gain is recognised and, as collectibles gain, is 28-percent rate gain under § 1(h)(4).

questions.stem: In September 2025 a family took a $3,000 distribution from their son's § 529 account to buy curriculum materials for his secondary school. Does the distribution qualify?
options: Yes, the widened list of school expenses applies to distributions made after 4 July 2025
No, only tuition qualified at that level until taxable years beginning after 2025
Yes, but only if tuition was also paid in the same year
No, curriculum materials never qualify at the elementary and secondary level
questions.explanation: Pub. L. 119-21 § 70413(a) rewrote IRC § 529(c)(7) for distributions made after 4 July 2025, the date of enactment, so the September 2025 distribution draws on the wider expense list while remaining subject to that year's older dollar limit.

questions.stem: A grandfather sends a $1,500 cash contribution to his grandson's Coverdell account. The grandson turned 18 three weeks earlier. What happens?
options: It is accepted; the age limit applies only to distributions
It cannot be accepted, because no contribution may be made after the beneficiary reaches 18
It is accepted because it is in cash and below the annual cap
It is accepted if the grandson consents in writing
questions.explanation: IRC § 530(b)(1)(A)(iii) bars any contribution to a Coverdell account after the beneficiary attains age 18; a § 529 account, which has no such age limit, would have been the right vehicle.

questions.stem: A client takes the standard deduction and paid interest on a qualified education loan during 2026. His income is below the phase-out range. May he deduct the interest?
options: No, because he does not itemize
Yes, as an above-the-line deduction, up to the annual maximum
Only as a miscellaneous itemized deduction, which is currently disallowed
Only if his employer reimburses it under a § 127 programme
questions.explanation: IRC § 221 provides an above-the-line deduction, so it is available without itemising and survives the disallowance of miscellaneous itemized deductions, subject to the annual maximum and the 2026 phase-out.

questions.stem: A decedent dying in 2026 leaves a traditional IRA worth $600,000 to her daughter. What basis does the daughter take in the account?
options: Fair market value at death, like other inherited property
No step-up; the account passes with whatever basis the decedent had in it
The decedent's basis under § 1015, as if acquired by gift
Fair market value, but only if an estate tax return was filed
questions.explanation: IRC § 1014(c) excludes a right to receive an item of income in respect of a decedent from the fresh-basis rule, so a retirement account passes with the decedent's own basis rather than a basis stepped up to fair market value.

questions.stem: A single, never-married decedent dies in 2026 having made no lifetime gifts, with an estate that exceeds the basic exclusion amount by $600,000. How much of the estate is subject to estate tax?
options: The entire estate, because crossing the exclusion makes the whole estate taxable
$600,000, the excess over the basic exclusion amount only
Nothing, because a single decedent's estate is sheltered up to twice the exclusion
The whole estate less one annual exclusion
questions.explanation: IRC § 2010(c)(3) sets the basic exclusion amount, and it works as a threshold rather than a cliff: only the excess above it is subject to estate tax, and the assets passing to heirs still take a § 1014(a) basis.

questions.stem: A husband dies in 2026 leaving a $6,000,000 estate entirely to his wife, and his executor files a timely, complete estate tax return electing portability. What exclusion does the wife's own estate later have?
options: Her own basic exclusion amount only
Her own basic exclusion amount plus his deceased spousal unused exclusion amount
Exactly twice her own basic exclusion amount, whether or not the election was made
His unused exclusion amount in place of her own
questions.explanation: IRC § 2010(c)(2): a surviving spouse's applicable exclusion amount is her own basic exclusion amount plus the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount, which the timely election under § 2010(c)(5)(A) preserves — for a married couple the effective figure is twice the single exclusion.

questions.stem: Priya, aged 75, still works for the company that sponsors her 401(k) and has been deferring required distributions under the still-working exception while owning 4.5 percent of it. A stock grant this year takes her holding to 5.2 percent. What is the effect?
options: None, because the still-working exception continues until she actually retires
The exception is lost, and her required beginning date is fixed by the applicable age regardless of when she retires
She must begin distributions from the 401(k) but may keep deferring on any IRA she holds
The exception is lost only once her holding reaches 10 percent
questions.explanation: IRC § 401(a)(9)(C)(ii) denies the still-working deferral to a 5-percent owner, so once ownership exceeds 5 percent the required beginning date is set by the applicable age alone. The retirement limb never applied to an IRA in the first place.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old client asks her IRA trustee to send $10,000 directly to a donor advised fund she maintains at a community foundation. Is the transfer a qualified charitable distribution?
options: Yes, because she is past 70½ and the money went directly from the trustee
No, because she has not yet reached the applicable age for required distributions
No, because a donor advised fund is not a permitted recipient
Yes, but only up to her required minimum distribution for the year
questions.explanation: IRC § 408(d)(8)(B)(i): the distribution must go to an organization described in § 170(b)(1)(A) other than a supporting organization or a donor advised fund. Her age is not the obstacle, since the test is 70½ under § 408(d)(8)(B)(ii), not the required beginning date.

questions.stem: A client will turn 74 in 2034. She is not a 5-percent owner and holds only a traditional IRA. What is her applicable age for required distributions?
questions.explanation: IRC § 401(a)(9)(C)(v): the applicable age is 73 for an individual attaining 72 after 2022 and 73 before 2033, and 75 for one attaining 74 after 2032. A source giving 70½ predates 2019 and one giving 72 predates 2023; 70½ survives only as the qualified charitable distribution age in § 408(d)(8)(B)(ii).

questions.stem: A 2016 divorce decree requires monthly alimony. In 2026 the parties sign a modification reducing the amount, and the modification says nothing about the alimony rules. How are payments made after the modification treated?
options: Neither deductible nor includible, because any post-2018 modification brings the instrument under the current rules
Still deductible by the payer and includible by the recipient, because the modification did not expressly adopt the repeal
Deductible by the payer but no longer includible by the recipient
Includible by the recipient but no longer deductible by the payer
questions.explanation: Pub. L. 115-97 § 11051: a pre-2019 instrument keeps the old treatment unless it is modified after 2018 and the modification expressly provides that the repeal applies. The election is express, not automatic, so a silent modification leaves the old regime in place.

questions.stem: Divorced parents share custody, and their daughter lives with her mother for 220 nights a year. The mother signs Form 8332 releasing the claim to the father for the year. Which benefit moves to the father?
options: Head of household filing status
The earned income credit
The child tax credit
The child and dependent care credit
questions.explanation: IRC § 152(e): the custodial parent's release lets the noncustodial parent claim the dependency-linked benefits, the child tax credit and the education credits, but head of household status, the earned income credit and the dependent care credit stay with the parent the child actually lived with.

questions.stem: A divorce becomes final on 1 March 2026. Under the property settlement, one former spouse transfers a rental property to the other on 15 September 2026. Does § 1041 apply to the transfer?
options: No, because § 1041 covers only transfers made while the parties are still married
Yes, because a transfer within one year after the marriage ceases is incident to the divorce
Only if the transfer is also shown to be related to the cessation of the marriage
No, so the recipient recognises gain equal to the property's appreciation
questions.explanation: IRC § 1041(c)(1), (2): a transfer is incident to the divorce if it occurs within one year after the marriage ceases or is related to the cessation of the marriage. The two limbs are alternatives, so the September transfer qualifies on timing alone; no gain or loss is recognised and the recipient takes the transferor's basis under § 1041(b)(2).

questions.stem: A married taxpayer filing a separate return has a $9,000 net capital loss and no capital gains this year. Her spouse, also filing separately, has no capital transactions at all. How much of the loss may she deduct against ordinary income this year?
options: $3,000, the full annual allowance
$1,500, because the allowance is halved on a separate return
$9,000, because her spouse has no gains to absorb it
Nothing, because capital losses offset only capital gains
questions.explanation: IRC § 1211(b): the annual allowance against ordinary income is $3,000, or $1,500 for a married individual filing separately, and the remaining $7,500 carries forward subject to the same halved limit for each year the couple continues to file separately.
questions.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

questions.stem: A client owns two rental properties, each a separate passive activity, with $12,000 of suspended losses on the first and $9,000 on the second. This year she sells her entire interest in the first in a fully taxable sale. Which suspended losses are released?
options: Both, because disposing of any passive activity frees all suspended passive losses
Only the $12,000 from the property she sold
Neither, because suspended losses are released only when every passive activity has been disposed of
Half of each, prorated between the two activities
questions.explanation: IRC § 469(b), (g): a disallowed passive loss is allocable to the same activity in the next taxable year and is released on a fully taxable disposition of the entire interest in that activity. The carryover is tracked per activity, so disposing of one rental does not free the losses suspended on another.
questions.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

questions.stem: An individual has a general business credit for 2026 that exceeds the tax it can offset. How is the unused credit carried?
options: Forward indefinitely, with no carryback
Back two years and forward twenty
Back one year and forward twenty
Back five years and forward indefinitely
questions.explanation: IRC § 39(a): an unused general business credit is carried back one year and forward twenty. The two-year carryback belonged to pre-2018 net operating losses, and the five-year carryback was the temporary § 172(b)(1)(D) window for losses arising in 2018 through 2020, which has closed.
questions.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

questions.stem: A wife wants to be relieved of a deficiency assessed on a prior joint return, all of it attributable to her husband's unreported income. Which route applies?
options: An injured spouse allocation on Form 8379
A request for relief from joint and several liability under § 6015 on Form 8857
Either form, at her election
Form 8379 first, then Form 8857 if it is denied
questions.explanation: Relief under § 6015 on Form 8857 is relief from a liability, which is what she needs; an injured spouse claim under § 6402 allocates a refund taken for the other spouse's separate debt and does nothing about a liability she owes under § 6013(d)(3).

questions.stem: A joint refund was offset in March 2024 for the husband's pre-marital debt. The wife never filed Form 8379 and files it alone in September 2026. Is the claim in time?
options: No; a two-year deadline runs from the offset, as under § 6015
Yes, if it falls within the ordinary refund claim period under § 6511
No; the allocation can only be filed with the original return
Yes, but only if the husband also signs it
questions.explanation: The claim is governed by the ordinary refund claim rules in § 6511: an injured spouse allocation has no two-year limit of its own like § 6015's, it may be filed on its own after the offset, and the debtor spouse's signature is not required.

questions.stem: A couple's joint refund is taken for the wife's unpaid state income tax from a year before the marriage. Is the husband an injured spouse?
options: Yes; a past-due state income tax obligation is one of the offsets that trigger the allocation
No; only debts to federal agencies can offset a federal refund
No; a state debt is collected by the state, not through the refund
Yes, but only in a community property state
questions.explanation: IRC § 6402(e) authorises the offset of a refund for a past-due state income tax obligation, one of the four categories in § 6402(c) to (f), and the debt is the wife's alone, so his share of the overpayment is recoverable on Form 8379.

questions.stem: A deficiency on a joint return is attributable entirely to the husband's erroneous items. The couple are still married and living together. May the wife elect separate allocation under § 6015(c)?
options: Yes, allocation is available to any joint filer
No; the election needs divorce, legal separation, or twelve months in separate households ending on the election date
Yes, but only if the husband consents
No, because § 6015(c) applies only to unpaid liabilities
questions.explanation: IRC § 6015(c)(3)(A) limits the election to a spouse no longer married to, or legally separated from, the other, or not a member of the same household at any time in the twelve months ending on the election date; a couple living together are left to § 6015(b) or (f).

questions.stem: A divorced taxpayer validly elects allocation under § 6015(c). The Secretary proves she had actual knowledge, when signing, of $20,000 of the $60,000 of income her ex-husband omitted. What is the effect?
options: The whole election is invalid
The election is invalid as to the $20,000 item only
None; knowledge is irrelevant under § 6015(c)
The election is invalid unless she proves she lacked reason to know of the remaining $40,000
questions.explanation: IRC § 6015(c)(3)(C) makes the election invalid as to any item of which the Secretary shows the electing spouse had actual knowledge when signing; the burden is on the Secretary, and only that item is affected.

questions.stem: Three years ago a taxpayer paid in full a joint liability that was correctly reported but attributable to her former husband. She now seeks equitable relief and a refund under § 6015(f). What deadline applies?
options: Two years from the start of collection activity
Any time before the § 6502 collection period expires
Within the period for a timely refund claim, because the amount has been paid
There is no deadline for equitable relief
questions.explanation: IRC § 6015(f)(2): a request as to an unpaid amount may be made before the § 6502 collection period expires, but as to a paid amount within the period for a timely refund claim — and the refund itself is subject to § 6511.

questions.stem: A self-employed client is in her first profitable year and expects $14,000 of tax. She had no tax liability for the preceding year, which was a full twelve months, and was a citizen throughout it. Must she pay estimated tax to avoid the addition?
options: Yes, because her current-year tax is well above the de minimis amount
No; with no prior-year liability, a full twelve-month prior year and citizenship throughout, no addition applies whatever this year's tax
Only if she cannot meet the 90 percent test
Yes, unless she files and pays by 31 January
questions.explanation: IRC § 6654(e)(2): no addition to tax where the preceding taxable year was a full 12 months, the individual had no tax liability for it, and the individual was a citizen or resident throughout it — the three conditions are cumulative, and she meets all three.
questions.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

questions.stem: A taxpayer's 2026 return shows total tax of $9,400. Withholding was $8,700 and he made no estimated payments. Is an addition to tax imposed?
options: No; the tax shown, reduced by withholding, is below the de minimis amount
Yes, computed on the full $9,400
Yes, computed on the $700 balance
No, but only if he also met the prior-year harbour
questions.explanation: IRC § 6654(e)(1): no addition applies where the tax shown on the return, reduced by the credit for tax withheld, is less than the de minimis figure; his $700 balance is under it, and the test runs against tax net of withholding rather than gross tax.
questions.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

questions.stem: A client elects on her 2025 return to have her $4,000 overpayment applied to her 2026 estimated tax. How is that amount credited against the 2026 installments?
options: As an estimated tax payment on the first installment due date
In four equal parts on each due date, like withholding
On the date the 2025 return was filed
Against the fourth installment only
questions.explanation: IRC § 6402(b): an overpayment of the preceding year's income tax may be credited against the current year's estimated tax; the amount is treated as an estimated tax payment and lands on the first installment date, which is why crediting forward is a clean way to cover the first quarter.
questions.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

questions.stem: A cash-method client charges a $3,200 deductible medical bill to her credit card on 30 December and pays the card issuer on 25 January. In which year is the expense treated as paid?
options: The year the card was charged
The year the card issuer was paid
Neither year, because borrowed funds are not payment
Half in each year
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.461-1(a)(1): deductions are taken in the year paid, and payment by credit card is made when the card is charged because the issuer has paid the payee; her later debt to the card issuer is a separate matter and is not deductible.
questions.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

questions.stem: A client carries a large nonrefundable credit into a year in which his regular tax will be very small. Which year-end move actually preserves the credit's value?
options: Deferring income into the following year
Accelerating income into the current year so there is tax for the credit to reduce
Claiming the unused portion as a refund
Electing to itemize instead of taking the standard deduction
questions.explanation: IRC § 26(a) caps the nonrefundable credits at regular tax liability, so a year with too little tax wastes them; this is the one situation where the standard advice to defer income runs backwards.
questions.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

questions.stem: A married couple give $9,000 to charity and pay $6,000 of deductible state taxes each year, and cannot clear the standard deduction in either year. They make two years of gifts in December 2026. What makes this bunching work?
options: Excess charitable gifts carry forward automatically to fill the next year
Itemizing is an annual election, so they itemize for 2026 and take the standard deduction for 2027
The standard deduction is reduced by charitable gifts made in the year
Deductions may be averaged across two consecutive years
questions.explanation: IRC § 63(e): no itemized deduction is allowed unless the individual elects to itemize on the return, and the election is made year by year, so a year of large deductions next to a year of none is worth more than two average years.
questions.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

questions.stem: A sole proprietor sells equipment for $92,000. Cost was $80,000 and depreciation taken was $50,000. How is the $62,000 gain characterised?
options: $62,000 ordinary income
$50,000 ordinary income and $12,000 section 1231 gain
$12,000 ordinary income and $50,000 section 1231 gain
$62,000 long-term capital gain
questions.explanation: IRC § 1245(a): recomputed basis is $80,000, the amount realised is $92,000, and ordinary income is the lower of the two ($80,000) less the $30,000 adjusted basis, or $50,000 — the whole of the depreciation taken; the remaining $12,000 of gain is section 1231 gain.
questions.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

questions.stem: A landlord sells an office building held twelve years at a $350,000 gain, having taken $200,000 of straight-line depreciation. How is the $200,000 attributable to depreciation treated?
options: Ordinary income recaptured under section 1250
Unrecaptured section 1250 gain, taxed at a maximum of 25 percent
Long-term capital gain at the 20 percent rate
Ordinary income recaptured under section 1245
questions.explanation: IRC § 1(h)(1)(D): straight-line depreciation produces no additional depreciation for section 1250 to recapture, so the gain instead falls into the 25 percent unrecaptured section 1250 gain bucket — a rate ceiling on capital gain, not a recharacterisation.
questions.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

questions.stem: A client acquired qualified small business stock in October 2025 and sells it in December 2028, after just over three years, at a $2,000,000 gain that is within the per-issuer limit. How much is excluded?
options: Nothing, because the holding period must exceed five years
questions.explanation: IRC § 1202(a)(5): for stock acquired after 4 July 2025 the applicable percentage is 50 percent at three years, 75 at four and 100 at five or more, so three years held excludes half the gain.
questions.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

questions.stem: A married couple live together all year and file separate returns. The wife has earned income within the credit range and a qualifying child who lives with her. What earned income credit may she claim?
options: The full credit on her own return
Half the credit a joint return would have produced
None, because the credit is allowed to a married individual only on a joint return
The full credit, provided her husband does not also claim the child
questions.explanation: IRC § 32(d)(1) makes the earned income credit unavailable on a separate return; it is denied outright rather than reduced, unless the taxpayer meets the narrower separated-spouse rule in § 32(d)(2)(B), which a couple living together cannot.
questions.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

questions.stem: A married woman has lived apart from her husband since February, files a separate return, and pays the whole cost of the home she shares all year with her dependent mother. May she file as head of household?
options: Yes, she is considered unmarried under § 7703(b)
No, the qualifying individual for the considered-unmarried test must be a child
No, a married person can never file as head of household
Yes, because her husband was absent for the last six months of the year
questions.explanation: IRC § 7703(b) requires a household that is the principal place of abode of a child; a qualifying relative who is not a child does not satisfy that condition, so she remains married and her choices are joint or separate.
questions.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

questions.stem: A couple who live together all year file separate returns. The husband actively participates in a rental activity that produces a $9,000 loss. How much of the rental real estate special allowance may he use?
options: The full allowance available on a joint return
Half the allowance, with a halved phase-out range
None; the allowance is denied entirely to a separate filer who did not live apart from the spouse at all times
The $9,000 loss in full, because the allowance is not limited on a separate return
questions.explanation: IRC § 469(i)(5) halves the allowance and its phase-out range only for a married individual filing separately who lives apart from the spouse at all times during the year, and denies it entirely to one who does not.
questions.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid foreign income taxes in 2019 and filed her 2019 return on time. In 2026 she discovers she under-claimed the foreign tax credit for that year. Is a refund claim still possible?
options: No, the ordinary three-year period closed in 2023
Yes, a ten-year period runs from the due date of the return for the year the foreign tax was paid or accrued
Yes, a seven-year period applies
Only if she was financially disabled
questions.explanation: IRC § 6511(d)(3)(A) substitutes 10 years from the date prescribed for filing the return for the year in which the foreign taxes were actually paid or accrued, in place of the ordinary period.
questions.pageTitle: Conditions for filing a claim for refund (amended returns)

questions.stem: A taxpayer's timely refund claim for 2023 is allowed in the amount of $4,000. She also owes $2,500 of assessed income tax for 2021. What does she receive?
options: $4,000, because the 2021 balance must be collected separately
$1,500, after the overpayment is credited against the 2021 liability
Nothing until the 2021 year is resolved
$4,000, provided she files an injured spouse allocation
questions.explanation: IRC § 6402(a) lets the Secretary credit an overpayment against any liability for internal revenue tax of the person who made it and refund only the balance; the § 6402(c) to (f) offsets for other debts come after that.
questions.pageTitle: Conditions for filing a claim for refund (amended returns)

questions.stem: A taxpayer lives in an area given a postponement period under a federal disaster declaration. Her refund claim is timely, but the look-back window would otherwise cap the refund at nothing. What is the effect of the postponement?
options: None; postponements reach only filing and payment deadlines
The postponement period is also disregarded in determining the amount of any credit or refund
It converts the two-year look-back into a three-year one
It applies only to combat-zone service, not to disasters
questions.explanation: IRC § 7508A(a)(3) reaches "the amount of any credit or refund" and not merely the filing act, so a disaster postponement can preserve a claim that the ordinary look-back would have capped at nothing.
questions.pageTitle: Conditions for filing a claim for refund (amended returns)

questions.stem: An individual is convicted under IRC § 7206(1). The section itself prints a maximum fine of $100,000. What is the default statutory maximum fine under 18 U.S.C. § 3571(b)(3), which supersedes that printed figure?
options: $100,000, because the Code section controls its own penalty
$250,000, the felony maximum for an individual under § 3571(b)(3)
$500,000, the figure printed for organizations
No fine at all, because the section provides only for imprisonment
questions.explanation: 18 U.S.C. § 3571(b)(3): an individual convicted of a felony may be fined up to $250,000, and § 3571(e) preserves a lower statutory figure only where the offence provision exempts itself by specific reference, which § 7206 does not do. The same is true of § 7201.

questions.stem: Which element must the government prove for evasion under IRC § 7201 that it need not prove for the false-return offence under IRC § 7206(1)?
options: A signed document verified by a penalties-of-perjury declaration
An affirmative act of evasion and a tax owing
Willfulness
A false statement about a material matter
questions.explanation: IRC § 7201 requires an affirmative act of evasion and an unpaid tax; § 7206(1) requires a willfully signed false document and no deficiency at all. Willfulness is an element of both, and neither offence is a lesser included version of the other.

questions.stem: A client took a home office deduction on her preparer's advice that a guest room used a few evenings a week for client calls qualified. It did not, and the deduction is disallowed on audit. What is her exposure?
options: A § 7206(1) felony, because she signed a return that was wrong as to a material matter
The civil fraud penalty, because the deduction was disallowed in full
A civil adjustment only, because she was not willful
A § 7207 misdemeanor, because the return was false but no tax was evaded
questions.explanation: IRC § 7206(1) requires willfulness, the voluntary and intentional violation of a known legal duty, and reliance on a preparer's advice about a genuinely debatable position cuts against it. An honest but wrong position is a civil adjustment, with no § 6663 fraud penalty and no criminal referral.

questions.stem: What is the applicable credit amount that is subtracted in the final step of the estate tax computation?
options: The basic exclusion amount, subtracted from the gross estate before deductions
The tentative tax that the unified rate schedule would produce on the applicable exclusion amount
Forty percent of the taxable estate
The basic exclusion amount less the decedent's adjusted taxable gifts
questions.explanation: IRC § 2010(c)(1) defines the credit as the tentative tax that § 2001(c) would produce on the applicable exclusion amount; it is a credit against tax, not a dollar-for-dollar reduction of the estate, and describing it as a deduction gives the right answer only because the top bracket is flat.
questions.pageTitle: Gross estate, taxable estate (calculations and payments), unified credit, life insurance, and filing requirements

questions.stem: An unmarried decedent gave her niece $500,000 in cash in each of two years before her death and made no other lifetime gifts. In computing the tentative tax, what is added to the taxable estate as adjusted taxable gifts?
options: $1,000,000, the gross amount given
Each gift less the annual exclusion for the year it was made
Nothing, because lifetime gifts reduce the exclusion instead of enlarging the base
$1,000,000 less the basic exclusion amount
questions.explanation: IRC § 2001(b)(1)(B) adds post-1976 adjusted taxable gifts to the base, and adjusted taxable gifts are taxable gifts within the meaning of § 2503 — the annual exclusion comes off first, so using gross gifts is the trap the page warns against.
questions.pageTitle: Gross estate, taxable estate (calculations and payments), unified credit, life insurance, and filing requirements

questions.stem: An estate is illiquid because most of its value is an interest in a closely held business. Against what measure is the 35 percent test applied before the executor may elect under § 6166 to pay the attributable estate tax in installments?
options: The adjusted gross estate, so how administration expenses are claimed can affect whether the estate qualifies
The gross estate before any deductions
The taxable estate after the marital and charitable deductions
The sum of the taxable estate and adjusted taxable gifts
questions.explanation: IRC § 6166 measures the 35 percent test against the adjusted gross estate, which is why the page says the election is worth checking early — the way expenses are claimed can move the estate across the line.
questions.pageTitle: Gross estate, taxable estate (calculations and payments), unified credit, life insurance, and filing requirements

questions.stem: Three siblings inherit a farm from their mother as joint tenants with right of survivorship. None of them paid anything for it. The eldest dies. How much of the farm is in his gross estate?
options: Nothing, because he furnished no consideration
One-third, with no consideration tracing required or permitted
The whole value, unless the surviving siblings can prove their contributions
One-half
questions.explanation: Under the IRC § 2040(a) second proviso and Reg. § 20.2040-1(a)(1), where the joint interest was itself acquired by gift, devise, bequest or inheritance the decedent's fractional share is included and the consideration test never runs.

questions.stem: Two friends own a building as tenants in common, each holding an undivided one-half. One of them dies. What is included in her gross estate, and where does it go?
options: The whole value, less whatever the co-owner can prove she paid
One-half automatically, passing to the co-owner by survivorship
Her undivided one-half, passing under her will or intestacy rather than to the co-owner
Nothing, because a tenancy in common is outside the estate tax
questions.explanation: A tenancy in common has no right of survivorship, so § 2040 never applies; the decedent's fractional interest is in the gross estate under IRC § 2033 and passes by will or intestacy, not to the co-tenant.

questions.stem: Unmarried partners own a house as joint tenants. It cost $200,000 and is worth $1,000,000 when one dies. The survivor proves with bank records that she furnished 70 percent of the purchase price. What is her basis in the house after the death?
questions.explanation: Basis follows inclusion under IRC § 1014(b)(9): the 30 percent included in the gross estate takes a date-of-death basis of $300,000, while her excluded 70 percent keeps its original basis of $140,000, for $440,000 in total — the proof that kept value out of the estate also kept the old basis.

questions.stem: An executor elects to treat a trust paying all its income annually to the surviving spouse as qualified terminable interest property. What are the consequences?
options: The property is deductible now and is never subject to estate tax again
The property is deductible now and is included in the surviving spouse's gross estate at her death
The property is not deductible, because the spouse's interest terminates at death
Only one-half of the property is deductible
questions.explanation: Under IRC § 2056(b)(7) the executor's election treats the property as passing to the spouse, so it qualifies for the marital deduction in the first estate and is then in the survivor's gross estate at her death; the election can be partial and is made property by property.
questions.pageTitle: Marital deduction and other marital issues (e.g., portability election)

questions.stem: A husband who has no deceased spousal unused exclusion amount of his own dies in 2026, and his executor makes a timely portability election. The tentative tax on his estate was determined on $4,000,000. What is his widow's deceased spousal unused exclusion amount?
options: His basic exclusion amount less $4,000,000
Whatever remained after the deductions claimed on his return
Nil, because his estate paid no tax
questions.explanation: IRC § 2010(c)(4) defines the amount as the lesser of the basic exclusion amount or the last deceased spouse's applicable exclusion amount reduced by the amount on which the tentative tax was determined under § 2001(b)(1) — not simply whatever was left over.
questions.pageTitle: Marital deduction and other marital issues (e.g., portability election)

questions.stem: A widow's late husband died in 2026 and his estate made the portability election. She dies in 2036. The ordinary assessment period for his estate closed years ago. May the IRS still examine his return when auditing hers?
options: No; once the assessment period has run the first return is closed for every purpose
Yes, but only to the extent needed to determine the unused exclusion amount
Only if the first estate actually paid estate tax
Only within three years of her death
questions.explanation: IRC § 2010(c)(5)(B) lets the Secretary examine the deceased spouse's return to determine the unused exclusion amount notwithstanding § 6501, long after assessment against that estate is time-barred.
questions.pageTitle: Marital deduction and other marital issues (e.g., portability election)

questions.stem: A decedent owned a $1,000,000 policy on his own life, payable to his daughter, and retained the right to change the beneficiary until his death. How are the proceeds treated?
options: Excluded from the daughter's income and outside the gross estate, because she was the beneficiary
Excluded from the daughter's income but included in the gross estate
Taxable to the daughter as income and included in the gross estate
Taxable to the daughter as income but outside the gross estate
questions.explanation: IRC § 101(a) excludes proceeds paid by reason of death from gross income, while § 2042(2) includes proceeds receivable by anyone where the decedent held an incident of ownership at death — and the right to change the beneficiary is one; the two exclusions are different taxes and both apply here.
questions.pageTitle: Life insurance, IRAs and retirement plans

questions.stem: Ottilie inherits her father's IRA at age 12 and, as a minor child of the employee, takes distributions over her life expectancy. What happens when she reaches the age of majority?
options: Distributions continue over her life expectancy for the rest of her life
The remainder must be distributed within 10 years of the date she reaches majority
The remainder must be distributed within 10 years of her father's death
The whole account must be distributed immediately
questions.explanation: IRC § 401(a)(9)(E)(iii) ends the minor-child exception at majority and requires the remainder to be distributed within 10 years of that date, so the stretch runs for a few years and then converts to a deadline.
questions.pageTitle: Life insurance, IRAs and retirement plans

questions.stem: Estate tax was actually paid on a decedent's traditional IRA. The beneficiary now takes distributions and reports them as income in respect of a decedent. What relief is available to the beneficiary?
options: A basis step-up equal to the estate tax paid
An income tax deduction for the estate tax attributable to the account as it is drawn down
A credit against income tax equal to the estate tax paid
None; the estate's payment of the tax is final
questions.explanation: IRC § 691(c) allows the beneficiary a deduction for the estate tax attributable to the item, in the same ratio the item's estate tax value bears to all such items — frequently missed because the beneficiary receiving the Form 1099-R never sees the estate tax return.
questions.pageTitle: Life insurance, IRAs and retirement plans

questions.stem: A decedent whose gross estate exceeds the filing threshold dies on 20 February 2026. Absent an extension, when is Form 706 due?
options: 20 November 2026
15 April 2027
20 February 2027
15 June 2026
questions.explanation: IRC § 6075(a) sets the Form 706 due date at nine months after the date of death, and the estate tax is payable on that same date; the fourth-month rule in § 6072(a) governs Form 1041, not Form 706.
questions.pageTitle: Estate filing requirements and due dates (Form 706, Form 1041)

questions.stem: A decedent's assets were held in a revocable trust that became irrevocable at death, and an executor was appointed to probate the residue of the estate. Who must make the election that treats the trust as part of the estate for income tax purposes, and what is its effect?
options: The executor alone; the trust adopts the estate's fiscal year
The trustee alone; the trust files its own Form 1041 on a calendar year
Both the executor and the trustee; the trust is treated and taxed as part of the estate on one return
The residuary beneficiaries; the trust is disregarded entirely
questions.explanation: IRC § 645(a) requires both the executor and the trustee of the qualified revocable trust to elect, after which the trust is treated and taxed as part of the estate rather than as a separate trust — collapsing two returns into one and extending the estate's fiscal year advantage to the trust's income.
questions.pageTitle: Estate filing requirements and due dates (Form 706, Form 1041)

questions.stem: A domestic estate has gross income of $250 for its first taxable year. One of its three beneficiaries is a nonresident alien. Must the estate file Form 1041?
options: No; gross income is below the filing threshold
Yes; any beneficiary who is a nonresident alien triggers a return whatever the income
Only if the estate has positive taxable income
Only if the nonresident alien beneficiary actually received a distribution
questions.explanation: IRC § 6012(a)(5) requires a return from an estate with any nonresident alien beneficiary regardless of income, so the gross income test in § 6012(a)(3) is not the only route to a filing obligation.
questions.pageTitle: Estate filing requirements and due dates (Form 706, Form 1041)

questions.stem: A husband gives his niece $36,000 from an account in his sole name in 2026. His wife consents to split, and neither spouse has a taxable gift as a result. Must the husband file a gift tax return?
options: No; splitting leaves no taxable gift to report
No, provided the wife files a return signifying her consent
Yes; the gift he actually made exceeded one annual exclusion, and the consent is signified on the return
Yes, but only if the couple also made gifts to other donees
questions.explanation: IRC § 6019 keys off the transfer the donor actually made, before splitting, so a gift over one annual exclusion requires a return even where splitting produces no taxable gift, and the § 2513 consent has to be signified on a return in any event.

questions.stem: A United States citizen married to a non-resident alien gives $50,000 to her brother from her own funds. May the spouses split the gift?
options: Yes, if both sign the consent on her return
Yes, but only up to the special exclusion for gifts to a non-citizen spouse
No; each spouse must be a citizen or resident at the time of the gift
No, unless the husband files his own Form 709
questions.explanation: IRC § 2513(a)(1) permits splitting only where both spouses were citizens or residents of the United States at the time of the gift.

questions.stem: The husband filed his 2026 gift tax return on 10 April 2027 without any consent. On 20 April 2027 the couple sign a consent to split. Is it effective?
options: Yes; consent may be signified any time before the extended return due date
Yes; the wife has not yet filed, so the door remains open
No; consent may not be signified after 15 April unless neither spouse has filed by then
Yes, but it becomes irrevocable on signing
questions.explanation: IRC § 2513(b)(2)(A) closes the door on 15 April unless neither spouse has yet filed for the year; the husband's 10 April return means the exception is not available.

questions.stem: Rosalind, who is married, makes outright cash gifts to each of her four grandchildren in 2026, and her husband consents to split the gifts. How many annual exclusions are available for the year?
options: One, because the exclusion is an annual allowance for the donor
Four
Eight
Two
questions.explanation: IRC § 2503(b)(1) makes the exclusion per donee per calendar year, and under the gift-splitting rule in IRC § 2513(a)(1) each gift is treated as made one-half by each spouse — four donees times two donors gives eight exclusions.

questions.stem: In 2026 Ignatius contributes $95,000 to a qualified tuition program for his daughter and elects to spread the excess ratably over five years. In 2028 he gives her a $2,000 birthday cheque. What is the result?
options: The cheque is covered by that year's annual exclusion
The cheque is a taxable gift, because the exclusion for that year has already been committed to the contribution
The cheque is a qualified transfer and not a gift at all
The election is revoked and the whole contribution becomes taxable
questions.explanation: IRC § 529(c)(2)(B) takes the excess into account ratably over the five years beginning with the contribution year, so the daughter's annual exclusion for each of those years is already spoken for; the election buys front-loading, not extra exclusion.

questions.stem: Inflation rose during the year, yet the annual exclusion for the following year is unchanged. Which best explains this?
options: Congress must enact each increase separately
The figure is indexed but rounded down to the next lowest multiple of $1,000, so it can stand still
The exclusion is fixed at the figure printed in the statute
The exclusion moves only when the basic exclusion amount moves
questions.explanation: IRC § 2503(b)(2) indexes the exclusion from the statutory figure and rounds down to the next lowest multiple of $1,000, which is why it moves in whole thousands and can stand still for a year or more.

questions.stem: A client asks for the "lifetime gift tax exemption" as a figure separate from the estate tax exclusion. What is the correct response?
options: It is a separate amount fixed in IRC § 2503
There is no separate figure; the gift tax credit is measured by the applicable credit amount under an estate tax provision
It is half the basic exclusion amount
It is the annual exclusion multiplied by the number of donees
questions.explanation: IRC § 2505(a)(1) points at the applicable credit amount under § 2010(c), an estate tax provision; there is one credit shared by the two taxes, not two.

questions.stem: In computing this year's unified credit, a donor's credit allowable for gifts made in preceding calendar periods is determined at which rates?
options: The rates in force when each prior gift was made
The current year's rates
The rates expected to apply at death
An average of the rates over the prior periods
questions.explanation: The closing sentence of IRC § 2505(a) recomputes the credit allowed for preceding calendar periods at the current year's rates rather than the rates that applied when those gifts were made.

questions.stem: A client uses a large basic exclusion amount against lifetime gifts, and the exclusion in force at her death is later reduced by Congress. Which provision addresses the difference?
options: The ceiling that caps the credit at the year's tax
The direction to prescribe regulations dealing with any difference between the exclusion at death and the amount applicable to gifts already made
The gross-up of gift tax paid within three years of death
The portability election for a surviving spouse
questions.explanation: IRC § 2001(g)(2) is the statutory direction that handles the clawback problem; with the higher figure now permanent the problem has receded, but a future reduction would revive it immediately.

questions.stem: A donor whose credit is exhausted gives her daughter $4,000,000 and dies five years later. In computing her estate tax, what happens to the gift?
options: Nothing; a completed gift is outside the estate
The $4,000,000 is added to the estate tax base as an adjusted taxable gift, though the growth on it since the gift is not
The gift plus its appreciation to the date of death is included in the gross estate
The gift tax she paid on it is added to the gross estate under the three-year rule
questions.explanation: IRC § 2001(b)(1)(B) brings a taxable gift back into the estate tax base as an adjusted taxable gift; a gift removes future growth from the estate, not the gift itself, and the § 2035(b) gross-up does not apply because she survived three years.
questions.pageTitle: Effect on estate tax (e.g., Generation skipping transfer tax)

questions.stem: A transferor gives $300,000 to a long-time employee who is no relation and was born 41 years after him. Is the employee a skip person?
options: No; the age bands apply only to relatives
No; anyone born within 50 years of the transferor is one generation down
Yes; an individual not placed by the family rules who was born more than 37½ years after the transferor is two generations below
Yes, but only if the transferor allocates no exemption
questions.explanation: IRC § 2651(d) assigns generation by age only for someone the family rules do not place: more than 12½ but not more than 37½ years after the transferor is one generation down, so an employee born 41 years after him falls beyond that band into the next generation, two generations below, and is a skip person under § 2613(a).
questions.pageTitle: Effect on estate tax (e.g., Generation skipping transfer tax)

questions.stem: A husband dies in 2026 having allocated none of his GST exemption. His executor makes a valid portability election. What GST exemption does the surviving wife now have?
options: Her own plus her husband's unused GST exemption
Her own only; the GST exemption is not portable and his unused amount is lost
Her own plus his unused amount, but only for direct skips
Double her own, because the exemption equals the basic exclusion amount
questions.explanation: IRC § 2631 gives each individual an exemption equal to the § 2010(c) basic exclusion amount, but only the basic exclusion amount ports to a surviving spouse; an unused GST exemption dies with the first spouse.
questions.pageTitle: Effect on estate tax (e.g., Generation skipping transfer tax)

questions.stem: A donor makes a taxable gift in 2026 that her credit does not fully absorb. Who is liable for the gift tax, and when is it ordinarily due?
options: The donee, by 15 April 2027
The donor, by 15 April 2027, the date fixed for filing the return
The donor, within 90 days of the gift
The donor, with the estate tax return
questions.explanation: IRC § 2502(c) makes the tax the donor's; § 6075(b)(1) fixes the return for 15 April following the close of the calendar year, and § 6151(a) requires payment at the time fixed for filing, determined without regard to any extension.

questions.stem: A client gives her children discounted interests in a family LLC; her credit absorbs all the tax. Her Form 709 describes the entity, the valuation method, the discount claimed and its basis. What is the effect on the assessment period for that gift?
options: It never begins to run, because no tax was paid
It runs in the ordinary way, so the valuation cannot be challenged once it expires
It runs, but only for six years because a discount was claimed
It runs only if the Service accepts the valuation in writing
questions.explanation: The second sentence of IRC § 6501(c)(9) closes the otherwise unlimited period where the item is disclosed on the return or an attached statement in a manner adequate to apprise the Secretary of its nature.

questions.stem: A grandmother gives $60,000 outright to her grandson, whose parents are living, and files Form 709 without addressing GST exemption. What happens to her exemption?
options: None is allocated, and the direct skip is taxed at the flat rate
Exemption is allocated automatically so far as needed to bring the inclusion ratio to zero, unless she elects out
Allocation must wait until her estate tax return is due
Exemption is allocated automatically but may be withdrawn on a later return
questions.explanation: IRC § 2632(b) deems exemption allocated to a lifetime direct skip unless the individual elects out of that treatment, and an allocation once made is irrevocable, which is why the default has permanent consequences.

questions.stem: A client's only foreign account peaked at €90,000 in June and was closed with a nil balance in November. What does she report on the FBAR?
options: Nothing, because the account was closed before the year end
The closing balance, nil
The June maximum, taken from the periodic statements in euros and converted at the end-of-calendar-year rate
The June maximum converted at the June exchange rate
questions.explanation: The FBAR reports the maximum value of each account during the year, taken from periodic account statements in the currency of the account and converted at the end-of-calendar-year exchange rate; it is the maximum balance, not the closing balance.
questions.pageTitle: Filing and reporting requirements and due dates (e.g., FBAR, Form 8938, Form 8865, Form 5471, Form 3520)

questions.stem: A married couple filing jointly and living in Texas hold one account abroad. It peaked at $160,000 in March and closed the year at $90,000. What must they file?
options: The FBAR only; the last-day balance is under the joint domestic threshold
Both the FBAR and Form 8938; the March peak exceeded the joint domestic any-time figure
Form 8938 only
Neither; the last-day balance is below both thresholds
questions.explanation: The FBAR is required because the aggregate exceeded the FBAR threshold at a time during the year; Form 8938 is required because for a couple filing jointly and living in the United States the thresholds are $100,000 on the last day of the year or $150,000 at any time, and the $160,000 peak meets the second.
questions.pageTitle: Filing and reporting requirements and due dates (e.g., FBAR, Form 8938, Form 8865, Form 5471, Form 3520)

questions.stem: A preparer reads the $50,000 aggregate-value figure printed in IRC § 6038D(a) and applies it to every client. For which filer is that figure actually the operative last-day threshold?
options: Every specified individual
A specified individual living in the United States who is unmarried or married filing separately; for every other filer the regulatory thresholds are higher
A married couple filing jointly and living in the United States
No one; the figure has been superseded entirely
questions.explanation: IRC § 6038D(a) prints $50,000 subject to such higher dollar amount as the Secretary may prescribe; the four threshold pairs that apply are regulatory, and the section alone understates the requirement for every filer but an unmarried or separately filing one living in the United States.
questions.pageTitle: Filing and reporting requirements and due dates (e.g., FBAR, Form 8938, Form 8865, Form 5471, Form 3520)

questions.stem: A client holds a $150,000 account at the New York branch of a Japanese bank. Which form reaches it?
options: Both forms
The FBAR only, because the institution is foreign
Form 8938 only, because the account is in the United States
Neither form
questions.explanation: Under the branch rule the location of the branch decides the FBAR and the status of the institution decides Form 8938: an account at a United States branch of a foreign institution is on neither form, the reverse of the foreign-branch case.

questions.stem: A client holds two funds: a United States mutual fund that invests entirely in foreign stocks, and a foreign mutual fund. Which is reportable?
options: Both, on both forms
The domestic fund only, on Form 8938
The foreign fund on both forms; the domestic fund on neither
Neither, because mutual funds are not accounts
questions.explanation: As the Service's Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements sets out, a foreign mutual fund is reportable on both forms, while a domestic mutual fund investing in foreign stocks and securities is reportable on neither.

questions.stem: A client owns 70 percent of a foreign company, which holds an account at a foreign bank. Which form reaches the company's account itself?
options: Form 8938 only, as an indirect interest in a foreign account
The FBAR only; her majority ownership of the company gives her a financial interest in its account, while for Form 8938 it is her interest in the company, not the account, that is the asset
Both forms, as the account is foreign
Neither, because the company and not the client owns it
questions.explanation: As the Service's Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements sets out, an indirect interest in foreign financial assets through an entity is not itself a Form 8938 asset but gives an FBAR financial interest where the ownership or beneficial interest in the entity is sufficient, as a majority holding is; her interest in the company itself is a specified foreign financial asset under IRC § 6038D(b).

questions.stem: A taxpayer's underpayment is partly attributable to interest from a foreign account that should have been reported on Form 8938 and was not. What accuracy-related penalty rate applies to that portion?
options: 20 percent, the ordinary rate
40 percent
50 percent of the account balance
75 percent
questions.explanation: IRC § 6662(j): the accuracy-related penalty is 40 percent instead of 20 percent on the portion of an underpayment attributable to an undisclosed foreign financial asset.
questions.pageTitle: Potential penalties (e.g., failure to file, underreporting, substantially incomplete, statute of limitations, reduction of tax attributes)

questions.stem: A client has an unreported foreign trust that holds an unreported foreign account, and the income from the account was never reported. How do the resulting penalties relate to one another?
options: Only the largest single penalty applies
The § 6677 trust penalty, the FBAR penalty and the § 6662(j) understatement penalty all apply, cumulatively
The FBAR penalty displaces the Code penalties
The § 6662(j) penalty is an alternative to the information return penalties
questions.explanation: IRC §§ 6677 and 6662(j) and the FBAR penalty in 31 U.S.C. § 5321 are per-form and cumulative; none is an alternative to any other, and the § 6501(c)(8) limitation period stays open on top of them.
questions.pageTitle: Potential penalties (e.g., failure to file, underreporting, substantially incomplete, statute of limitations, reduction of tax attributes)

questions.stem: A taxpayer non-willfully failed to file an FBAR for an account whose balance was properly reported, and the failure was due to reasonable cause. What civil penalty applies?
options: The non-willful penalty, regardless of reasonable cause
None
The greater of $100,000 or 50 percent of the balance
40 percent of the underpayment
questions.explanation: 31 U.S.C. § 5321(a)(5): no non-willful penalty applies where the violation was due to reasonable cause and the balance in the account was properly reported — both conditions are required, not merely an innocent failure.
questions.pageTitle: Potential penalties (e.g., failure to file, underreporting, substantially incomplete, statute of limitations, reduction of tax attributes)

questions.stem: A daughter is named on her elderly father's account in Canada so she can manage his affairs. All the interest is reported on his return and she takes nothing from it. What must she file?
options: Both forms
The FBAR only
Form 8938 only
Neither form
questions.explanation: As the Service's Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements sets out, the FBAR interest test reaches an owner of record or holder of legal title regardless of whose income it is; the Form 8938 test asks whether anything from the asset must be reflected on her own income tax return, and nothing is.
questions.pageTitle: Distinctions between FBAR and Form 8938 requirements

questions.stem: A client extends her income tax return to 15 October. How does that affect her Form 8938 and her FBAR for the same year?
options: Both are due 15 October by virtue of the income tax extension
Form 8938 follows the extended return; the FBAR is due 15 April with its own automatic extension to 15 October, filed with FinCEN and never with the return
The FBAR must be attached to the extended return
Form 8938 follows the extended return; the FBAR has no extension and was due 15 April
questions.explanation: Form 8938 is attached to the return and follows its extensions under IRC § 6038D(a); the FBAR sits on the calendar year with its own automatic extension and goes to FinCEN electronically.
questions.pageTitle: Distinctions between FBAR and Form 8938 requirements

questions.stem: A client has filed an FBAR every year since 2004 for an account now worth $460,000 but has never filed Form 8938. What is the effect on the assessment period for those years?
options: It has run normally, because the FBAR disclosed the account
It remains open for every year in which Form 8938 was required, because the FBAR filing does nothing to close it
It is extended by three years from each FBAR filing
It is open only for the years in which the account produced income
questions.explanation: IRC § 6501(c)(8) keeps the assessment period open for every year in which the form was required; neither filing substitutes for the other, so diligence on the FBAR does not close the years on Form 8938.
questions.pageTitle: Distinctions between FBAR and Form 8938 requirements

questions.stem: A foreign corporation is owned 60 percent by a single foreign individual and 40 percent by one United States person. Is it a controlled foreign corporation?
options: Yes; a United States shareholder holds more than 10 percent
No; United States shareholders in aggregate do not own more than 50 percent, so there is no inclusion
Yes, because the foreign holder's stock is attributed to the United States person
No, because no single shareholder owns more than 50 percent
questions.explanation: IRC § 957(a) asks whether United States shareholders together own more than 50 percent of vote or value on any day of the year; the United States person is a United States shareholder under § 951(b), but at 40 percent in aggregate the corporation is not controlled.
questions.pageTitle: Ownership of a foreign corporation (GILTI, IRC Section 965 transition tax)

questions.stem: A client elected in 2018 to pay her § 965 transition tax in eight installments. What percentage of the net tax liability is the eighth and final installment?
options: 8 percent
15 percent
20 percent
25 percent
questions.explanation: IRC § 965(h): 8 percent for each of the first five installments, 15 percent for the sixth, 20 percent for the seventh and 25 percent for the eighth.
questions.pageTitle: Ownership of a foreign corporation (GILTI, IRC Section 965 transition tax)

questions.stem: An individual United States shareholder makes a § 962 election for his inclusion. When the controlled foreign corporation later distributes those earnings to him, how are they treated?
options: Tax-free, as previously taxed income
Taxable again to the extent the distribution exceeds the tax already paid under the election
Taxable only if the foreign tax rate was below the corporate rate
Tax-free, because the election is permanent once made
questions.explanation: IRC § 962 substitutes corporate rate treatment and opens the § 960 deemed-paid credit, but at the cost of a second layer of tax: the distribution is taxable again beyond the amount of tax already paid. The election is annual, not permanent.
questions.pageTitle: Ownership of a foreign corporation (GILTI, IRC Section 965 transition tax)

questions.stem: A client is under civil examination of his 2023 return over a charitable deduction, an issue unrelated to foreign assets. He now discovers an unreported account abroad and wants to use the streamlined procedures. May he?
options: Yes, because the examination does not concern foreign assets
Yes, for every year other than 2023
No; the streamlined procedures are unavailable once a civil examination of any taxable year has begun, whatever it concerns
No, unless he first pays the miscellaneous offshore penalty
questions.explanation: Under the streamlined filing compliance procedures, eligibility ends once the IRS has begun a civil examination of any taxable year, whether or not it concerns foreign assets.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who meets the non-residency requirement completes a streamlined submission and is later audited. What penalty exposure does she carry?
options: The 5 percent miscellaneous offshore penalty
None of the failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, accuracy-related, information return or FBAR penalties, unless the examination finds the noncompliance fraudulent or the FBAR violation willful
FBAR penalties only
Accuracy-related penalties only
questions.explanation: Under the streamlined procedures for U.S. taxpayers residing outside the United States, a taxpayer meeting the non-residency requirement who complies faces none of those penalties, and that protection survives a later audit unless the original noncompliance was fraudulent or the FBAR violation willful.

questions.stem: A client entering the Voluntary Disclosure Practice today asks whether the proposed six-year disclosure period and three-month deadline for filing and full payment apply to him. What is the correct advice?
options: Yes; the proposal took effect when its comment period closed
Yes, if he asks for the revised terms in his preclearance request
No; the proposal has not been finalised, nothing in it is law today, and the terms of any revised practice will be determined by the procedures in effect when the changes are finalised
No; the proposal was withdrawn when the comment period closed
questions.explanation: As the IRS Criminal Investigation Voluntary Disclosure Practice page states, the proposed revision has not been finalised or placed into effect; a client entering now proceeds under the practice as it currently stands, and the terms of a revised practice would be determined by the procedures in effect when the changes are finalised.

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A client receives $9,000 from a friend who describes it as a gift, and $400 of interest earned on the money after depositing it. What is includible?
drills.answer: the $400. The value of property acquired by gift is excluded from gross income (IRC § 102(a)), but IRC § 102(b)(1) provides that the exclusion does not extend to the income from that property. The interest is § 61(a)(4) income.
drills.pageTitle: Sources of all worldwide taxable and nontaxable income

drills.sectionTitle: Preliminary work to prepare tax returns
drills.prompt: A United States citizen lived and worked in Portugal for the whole taxable year, was paid by a Portuguese employer, and received no United States information return. Is the salary reportable?
drills.answer: yes. All citizens of the United States, wherever resident, are liable to the income taxes imposed by the Code whether the income is received from sources within or without the United States (Reg. § 1.1-1(b)). Whether tax is ultimately due is a separate question — the § 911 exclusion and the foreign tax credit may reduce or eliminate it — but the salary is gross income and is reported.
