drills.prompt: A single taxpayer has $190,000 of wages and $22,000 of net investment income. What is the tax?
drills.answer: $456. Net investment income is $22,000 and modified adjusted gross income exceeds the $200,000 threshold by $12,000, so IRC § 1411(a)(1) applies 3.8 percent to the lesser figure of $12,000.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer with $600,000 of modified adjusted gross income takes a $150,000 distribution from a traditional individual retirement account. Is it subject to the tax?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 1411(c)(5) excludes any distribution from a plan or arrangement described in §§ 401(a), 403(a), 403(b), 408, 408A or 457(b) from net investment income. The distribution does, however, increase modified adjusted gross income and so can expose other investment income to the tax.

drills.prompt: Why is a sole proprietor's business profit not subject to the net investment income tax?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 1411(c)(6) excludes any item taken into account in determining self-employment income on which the § 1401(b) tax is imposed. The profit bears the hospital insurance component of self-employment tax instead, and the same dollar is never subject to both.

drills.prompt: Two taxpayers each have $40,000 of rental income and identical high incomes. Why might only one owe the tax?
drills.answer: Because § 1411(c)(2)(A) brings in a trade or business that is a passive activity within § 469. Where the taxpayer materially participates, the rents are derived in the ordinary course of a trade or business not described in that paragraph and are excluded by § 1411(c)(1)(A)(i); where they do not, the income is caught in full.

drills.prompt: Is the threshold adjusted for inflation?
drills.answer: No. The amounts in IRC § 1411(b) are fixed in the statute with no indexing provision, and have been unchanged since the tax took effect for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2012. Only the estate and trust threshold moves, because § 1411(a)(2)(B)(ii) points at the indexed start of the highest § 1(e) bracket.

drills.prompt: A single taxpayer has $185,000 of wages and $35,000 of self-employment income. What is the additional Medicare tax?
drills.answer: $180. The threshold applies to the combined $220,000, giving an excess of $20,000 taxed at 0.9 percent. Neither source alone crosses the threshold, and the employer withholds nothing because the wages are below the § 3102(f)(1) trigger.

drills.prompt: A married couple filing jointly earn $210,000 and $65,000. The higher earner's employer withheld the tax on wages above $200,000. What is payable with the return?
drills.answer: $135. Combined wages of $275,000 exceed the $250,000 joint threshold by $25,000, giving a liability of $225. The employer withheld 0.9 percent of $10,000, or $90, which is credited, leaving $135.

drills.prompt: Two employers each pay a single taxpayer $150,000. How much do they withhold?
drills.answer: Nothing. IRC § 3102(f)(1) requires withholding only to the extent the taxpayer receives wages from that employer in excess of $200,000, and expressly permits the employer to disregard other wages. The taxpayer owes 0.9 percent of $100,000 at filing.

drills.prompt: Does the additional Medicare tax on self-employment income enter the deduction for one half of self-employment tax?
drills.answer: No. The § 1401(b)(2) tax is disregarded both in the § 1402(a)(12) reduction of net earnings and in the § 164(f) deduction for one half of the tax. It is the only component of self-employment tax that receives neither halving.

drills.prompt: A married taxpayer files separately with $210,000 of wages. Is the employer's withholding enough?
drills.answer: No. The employer withholds on the $10,000 above $200,000, but the threshold for a married individual filing separately is $125,000 — half the joint figure — so the liability is 0.9 percent of $85,000. The difference is settled on Form 8959.

drills.prompt: A Form W-2 shows $310 in box 12 with code A. How is it treated?
drills.answer: As an addition to tax. Code A is uncollected social security tax on tips — the employee's share that the employer could not collect under IRC § 3102(c)(1) — and it is added to the individual's liability, not credited as withholding.
drills.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

drills.prompt: An employee receives $18 of cash tips in one month and $140 in the next. What is reportable?
drills.answer: Only the second month's. IRC § 3121(a)(12)(B) excludes cash tips received in a calendar month from wages unless they amount to $20 or more, so the $18 month is outside the employment tax system entirely — though the income tax on it is still due.
drills.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

drills.prompt: Why can an employer be unable to collect the tax on properly reported tips?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 3102(c)(1) permits collection only from wages of the employee excluding tips that are under the employer's control, and only within the period ending on the tenth day of the month following the month the tips were deemed paid. A tipped worker with little or no hourly pay leaves nothing to collect from.
drills.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

drills.prompt: What is the consequence of not reporting tips to the employer at all?
drills.answer: The employee owes the employee share of social security and Medicare tax on them directly, computed on Form 4137, and is liable under IRC § 6652(b) for an additional 50 percent of that tax unless the failure was due to reasonable cause and not wilful neglect.
drills.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

drills.prompt: Does the new deduction for qualified tips remove them from social security and Medicare tax?
drills.answer: No. The IRC § 224 deduction operates in computing taxable income only. Tips remain wages under § 3121(a) and (q), the § 6053(a) reporting obligation is unchanged, and the employee share of FICA is due on the same dollars.
drills.pageTitle: Uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax

drills.prompt: A taxpayer claimed the 2008 first-time homebuyer credit. How is it repaid?
drills.answer: In equal annual instalments of 6⅔ percent of the credit across a 15-year recapture period beginning with the second taxable year after the year of purchase — $500 a year on the maximum $7,500 credit (IRC § 36(f)(1), (7)).

drills.prompt: The same taxpayer sells the home to an unrelated buyer at a loss before the period ends. What is owed?
drills.answer: Nothing further. IRC § 36(f)(2) accelerates the unrecaptured balance into the year of disposition, but § 36(f)(3) limits the increase to the gain on a sale to an unrelated person, and there is no gain. Section 36(f)(2)(B) then switches off the annual instalments for that year and after.

drills.prompt: An excess individual retirement account contribution is left in place for four years. How many times is the § 4973 tax imposed?
drills.answer: Four. The tax is 6 percent of the excess determined as of the close of each taxable year, so it recurs for every year the excess remains in the account, capped at 6 percent of the account value.

drills.prompt: Does a taxpayer with no income tax liability owe the tax on a missed required minimum distribution?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 4974(a) imposes the tax on the payee at 25 percent of the shortfall regardless of income tax liability, and nonrefundable credits do not reduce it.

drills.prompt: What is the shared responsibility payment for 2026?
drills.answer: Zero. IRC § 5000A(a) and (b) still state the requirement and the penalty, but § 5000A(c)(2)(B)(iii) sets the percentage of income at zero for taxable years beginning after 2018 and § 5000A(c)(3)(A) sets the applicable dollar amount at $0, so the monthly penalty amount is the greater of two zeros.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer receives $12,000 across 300 transactions through an online payment platform in 2026. Will a Form 1099-K be issued?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 6050W(e) as restored by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70432 requires both the dollar amount and the transaction count to be exceeded. The count is met and the amount is not, so no return is required. The income, if any, is reportable regardless.

drills.prompt: A business pays an unincorporated contractor $1,500 during 2026. Is an information return required?
drills.answer: No. The IRC § 6041(a) threshold for payments made after 31 December 2025 exceeds that amount, following Pub. L. 119-21 § 70433(a), so no return is required. The contractor's income is taxable all the same.

drills.prompt: A dealer receives $6,500 in cash on one day and $4,800 in cash a week later for the same vehicle. What is required?
drills.answer: A Form 8300. IRC § 6050I(a) applies where more than $10,000 in cash is received in one transaction or two or more related transactions, and payments for a single vehicle are related. The aggregate of $11,300 exceeds the threshold.

drills.prompt: Two professionals exchange services of equal value with no barter exchange involved. What are the consequences?
drills.answer: Each has gross income equal to the fair market value of what they received under IRC § 61(a), and each may have a deductible business expense of the same amount. No information return is required, because neither is a barter exchange within § 6045(c)(3), and the absence of a form does not affect taxability.

drills.prompt: A payer files 100 incorrect information returns through intentional disregard. What is the exposure?
drills.answer: Under IRC § 6721(e)(2)(A) the penalty is the greater of $690 per return or 10 percent of the aggregate amount required to be reported correctly, with no calendar year maximum — and a parallel penalty applies under § 6722 for the corresponding payee statements.

drills.prompt: Which of a copyright, a vehicle, land and a collectible is not personal property?
drills.answer: Land. Personal property is all property other than real property, and real property is land and what is permanently affixed to it. A copyright, a vehicle and a collectible are all personal property, though they are taxed very differently from one another on sale.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer sells a coin collection held for six years at a $40,000 gain. What rate applies?
drills.answer: 28 percent, as 28-percent rate gain. Coins are collectibles within IRC § 408(m) as applied by § 1(h)(5)(A), and § 1(h)(4) combines collectibles gain with § 1202 gain into a category taxed at a maximum of 28 percent — reduced by collectibles losses, net short-term capital loss and long-term capital loss carried forward.

drills.prompt: A rental property is sold at a gain after $85,000 of straight-line depreciation. How is that $85,000 taxed?
drills.answer: As unrecaptured section 1250 gain, at a maximum rate of 25 percent under IRC § 1(h)(1)(E) and (6). It is not ordinary income — that is § 1245 recapture, which applies to personal property — and it is not eligible for the zero, 15 or 20 percent rates.

drills.prompt: Does selling a partnership interest instead of the underlying artwork change the rate?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 1(h)(5)(B) treats gain on the sale of an interest in a partnership, S corporation or trust attributable to unrealised appreciation in collectibles as collectibles gain, applying rules similar to § 751. The 28 percent rate follows the underlying asset.

drills.prompt: A single taxpayer with $42,000 of other taxable income realises a $30,000 long-term gain. Is the whole gain taxed at zero?
drills.answer: No. The zero rate applies only to so much of the adjusted net capital gain as fits below the maximum zero rate amount for the filing status, measured by taxable income. The gain itself lifts the taxpayer past that ceiling, and the excess is taxed at 15 percent.

drills.prompt: What is the maximum § 529 distribution for elementary and secondary expenses in 2026?
drills.answer: $20,000 per beneficiary for the year. Pub. L. 119-21 § 70413(b) doubled the previous $10,000 figure for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025. Any source giving $10,000 is describing 2025 and earlier.

drills.prompt: May a § 529 account pay for private tutoring?
drills.answer: Yes, within limits. IRC § 529(c)(7)(E) covers tuition for tutoring or educational classes outside the home where the tutor is not related to the student and is either licensed as a teacher in any State, has taught at an eligible educational institution, or is a subject matter expert in the relevant subject.

drills.prompt: A client's son is in a recognised electrician credential programme. Can the § 529 account pay the testing fee for the licence?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 529(f)(1)(B) treats fees for testing required to obtain or maintain a recognised postsecondary credential as qualified postsecondary credentialing expenses, which § 529(e)(3)(C) brings within qualified higher education expenses.

drills.prompt: Can an employer permanently exclude payments toward an employee's student loans?
drills.answer: Yes. Pub. L. 119-21 § 70412(a) struck the 1 January 2026 cut-off from IRC § 127(c)(1)(B), so employer payments of principal or interest on a qualified education loan remain within the exclusion indefinitely, subject to the annual limit — which § 127(d) now indexes from 2027.

drills.prompt: A family pays $12,000 of tuition entirely from a § 529 distribution and claims an education credit on it. What is wrong?
drills.answer: The same expenses cannot support both a tax-free qualified tuition program distribution and an education credit. Allocating part of the tuition to other funds preserves the credit while still using the account for the balance.

drills.prompt: A client gives appreciated shares to a child instead of leaving them by will. What is the income tax consequence?
drills.answer: The child takes the donor's basis under IRC § 1015(a), so the whole appreciation remains taxable on a later sale. Had the shares passed at death, § 1014(a) would have given a basis equal to fair market value at death and the appreciation would never have been taxed.

drills.prompt: An estate passes entirely to a surviving spouse and owes no estate tax. Is a return needed?
drills.answer: Yes, if portability is wanted. IRC § 2010(c)(5)(A) makes the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount available only where the first estate filed a timely and complete estate tax return electing it. The tax owed is irrelevant to that requirement.

drills.prompt: Are life insurance proceeds taxable?
drills.answer: Not for income tax — IRC § 101(a)(1) excludes amounts paid by reason of the insured's death. But § 2042 includes them in the gross estate if receivable by the executor, or if the decedent possessed any incident of ownership at death. The two systems reach opposite answers on the same money.

drills.prompt: How many donees can receive an annual exclusion gift?
drills.answer: Any number. The IRC § 2503(b) exclusion applies per donee per calendar year with no limit on the number of donees, provided each gift is of a present interest rather than a future interest.

drills.prompt: Does the basic exclusion amount fall back after 2025?
drills.answer: No. Pub. L. 119-21 § 70106 amended IRC § 2010(c)(3) to set a new amount for calendar year 2026, indexed from calendar year 2025 for decedents dying after 2026. The scheduled reduction that drove much 2018–2025 planning no longer applies.

drills.prompt: A nephew inherits a traditional IRA. Which option is unavailable to him?
drills.answer: Rolling the balance into an IRA of his own. Only a surviving spouse may treat an inherited account as their own or roll it over; a non-spouse beneficiary must take it as an inherited account under the IRC § 401(a)(9)(B) distribution rules. A lump sum, distributions over a period, or an annuity where available are all possible.

drills.prompt: A 74-year-old still working for an unrelated employer owns 2 percent of it. When must distributions from the employer plan begin?
drills.answer: Not until 1 April of the year following retirement. IRC § 401(a)(9)(C)(i) uses the later of the applicable age and retirement, and the § 401(a)(9)(C)(ii) exception for 5-percent owners does not reach a 2 percent holding. Any IRA of theirs is a different matter — the retirement limb never applies to one.

drills.prompt: Why is a qualified charitable distribution better than writing a cheque for a client who does not itemise?
drills.answer: Because it is an exclusion from gross income under IRC § 408(d)(8)(A) rather than a deduction. The amount never enters adjusted gross income, so the benefit is available regardless of the standard deduction, and the lower adjusted gross income can reduce the taxable portion of social security and other income-linked amounts. It also counts toward the required distribution.

drills.prompt: A client aged 72 has deducted IRA contributions since turning 70½. Does that affect a qualified charitable distribution?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 408(d)(8)(A) reduces the excludable amount by the aggregate deductions allowed under § 219 for all taxable years ending on or after the individual attained age 70½, less reductions already applied in earlier years. The offset is cumulative and does not reset.

drills.prompt: A single taxpayer with no workplace retirement plan and adjusted gross income of $200,000 wants to deduct an IRA contribution. Can they?
drills.answer: Yes, in full. The IRC § 219(g) phase-out applies only to an active participant in an employer plan. With no such plan and no spouse who is a participant, there is no income limit on the deduction.

drills.prompt: A couple divorce on 5 December. What filing status is available for that year?
drills.answer: Single, or head of household if its separate conditions are met. IRC § 7703(a)(1) determines marital status as of the close of the taxable year, so a decree entered in December makes both parties unmarried for the whole year regardless of how long they were married during it.

drills.prompt: A 2015 divorce decree requires alimony. Is a payment made in 2026 deductible?
drills.answer: Yes. Pub. L. 115-97 § 11051 repealed IRC §§ 71 and 215 only for instruments executed after 31 December 2018. A pre-2019 instrument keeps the deduction and the corresponding inclusion, unless it has been modified after 2018 with an express provision that the repeal applies.

drills.prompt: One spouse takes a house with a low basis and the other an account of equal value with a high basis. Is the division tax-neutral?
drills.answer: Not economically. IRC § 1041(a) means neither recognises gain on the transfer, but § 1041(b)(2) gives each the transferor's adjusted basis, so the spouse taking the low-basis asset carries the larger unrealised gain. Equal value is not equal after tax.

drills.prompt: A married taxpayer files separately and lived with their spouse for part of the year. What is the base amount for taxing social security benefits?
drills.answer: Zero. IRC § 86(c)(1)(C) sets the base amount at zero for a taxpayer who is married at the close of the year, does not file a joint return, and does not live apart from their spouse at all times during the year. Benefits are taxable from the first dollar of other income.

drills.prompt: Does a divorce decree assigning the tax liability to one spouse protect the other from the IRS?
drills.answer: No. A joint return creates joint and several liability under IRC § 6013(d)(3), and a decree binds the spouses rather than the Service. The only relief runs through § 6015, on its own conditions and deadlines.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer carries forward a $2,500 long-term capital loss into a year with a $1,500 long-term gain and a $3,000 short-term gain. What is the result?
drills.answer: A $2,000 net short-term gain. Under IRC § 1212(b)(1)(B) the carryover retains its long-term character, offsets the long-term gain first, and the remaining $1,000 then reduces the short-term gain.
drills.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

drills.prompt: Which is not a component of the general business credit — the investment credit, the minimum tax credit, the work opportunity credit or the energy efficient home credit?
drills.answer: The minimum tax credit. It is allowed under IRC § 53 as a credit for prior year minimum tax liability and is not among the credits aggregated into the general business credit under § 38.
drills.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

drills.prompt: How long may an individual carry forward a charitable contribution that exceeded the percentage limitation?
drills.answer: Five succeeding taxable years, in order of time, under IRC § 170(d)(1)(A). In each of those years it is used after the current year's contributions and remains subject to the applicable percentage limitation.
drills.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

drills.prompt: A client has net operating losses from 2016 and 2022. Which is used first?
drills.answer: The 2016 loss. IRC § 172(a)(2)(A) allows losses arising in taxable years beginning before 1 January 2018 in full and before the post-2017 pool, which is separately limited to 80 percent of taxable income computed without the § 172, § 199A and § 250 deductions.
drills.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

drills.prompt: A business has a qualified business income loss this year and profits next year. What happens?
drills.answer: IRC § 199A(c)(2) treats the negative net amount as a loss from a qualified trade or business in the succeeding taxable year, reducing next year's qualified business income and therefore the deduction. Nothing on the loss year's return records it, so it has to be tracked deliberately.
drills.pageTitle: Items that will affect future and past returns

drills.prompt: A couple's joint refund is taken to pay one spouse's pre-marital defaulted federal student loan. What is the remedy?
drills.answer: An injured spouse allocation on Form 8379. The debt is a past-due legally enforceable debt owed to a federal agency within IRC § 6402(d), and the non-debtor spouse claims the portion of the joint overpayment attributable to their own income, withholding and credits.

drills.prompt: The same couple's refund is instead applied to their own joint balance from a prior year. Does Form 8379 help?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 6402(a) credits an overpayment against a liability of the person who made it, and a joint return makes that liability joint and several under § 6013(d)(3). The debt is the claimant's own, so there is no injured spouse claim — relief, if any, would have to come under § 6015.

drills.prompt: Who notifies the taxpayer of an offset, and who should they contact?
drills.answer: The Bureau of the Fiscal Service, which administers the Treasury Offset Program, sends a notice showing the original refund, the offset and the agency paid. The details are not provided to the IRS, so the taxpayer should contact the Bureau unless the refund amount on the notice differs from the amount on the return.

drills.prompt: Why might an injured spouse in a community property state recover less?
drills.answer: Because community income and the withholding on it are generally treated as belonging half to each spouse under state law, which the Service applies to the allocation. A larger share of the overpayment is therefore attributable to the debtor spouse than the same facts would produce in a common law state.

drills.prompt: When is the best time to file the allocation?
drills.answer: With the original return, where the couple already knows an offset is likely. That prevents the offset rather than reversing it and avoids the months a post-offset claim takes to work.

drills.prompt: A couple filed accurately, owe $30,000 they never paid, and have since separated. Which route is available?
drills.answer: Equitable relief under IRC § 6015(f) only. Subsections (b) and (c) require an understatement or a deficiency, and there is neither — the liability was correctly reported. The request must be made before the § 6502 collection period expires.

drills.prompt: A divorced taxpayer elects allocation under § 6015(c) after paying part of the deficiency. What happens to the payment?
drills.answer: Nothing. IRC § 6015(g)(3) allows no credit or refund as a result of a § 6015(c) election. To recover an amount already paid the request has to rest on § 6015(b) or § 6015(f), subject to the § 6511 refund claim period.

drills.prompt: When does the two-year period for a § 6015(b) election begin?
drills.answer: On the date the Secretary began collection activities with respect to the individual making the election (IRC § 6015(b)(1)(E)) — not on assessment, not on filing, and not on divorce.

drills.prompt: A requesting spouse knew of part of an understatement but not its size. What relief is available under § 6015(b)?
drills.answer: Partial. IRC § 6015(b)(2) relieves the individual of liability to the extent attributable to the portion of the understatement of which they did not know and had no reason to know, provided the other conditions are met.

drills.prompt: Six months after filing a request, the Service has not determined it. What can the taxpayer do?
drills.answer: Petition the Tax Court. IRC § 6015(e)(1)(A)(i)(II) allows a petition at any time after the date six months after the election or request, without waiting for a final determination notice; where such a notice is issued, the petition must be filed within 90 days of it.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer's preceding year showed tax of $30,000 and adjusted gross income of $190,000. Her current-year tax is $26,000. What is her required annual payment?
drills.answer: $33,000. Because the preceding year's adjusted gross income exceeded $150,000, IRC § 6654(d)(1)(C)(i) substitutes 110 percent for 100 percent, giving $33,000 on the prior-year branch. The current-year branch is 90 percent of $26,000, or $23,400, and the required annual payment is the lesser of the two — but the taxpayer must know the current year's tax to rely on it, which she does not until the year ends.
drills.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

drills.prompt: A client with no estimated tax payments increases his withholding sharply in December, ending the year with total withholding equal to his prior-year tax. Has he underpaid any installment?
drills.answer: No. Under IRC § 6654(g)(1) the credit allowed under § 31 is deemed a payment of estimated tax paid in equal parts on each due date, unless the taxpayer establishes the actual dates. The December withholding is treated as one quarter paid in April, one in June, one in September and one in January.
drills.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer files her return and pays the balance in full on 28 January. Which installments does that protect?
drills.answer: The fourth only. IRC § 6654(h) removes the addition with respect to an underpayment of the fourth required installment where the return is filed and paid in full on or before 31 January. Any shortfall in the first three installments is unaffected.
drills.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

drills.prompt: A farmer's gross income from farming is 70 percent of his total gross income. How many installments must he make, and when?
drills.answer: One, due 15 January of the following year. IRC § 6654(i)(1) allows a single required installment for a farmer or fisherman — defined in § 6654(i)(2) as one whose farming or fishing gross income is at least 66⅔ percent of gross income from all sources for the year or the preceding year — computed by substituting 66⅔ percent for 90 percent and disregarding the 110 percent rule.
drills.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer annualises and pays nothing for the first installment. What happens to the amount he did not pay?
drills.answer: It is recaptured. IRC § 6654(d)(2)(A)(ii) increases the next required installment determined under the flat method by the amount of the reduction, and increases later installments to the extent it has not yet been recaptured. Annualising changes when the money is due, not how much is due for the year.
drills.pageTitle: Estimated tax and penalty avoidance (mid-year estimated tax planning)

drills.prompt: A client mails a cheque to a qualified charity on 31 December. The charity deposits it on 6 January and it clears on 9 January. In which year is the contribution deductible?
drills.answer: The year of mailing. Under Reg. § 1.170A-1(b) the unconditional delivery or mailing of a cheque that subsequently clears in due course is an effective contribution on the date of delivery or mailing.
drills.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

drills.prompt: An employer tells an employee on 15 December that her bonus is available for collection any time after 20 December. She asks the employer to hold it until January and it is paid on 4 January. When is it income?
drills.answer: In the earlier year. Reg. § 1.451-2(a) treats income as constructively received when it is set apart or otherwise made available so that the taxpayer may draw on it. Her own request to defer collection is not a substantial limitation or restriction on her control.
drills.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

drills.prompt: A cash-method taxpayer pays her January mortgage instalment in December. What happens to the interest portion?
drills.answer: It is charged to capital account and treated as paid in January. IRC § 461(g)(1) applies to interest allocable to a period after the close of the taxable year in which it is paid. The points exception in § 461(g)(2) does not reach an ordinary instalment.
drills.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer files on extension in September and funds an IRA for the prior year at the same time. Is the contribution deductible for the prior year?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 219(f)(3) deems a contribution made on the last day of the preceding year only if it is made by the time prescribed by law for filing the return for that year, not including extensions.
drills.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer sells stock at a loss on 10 December, having bought additional shares of the same stock on 20 November. Is the loss allowed?
drills.answer: No, to the extent of the replacement shares. IRC § 1091(a) disallows a loss where substantially identical stock is acquired within the period beginning 30 days before the sale and ending 30 days after it. The 20 November purchase falls inside the window, and the disallowed loss is added to the basis of those shares.
drills.pageTitle: Adjustments, deductions, and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer acquires stock on 2 February and sells it on 2 February of the following year. Is the gain long-term?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 1222 requires the property to be held for more than one year. The day of acquisition is excluded from the count, so the holding period first exceeds one year on 3 February. A sale on 2 February produces short-term gain.
drills.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

drills.prompt: A sole proprietor sells equipment for $48,000. Cost was $80,000 and depreciation taken was $50,000. How is the $18,000 gain characterised?
drills.answer: All ordinary income. Recomputed basis is $80,000, adjusted basis is $30,000, and IRC § 1245(a) makes ordinary the excess over adjusted basis of the lower of recomputed basis ($80,000) or amount realised ($48,000) — that is $18,000, the entire gain. Nothing is left for § 1231.
drills.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer has a net section 1231 gain of $25,000 this year and had a net section 1231 loss of $18,000 two years ago that has not been recaptured. What is the character of this year's gain?
drills.answer: $18,000 ordinary and $7,000 long-term capital. IRC § 1231(c)(1) treats net section 1231 gain as ordinary income to the extent of non-recaptured net section 1231 losses from the five most recent preceding taxable years.
drills.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

drills.prompt: A collector sells an antique held for eleven years at a $40,000 gain. Her other income puts her in the top bracket. What rate applies to the gain?
drills.answer: 28 percent. Collectibles gain is taken out of the adjusted net capital gain that receives the 0, 15 and 20 percent rates and is taxed under the separate 28-percent rate gain rule in IRC § 1(h)(4).
drills.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer acquired qualified small business stock in 2023 and sells it after four years. How much of the gain is excluded?
drills.answer: None. The stock was acquired on or before the applicable date of 4 July 2025, so it is governed by IRC § 1202(a)(1)(A), which requires a holding period of more than five years. The tiered percentages in § 1202(a)(5) apply only to stock acquired after that date.
drills.pageTitle: Character of transaction (e.g., use of capital gain rates versus ordinary income rates)

drills.prompt: A married couple filed separate returns for a year. Eighteen months after the due date they want to file jointly instead. May they?
drills.answer: Yes, provided none of the bars applies. IRC § 6013(b)(1) permits a joint return after separate returns, and § 6013(b)(2) closes the election only after 3 years from the unextended due date, or after a notice of deficiency has been mailed and the spouse has petitioned the Tax Court, or after a suit for recovery, closing agreement or compromise.
drills.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

drills.prompt: A married couple filed a joint return and now wish to file separately for that year. The due date has passed. May they?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 6013(b) provides only for a joint return after separate returns. There is no corresponding provision allowing the reverse after the due date, so the joint return — and the joint and several liability under § 6013(d)(3) — stands.
drills.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

drills.prompt: A married individual files a separate return. Her husband itemizes deductions. Her own itemized deductions total less than the standard deduction. What is her standard deduction?
drills.answer: Zero. IRC § 63(c)(6)(A) sets the standard deduction at zero for a married individual filing a separate return where either spouse itemizes. She must itemize whatever her own deductions come to.
drills.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

drills.prompt: A married man lived with his wife until 4 July, then moved out. His son lived with him all year and he paid the whole cost of the home. Can he be considered unmarried?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 7703(b)(3) requires the spouse not to be a member of the household during the last 6 months of the taxable year, which begins 1 July. She was a member on 1 to 4 July, so the test fails and he is married for the year.
drills.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

drills.prompt: A couple who live together file separate returns. One receives social security benefits. How much of the base amount does she get?
drills.answer: None. Under IRC § 86(c)(1)(C) the base amount is zero for a taxpayer who is married at the close of the year within the meaning of § 7703, does not file a joint return, and does not live apart from the spouse at all times during the year. The adjusted base amount is zero as well under § 86(c)(2)(C).
drills.pageTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of MFJ/MFS/HOH filing statuses in various scenarios. (joint and several liability)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer filed her 2022 return on 3 March 2023. The due date was 18 April 2023. She now wants to claim a refund. What is the last day to file the claim?
drills.answer: 18 April 2026. Under IRC § 6513(a) the early return is considered filed on the last day prescribed for filing, so the three-year period in § 6511(a) runs from 18 April 2023 rather than from 3 March.
drills.pageTitle: Conditions for filing a claim for refund (amended returns)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer never filed for a year in which $9,000 was withheld from his wages and no other payments were made. He files a return claiming a refund four years later. What does he recover?
drills.answer: Nothing. With no return previously filed, IRC § 6511(a) gives 2 years from the time the tax was paid, and § 6513(b)(1) deems the withholding paid on the 15th day of the fourth month after the year closed. The claim is out of time, and § 6511(b)(2)(B) would independently cap the refund at tax paid in the preceding two years, which is nil.
drills.pageTitle: Conditions for filing a claim for refund (amended returns)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer has an overpayment for 2020 caused by a net operating loss arising in 2023. From which year does the period for the refund claim run?
drills.answer: From 2023, the loss year. IRC § 6511(d)(2)(A) gives a period ending 3 years after the time prescribed for filing the return, including extensions, for the taxable year of the loss that produces the carryback.
drills.pageTitle: Conditions for filing a claim for refund (amended returns)

drills.prompt: A client was hospitalised and unable to manage his affairs for fourteen months, during which his sister held a power of attorney over his finances. Does § 6511(h) suspend the limitation period?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 6511(h)(2)(B) provides that an individual is not treated as financially disabled during any period in which a spouse or any other person is authorised to act on the individual's behalf in financial matters.
drills.pageTitle: Conditions for filing a claim for refund (amended returns)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer's claim relates to an overpayment caused by a security that became worthless. How long does she have to file it?
drills.answer: 7 years from the date prescribed by law for filing the return for the year concerned, under IRC § 6511(d)(1), in place of the ordinary 3-year period.
drills.pageTitle: Conditions for filing a claim for refund (amended returns)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer signs a return containing a deduction she knows is fabricated. The correction would produce no additional tax. Has she committed an offence under IRC § 7206(1)?
drills.answer: Yes. Section 7206(1) requires willfully making and subscribing a document verified by a penalties-of-perjury declaration that the signer does not believe to be true and correct as to every material matter. There is no requirement that any tax be due.

drills.prompt: What is the maximum term of imprisonment under IRC § 7206, and under IRC § 7201?
drills.answer: 3 years under § 7206 and 5 years under § 7201. Both are felonies; the imprisonment terms printed in those sections are current, unlike the fines.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer denies signing a return that bears his name. What is the evidentiary starting point?
drills.answer: The signature is prima facie evidence for all purposes that he signed it, under IRC § 6064. The burden of displacing that presumption is his.

drills.prompt: The Secretary establishes that $12,000 of a $40,000 underpayment is attributable to fraud. To what amount does the 75 percent penalty apply?
drills.answer: To the whole $40,000, unless the taxpayer establishes that a portion is not attributable to fraud. IRC § 6663(b) treats the entire underpayment as attributable to fraud once any portion is established as such.

drills.prompt: Does the penalties-of-perjury declaration apply to a statement attached to a return?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 6065 applies to any return, declaration, statement or other document required to be made under any provision of the internal revenue laws or regulations, except as the Secretary otherwise provides.

drills.prompt: An estate has a taxable estate of $4,000,000 and adjusted taxable gifts of $2,000,000. On what amount is the tentative tax computed?
drills.answer: $6,000,000. IRC § 2001(b)(1) computes the tentative tax on the sum of the taxable estate and adjusted taxable gifts. The gifts are added to the base; they do not reduce the exclusion.
drills.pageTitle: Gross estate, taxable estate (calculations and payments), unified credit, life insurance, and filing requirements

drills.prompt: A decedent's gross estate is valued at more than the basic exclusion amount, but deductions bring the taxable estate below it. Is a return required?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 6018(a)(1) measures the filing requirement against the *gross* estate at death, not the taxable estate, so a return is required even though no tax may be due.
drills.pageTitle: Gross estate, taxable estate (calculations and payments), unified credit, life insurance, and filing requirements

drills.prompt: An executor wants to elect alternate valuation for an estate that will owe no tax either way. May he?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2032(c) permits the election only where it decreases both the value of the gross estate and the sum of the estate and generation-skipping taxes after credits. Where no tax is payable, the second condition fails.
drills.pageTitle: Gross estate, taxable estate (calculations and payments), unified credit, life insurance, and filing requirements

drills.prompt: A decedent transferred a life insurance policy on her own life to her son 30 months before her death, retaining nothing. Are the proceeds in her gross estate?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 2035(a) includes property transferred within the 3-year period ending at death where it would have been included under § 2042 had the interest been retained. A transfer more than three years before death would have been outside the estate.
drills.pageTitle: Gross estate, taxable estate (calculations and payments), unified credit, life insurance, and filing requirements

drills.prompt: When is the estate tax return due, and when is the tax due?
drills.answer: Both 9 months after the date of death. IRC § 6075(a) sets the filing date, and the tax is payable on the same date; an extension of time to file does not extend the time to pay.
drills.pageTitle: Gross estate, taxable estate (calculations and payments), unified credit, life insurance, and filing requirements

drills.prompt: A brother and sister hold land as joint tenants with right of survivorship. The brother paid $180,000 of the $300,000 purchase price from his own funds; the sister paid the rest from hers. The brother dies when the land is worth $500,000. How much is in his gross estate?
drills.answer: $300,000. Under IRC § 2040(a) the whole value is included except the part attributable to the sister's own consideration — 40 percent, or $200,000 — leaving 60 percent of the $500,000 date-of-death value.

drills.prompt: Same facts, except the sister's $120,000 was a gift from the brother two years before the purchase. How much is in his gross estate?
drills.answer: The whole $500,000. Reg. § 20.2040-1(a)(2) takes into account only consideration not attributable to property acquired from the decedent for less than full and adequate consideration, so the gifted funds are not the sister's contribution.

drills.prompt: A married couple hold a brokerage account as joint tenants with right of survivorship, and they are the only joint tenants. The wife funded all of it. She dies. How much is in her gross estate?
drills.answer: One-half. IRC § 2040(b) makes a qualified joint interest exactly half regardless of who furnished the consideration.

drills.prompt: The same couple had also added their son as a third joint tenant. How much is in her gross estate?
drills.answer: All of it. IRC § 2040(b)(2)(B) requires the decedent and the spouse to be the only joint tenants, so § 2040(a) applies instead and she furnished the entire consideration.

drills.prompt: A surviving spouse who is not a United States citizen held a home with the decedent as tenants by the entirety. Does the one-half rule apply?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2056(d)(1)(B) provides that § 2040 (b) shall not apply where the surviving spouse is not a citizen, so the consideration-furnished test in § 2040(a) governs.

drills.prompt: A decedent leaves his wife the income from a trust for her life, with the remainder to his brother. No election is made. Is the interest deductible?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2056(b)(1) denies the deduction where the spouse's interest will terminate, an interest in the same property passed from the decedent to another person for less than adequate consideration, and that person may enjoy the property afterwards. All three are satisfied.
drills.pageTitle: Marital deduction and other marital issues (e.g., portability election)

drills.prompt: Who makes the portability election, and on what return?
drills.answer: The executor of the estate of the deceased spouse, on an estate tax return for that estate on which the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount is computed, filed within the time prescribed including extensions (IRC § 2010(c)(5)(A)). The election is irrevocable.
drills.pageTitle: Marital deduction and other marital issues (e.g., portability election)

drills.prompt: A surviving spouse received a deceased spousal unused exclusion amount from her first husband. She remarries; her second husband dies having used his entire applicable exclusion amount, and his executor makes no election. What is her deceased spousal unused exclusion amount?
drills.answer: Nil. IRC § 2010(c)(4)(B) measures it against the applicable exclusion amount of the last deceased spouse, and amounts from earlier spouses are neither preserved nor added.
drills.pageTitle: Marital deduction and other marital issues (e.g., portability election)

drills.prompt: A decedent's estate is well below the filing threshold and all of it passes to his spouse. Is there any reason to file Form 706?
drills.answer: Yes — to make the portability election. It can only be made on a timely filed estate tax return for that estate, so an estate that files nothing loses the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount permanently.
drills.pageTitle: Marital deduction and other marital issues (e.g., portability election)

drills.prompt: A decedent leaves property outright to his surviving spouse, who is not a United States citizen. Is a marital deduction allowed?
drills.answer: No, unless the property passes in a qualified domestic trust meeting IRC § 2056A(a). Section 2056(d)(1)(A) disallows the deduction where the surviving spouse is not a citizen.
drills.pageTitle: Marital deduction and other marital issues (e.g., portability election)

drills.prompt: A decedent's employer owned and paid for a policy on his life, payable to his widow. He held no rights under it. Is it in his gross estate?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2042(2) includes proceeds receivable by other beneficiaries only where the decedent possessed an incident of ownership at death, and § 2042(1) reaches only amounts receivable by the executor. He held neither.
drills.pageTitle: Life insurance, IRAs and retirement plans

drills.prompt: A taxpayer inherits her father's traditional IRA. What is her basis in it?
drills.answer: She has no stepped-up basis. The account is income in respect of a decedent, and IRC § 1014(c) excepts such property from the fair market value basis rule, so distributions are ordinary income under § 691(a).
drills.pageTitle: Life insurance, IRAs and retirement plans

drills.prompt: A decedent assigned a policy on his own life to his brother 40 months before dying. Are the proceeds in his gross estate?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2035(a) reaches transfers within the 3-year period ending at death; 40 months is outside it, and he held no incident of ownership at death for § 2042 to reach.
drills.pageTitle: Life insurance, IRAs and retirement plans

drills.prompt: Who qualifies as an eligible designated beneficiary?
drills.answer: Under IRC § 401(a)(9)(E)(ii), the surviving spouse, a child of the employee who has not reached majority, a disabled individual, a chronically ill individual, or an individual not more than 10 years younger than the employee — tested as of the date of the employee's death.
drills.pageTitle: Life insurance, IRAs and retirement plans

drills.prompt: A grandson inherits a defined contribution account from his grandmother, who died at 80. Over what period must he take it?
drills.answer: Within 10 years of her death. He is a designated beneficiary but not an eligible designated beneficiary, so IRC § 401(a)(9)(H)(i) applies, whether or not she had begun taking distributions.
drills.pageTitle: Life insurance, IRAs and retirement plans

drills.prompt: A domestic estate has gross income of $700 and taxable income of nil after deductions. Must it file Form 1041?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 6012(a)(3) requires a return from every estate whose gross income for the taxable year is $600 or more, regardless of what taxable income comes to after deductions.
drills.pageTitle: Estate filing requirements and due dates (Form 706, Form 1041)

drills.prompt: A decedent dies on 8 June. The executor selects a fiscal year ending 31 March. When is the estate's first Form 1041 due?
drills.answer: 15 July of the following year. IRC § 6072(a) sets the date at the 15th day of the fourth month following the close of the fiscal year, and the four months run from 31 March, not from the date of death.
drills.pageTitle: Estate filing requirements and due dates (Form 706, Form 1041)

drills.prompt: A decedent's gross estate is $3,000,000 and she made post-1976 adjusted taxable gifts of $13,500,000. Is a Form 706 required?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 6018(a)(3) reduces the filing threshold by adjusted taxable gifts, so the applicable figure is the basic exclusion amount less $13,500,000, and the gross estate exceeds it.
drills.pageTitle: Estate filing requirements and due dates (Form 706, Form 1041)

drills.prompt: An executor obtains an extension of time to file Form 706. Does the estate tax remain due at nine months?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 6081 extends the time to file only. An extension of time to pay must be sought separately under § 6161, and interest runs from the original date in any event.
drills.pageTitle: Estate filing requirements and due dates (Form 706, Form 1041)

drills.prompt: May an estate adopt a taxable year ending on 15 September?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 441(e) defines a fiscal year as a period of 12 months ending on the last day of a month other than December, so a year end must fall on the last day of a month.
drills.pageTitle: Estate filing requirements and due dates (Form 706, Form 1041)

drills.prompt: A wife gives her nephew $30,000 from her own funds. Her husband consents to split. What is each spouse's taxable gift for 2026?
drills.answer: Nil for each. Under IRC § 2513(a)(1) the gift is treated as made half by each, so each has made a $15,000 gift, and each is within a single annual exclusion of {fig:estate.annual_exclusion}.

drills.prompt: In the same year the husband separately gave his brother $40,000. May the couple split only the wife's gift?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2513(a)(2) applies the consent to all gifts made by either spouse to third parties during the calendar year. Splitting one gift splits them all.

drills.prompt: A couple signified consent on 10 March. On 1 May they wish to revoke it. May they?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2513(c)(1) provides that the right to revoke does not exist after 15 April where the consent was signified on or before that date.

drills.prompt: A husband makes a gift to a trust in which he gives his wife a general power of appointment over the interest transferred. May that gift be split?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2513(a)(1) expressly excludes a gift of an interest in property in which the donor creates a general power of appointment, as defined in § 2514(c), in the consenting spouse.

drills.prompt: After consenting to split, one spouse is assessed a gift tax deficiency. Who is liable?
drills.answer: Both, jointly and severally, for the entire gift tax of both spouses for that calendar year (IRC § 2513(d)).

drills.prompt: A donor transfers property to a trust that will pay income to her nephew beginning in ten years. How much annual exclusion is available?
drills.answer: None. The nephew's interest is limited to commence in use, possession or enjoyment at a future date, making it a future interest under Reg. § 25.2503-3(a), and no part of a gift of a future interest may be excluded.

drills.prompt: A grandmother pays $48,000 of tuition directly to her grandson's university and also gives him $15,000 in cash. What are the gift tax consequences?
drills.answer: The tuition is not a transfer by gift at all under IRC § 2503(e)(2)(A). The cash gift is covered by the annual exclusion, which the tuition payment has not consumed.

drills.prompt: Is a contribution to a qualified tuition program a qualified transfer under § 2503(e)?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 529(c)(2)(A)(ii) provides expressly that it shall not be treated as a qualified transfer. It is a completed gift of a present interest, so the annual exclusion applies to it.

drills.prompt: A trust for a 12-year-old permits expenditure for her benefit before 21 and distributes the remainder to her at 21, but provides that if she dies earlier the fund passes to her cousin. Does § 2503(c) apply?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2503(c)(2)(B) requires that on death before 21 the property be payable to the donee's estate or as she may appoint under a general power of appointment as defined in § 2514(c).

drills.prompt: Why is the annual exclusion for a non-citizen donee spouse larger than the ordinary one?
drills.answer: Because IRC § 2523(i)(1) denies the gift tax marital deduction where the donee spouse is not a citizen, and § 2523(i)(2) compensates by applying § 2503(b) to those gifts with $100,000 substituted for $10,000, indexed on the same basis.

drills.prompt: A donor used credit corresponding to $5,000,000 of exclusion on gifts in prior years. How much credit is available this year?
drills.answer: The applicable credit amount that would apply under IRC § 2010(c) if she died at the end of this year, reduced by the credit allowable for all preceding calendar periods (§ 2505(a)) — so the credit corresponding to the current basic exclusion amount less the $5,000,000 already used.

drills.prompt: A nonresident who is not a citizen of the United States gives United States real property to a friend. Is a unified credit available?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2505(a) allows the credit to a citizen or resident of the United States only. The annual exclusion under § 2503(b) remains available.

drills.prompt: In a year in which the credit exceeds the gift tax, what happens to the excess?
drills.answer: Nothing is refunded or carried forward as a separate item. IRC § 2505(c) limits the credit allowed to the tax imposed for the year; the unused exclusion simply remains available, because each year's credit is computed afresh and reduced only by amounts actually allowed.

drills.prompt: How is this year's gift tax rate determined for a donor with substantial prior gifts?
drills.answer: By the cumulative total. IRC § 2502(a) computes a tentative tax on the aggregate of this year's taxable gifts and all preceding calendar periods and subtracts a tentative tax on the preceding periods alone, so this year's gifts are taxed at the marginal rates the running total has reached.

drills.prompt: An executor is computing the subtraction for gift tax payable on gifts made when rates were higher. Which rates apply?
drills.answer: The rates in effect at the decedent's death. IRC § 2001(g)(1) substitutes them for the rates in force when the gifts were made, both for the chapter 12 tax and for the § 2505 credit against it.

drills.prompt: A donor pays $900,000 of gift tax on a gift made 14 months before her death. What is the effect on her gross estate?
drills.answer: It is increased by the $900,000. IRC § 2035(b) adds any gift tax paid by the decedent or the decedent's spouse on gifts made during the 3-year period ending at death.
drills.pageTitle: Effect on estate tax (e.g., Generation skipping transfer tax)

drills.prompt: A 68-year-old transfers property to his 26-year-old daughter. Is she a skip person?
drills.answer: No. She is a lineal descendant of a grandparent of the transferor, so IRC § 2651(b) assigns her by counting generations on the family tree — one generation below him. The age bands in § 2651(d) apply only where the family rules do not assign a generation.
drills.pageTitle: Effect on estate tax (e.g., Generation skipping transfer tax)

drills.prompt: A transferor makes a gift to his grandson. The grandson's mother, the transferor's daughter, died last year. Is this a generation-skipping transfer?
drills.answer: No. Under IRC § 2651(e) the grandson is treated as moving up a generation because his parent died before the transfer, so he is one generation below the transferor and not a skip person.
drills.pageTitle: Effect on estate tax (e.g., Generation skipping transfer tax)

drills.prompt: How is the generation-skipping transfer tax rate determined?
drills.answer: The applicable rate is the maximum federal estate tax rate multiplied by the inclusion ratio for the transfer (IRC § 2641(a)). It is flat, not graduated.
drills.pageTitle: Effect on estate tax (e.g., Generation skipping transfer tax)

drills.prompt: A grandmother pays her grandson's tuition directly to his college. Is that a generation-skipping transfer?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 2611(b)(1) excludes any transfer that, if made inter vivos, would not be a taxable gift by reason of § 2503(e) — which covers tuition paid directly to the educational organization.
drills.pageTitle: Effect on estate tax (e.g., Generation skipping transfer tax)

drills.prompt: A donor gives $10,000 to a trust that will pay the beneficiary at age 40. Is a gift tax return required?
drills.answer: Yes. The transfer is a future interest, so the annual exclusion in IRC § 2503(b) does not apply, and § 6019(1) excuses a return only where § 2503(b) or (e) keeps the transfer out of the total amount of gifts.

drills.prompt: A donor obtains an extension of time to file her Form 1040 for a calendar year. Does that extend her Form 709?
drills.answer: Yes, for filing. IRC § 6075(b)(2) deems an extension for the calendar-year income tax return to be also an extension for the gift tax return. It does not extend the time to pay, which § 6151(a) fixes at the unextended filing date.

drills.prompt: A donor made taxable gifts in March and died in August. When is the gift tax return for that year due?
drills.answer: No later than the due date, including extensions, of the estate tax return for that donor (IRC § 6075(b)(3)) — not the following 15 April.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer failed to report a gift that was required to be shown on a gift tax return. How long does the Service have to assess the gift tax?
drills.answer: Indefinitely. IRC § 6501(c)(9) permits assessment at any time for a gift required to be shown — determined without regard to the annual exclusion — that is not shown on the return, unless the item is disclosed on the return or an attached statement adequately.

drills.prompt: May spouses who elect to split gifts file a single joint gift tax return?
drills.answer: No. Each spouse files a separate return, and consent to splitting is signified on it under IRC § 2513(b); consent makes each spouse jointly and severally liable for the entire gift tax of both for that calendar year under § 2513(d).

drills.prompt: A taxpayer's foreign accounts totalled $9,000 for most of the year but reached $11,400 for two weeks in May. Is an FBAR required?
drills.answer: Yes. The test is whether the aggregate value of the foreign financial accounts exceeded $10,000 at any time during the calendar year reported, and the reported figure is the maximum value.
drills.pageTitle: Filing and reporting requirements and due dates (e.g., FBAR, Form 8938, Form 8865, Form 5471, Form 3520)

drills.prompt: When is Form 8938 due?
drills.answer: It is attached to the annual income tax return and due on the date of that return, including any applicable extensions (IRC § 6038D(a)). It is not a standalone filing.
drills.pageTitle: Filing and reporting requirements and due dates (e.g., FBAR, Form 8938, Form 8865, Form 5471, Form 3520)

drills.prompt: A United States person transfers property to a foreign trust on 1 October. By when must notice be given?
drills.answer: On or before the 90th day after the reportable event, or such later day as the Secretary prescribes (IRC § 6048(a)(1)) — so around 30 December, not with the following year's return.
drills.pageTitle: Filing and reporting requirements and due dates (e.g., FBAR, Form 8938, Form 8865, Form 5471, Form 3520)

drills.prompt: A client receives a $600,000 bequest from a non-resident alien relative. Is it reportable?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 6039F requires a United States person receiving aggregate foreign gifts above $10,000 in a taxable year to report them, and a bequest treated as such by the recipient is a foreign gift. That the receipt is not income and produces no tax is irrelevant.
drills.pageTitle: Filing and reporting requirements and due dates (e.g., FBAR, Form 8938, Form 8865, Form 5471, Form 3520)

drills.prompt: A married couple living abroad and filing jointly hold foreign assets worth $310,000 throughout the year. Must they file Form 8938?
drills.answer: No. For a married couple filing jointly and living abroad the thresholds are more than $400,000 on the last day of the tax year or more than $600,000 at any time during it, and neither is met.
drills.pageTitle: Filing and reporting requirements and due dates (e.g., FBAR, Form 8938, Form 8865, Form 5471, Form 3520)

drills.prompt: A client holds an account at the Singapore branch of a United States bank. Which form reaches it?
drills.answer: The FBAR only. The account is at a financial institution located outside the United States, so it is a foreign financial account; but the institution is not a foreign financial institution, so it is not a specified foreign financial asset for Form 8938.

drills.prompt: A client owns foreign partnership interests worth $220,000 and has no foreign accounts. What must she file?
drills.answer: Form 8938 if she is over the applicable threshold. Foreign partnership interests are specified foreign financial assets and are not FBAR accounts, so no FBAR arises.

drills.prompt: A client has signature authority over his employer's foreign bank account but no interest in it. What must he file?
drills.answer: An FBAR, subject to the exceptions for certain officers and employees. Signature or other authority triggers the FBAR; it is not an interest in a specified foreign financial asset, so Form 8938 does not apply.

drills.prompt: A client owns a villa in Italy directly, worth $900,000. Is it reportable?
drills.answer: No, on either form. Foreign real estate held directly is outside both regimes. Held through a foreign entity, the entity would be a specified foreign financial asset for Form 8938 and its maximum value would include the villa.

drills.prompt: A client holds foreign shares in an account at a foreign bank. Must the shares be listed separately?
drills.answer: No. Where foreign stock or securities are held in a financial account at a foreign financial institution, the account is subject to reporting but the contents of the account are not separately reported — on either form.

drills.prompt: A taxpayer fails to file Form 8938. The Service mails notice on 1 April; the taxpayer files on 20 June, 80 days later. What is the penalty?
drills.answer: $10,000. The additional penalty under IRC § 6038D(d)(2) applies only where the failure continues for more than 90 days after notice is mailed, and 80 days is inside that period.
drills.pageTitle: Potential penalties (e.g., failure to file, underreporting, substantially incomplete, statute of limitations, reduction of tax attributes)

drills.prompt: Same facts, but the taxpayer files 155 days after the notice. What is the penalty?
drills.answer: $30,000. The 90-day period expires, leaving 65 further days — three 30-day periods counting fractions — so $10,000 base plus $20,000 for the first two full periods and $10,000 for the fraction, capped well below the $50,000 ceiling on the additional penalty.
drills.pageTitle: Potential penalties (e.g., failure to file, underreporting, substantially incomplete, statute of limitations, reduction of tax attributes)

drills.prompt: What is the maximum civil penalty for a willful FBAR violation?
drills.answer: The greater of $100,000 or 50 percent of the balance in the account at the time of the violation (31 U.S.C. § 5321(a)(5)(C), (D)), with the reasonable cause exception unavailable. Title 31 maximums are adjusted annually for inflation.
drills.pageTitle: Potential penalties (e.g., failure to file, underreporting, substantially incomplete, statute of limitations, reduction of tax attributes)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer never filed Form 5471 for a controlled foreign corporation and the failure has continued for a year after notice. Beyond the dollar penalty, what else happens?
drills.answer: The foreign taxes paid or deemed paid for the year are reduced under IRC § 6038(c) — 10 percent initially, plus a further 5 percent for each 3-month period or fraction of one after the 90-day period expires.
drills.pageTitle: Potential penalties (e.g., failure to file, underreporting, substantially incomplete, statute of limitations, reduction of tax attributes)

drills.prompt: A taxpayer failed to file a required Form 8938 for a year six years ago. Has the assessment period expired?
drills.answer: No. Under IRC § 6501(c)(8) the time for assessment of any tax to which the information relates does not expire before 3 years after the information is furnished, and it has not been furnished. Where the failure was not due to reasonable cause the extension applies to the whole return, not only the foreign items.
drills.pageTitle: Potential penalties (e.g., failure to file, underreporting, substantially incomplete, statute of limitations, reduction of tax attributes)

drills.prompt: Which form reaches signature authority over an account in which the filer has no interest?
drills.answer: The FBAR only, subject to the exceptions for certain officers and employees. Signature authority is not an interest in a specified foreign financial asset for Form 8938.
drills.pageTitle: Distinctions between FBAR and Form 8938 requirements

drills.prompt: A specified individual holds an account at the London branch of a United States bank. Which form reaches it?
drills.answer: The FBAR only. The account is located outside the United States, but the institution maintaining it is not a foreign financial institution.
drills.pageTitle: Distinctions between FBAR and Form 8938 requirements

drills.prompt: Are United States territories part of the United States for these purposes?
drills.answer: They differ. For Form 8938 the territories are outside the United States; for the FBAR resident aliens of the territories and territory entities are subject to reporting.
drills.pageTitle: Distinctions between FBAR and Form 8938 requirements

drills.prompt: A client's foreign accounts peaked at $60,000 in June and stood at $48,000 on the last day of the year. She is unmarried and lives in the United States, and has no other foreign assets. What must she file?
drills.answer: The FBAR only. The aggregate exceeded $10,000 at a time during the year, so the FBAR is required. For Form 8938 the thresholds for an unmarried specified individual living in the United States are more than $50,000 on the last day of the year or more than $75,000 at any time during it, and neither is met — $48,000 on the last day and $60,000 at the peak.
drills.pageTitle: Distinctions between FBAR and Form 8938 requirements

drills.prompt: Does filing an FBAR satisfy the Form 8938 requirement?
drills.answer: No. The two are separate regimes under different titles of the United States Code, administered by different agencies, with separate penalties; neither filing substitutes for the other.
drills.pageTitle: Distinctions between FBAR and Form 8938 requirements

drills.prompt: A United States person owns 8 percent of a foreign corporation's stock by value and is treated as owning a further 4 percent under the attribution rules. Is he a United States shareholder?
drills.answer: Yes. IRC § 951(b) counts stock owned within the meaning of § 958(a) and stock considered owned under § 958(b), and 12 percent meets the 10 percent test.
drills.pageTitle: Ownership of a foreign corporation (GILTI, IRC Section 965 transition tax)

drills.prompt: Three unrelated United States persons own 20 percent each of a foreign corporation; the rest is owned by foreign persons. Is it a controlled foreign corporation?
drills.answer: Yes. Each is a United States shareholder at 10 percent or more, and together they own 60 percent — more than the 50 percent required by IRC § 957(a), which aggregates United States shareholders.
drills.pageTitle: Ownership of a foreign corporation (GILTI, IRC Section 965 transition tax)

drills.prompt: What happened to the qualified business asset investment offset?
drills.answer: It was repealed. Pub. L. 119-21 § 70323(a)(2) struck IRC § 951A(d), which had defined qualified business asset investment, so the inclusion is no longer reduced by a deemed return on tangible assets.
drills.pageTitle: Ownership of a foreign corporation (GILTI, IRC Section 965 transition tax)

drills.prompt: May an individual United States shareholder claim the IRC § 250 deduction?
drills.answer: No. Section 250(a)(1) allows it to a domestic corporation. An individual reaches comparable treatment only by electing under § 962 to be taxed on the inclusion at corporate rates.
drills.pageTitle: Ownership of a foreign corporation (GILTI, IRC Section 965 transition tax)

drills.prompt: Can a § 965 transition tax inclusion arise for a 2026 taxable year?
drills.answer: No. IRC § 965(a) applies to the last taxable year of a deferred foreign income corporation beginning before 1 January 2018. What can still arise in 2026 is an instalment obligation under § 965(h) or the consequences of a failure to have reported at the time.
drills.pageTitle: Ownership of a foreign corporation (GILTI, IRC Section 965 transition tax)

drills.prompt: What does a taxpayer certify to use the streamlined procedures?
drills.answer: That the failure to report all income, pay all tax and submit all required information returns, including FBARs, was due to non-willful conduct — conduct due to negligence, inadvertence or mistake, or resulting from a good faith misunderstanding of the requirements of the law.

drills.prompt: How many years of returns and how many years of FBARs must a streamlined submission cover?
drills.answer: The most recent 3 years for which the return due date, including any properly applied for extension, has passed, and the most recent 6 years for which the FBAR due date has passed.

drills.prompt: How is the Title 26 miscellaneous offshore penalty computed?
drills.answer: 5 percent of the highest aggregate balance or value of the foreign financial assets subject to it, found by aggregating year-end balances and values for each year in the covered tax return period and the covered FBAR period and taking the highest of those years.

drills.prompt: When is a voluntary disclosure no longer timely?
drills.answer: Once the IRS has commenced a civil examination or criminal investigation, has received information from a third party alerting it to the noncompliance, or has acquired information directly related to the noncompliance from a criminal enforcement action such as a search warrant or grand jury subpoena.

drills.prompt: Does a voluntary disclosure guarantee that the taxpayer will not be prosecuted?
drills.answer: No. It will not automatically guarantee immunity from prosecution. Criminal Investigation accepts timely, accurate and complete voluntary disclosures under consideration when determining whether to recommend prosecution, and a disclosure may result in prosecution not being recommended.
